Blade.title: Blade
Blade.blurb: A great action movie about Blade styling on a bunch of vampires. The plot and characters are lacking, but the action is kinetic and the villain genuinely theatening.
Blade.review:
The movie’s final one-liner as Blade delivers the killing blow to the big bad is “some motherfuckers are always trying to ice skate uphill”, and that line encapsulates the movie’s whole energy. The characters take everything seriously and are trying to be badass, but the editing, music, and writing are just so goofy. It’s an incredibly entertaining watch, but the movie is absolutely style over substance. Blade aura farms through a bunch of vampires, and Deacon Frost aura farms over a bunch of old vampires, but the characters and plot are not very compelling. Full marks to the action sequences though, they’re well-choreographed and the vampire disintegrating effects are very good, especially for 1998.

As for the characters, the movie makes an attempt. Blade is tortured by his past, but he’s already come to peace with it and kills vampires because it does in fact bring him peace. He has some depth, but he has no real arc. Dr Jenson gets credit for not being a love interest, and does become more capable as the movie progresses, fully becoming Blade’s partner by the end. On the other hand, her main subplot is creating a vampire cure, and while it seems to work on herself, it never seems to get spread to actually help people who’ve been turned, so her arc feels incomplete. She’s just helping Blade now that his adoptive father is dead. I feel like her arc’s culmination is actually making the anti-coagulant and accepting that you have to kill vampires and can’t cure them, but it’s never really given any focus, which is disappointing because her cure should work on those who were turned. There should be some thematic and inner conflict there, but it’s glossed over to blow people up. Which is fair, that’s just the kind of movie Blade is.

Deacon Frost is the main villain and his personality is great, just an evil vindictive prick, but his plan and motive are never fully formed. He feels resentful for being a turned vampire instead of being born a vampire, and the vampire council looks down on him, but these vampire social dynamics are never fully explored. Instead he just wants to turn the entire populace into vampires for reasons. Since the other vampires are rich, it might be an old-money/new-money thing, where Deacon wants to prove that he’s just as much a vampire as the old vampires are. Speaking of the money thing, the vampires are represented as both the establishment - the rich people who own the corporations, the politicians, and the police - and the outcasts - people who are into grunge. It feels weird, the implication that the poor and dispossessed are actually the ones running the country. But it’s Blade, the politics are set dressing for Blade’s sick swordfighting skills and explosive anti-coagulant.

Overall, it’s not an incredible movie by any means, but it is a fun one. It’s not a movie you watch when you want to be moved, but a movie you watch with your buddies while having popcorn and soda. Blade’s sword has retractable spikes on its hilt as a safety measure, which is awesome, while Deacon’s super-advanced computers have graphics that have been outdated for over a decade. They add to the vibe, but the movie is riding hard off that vibe. I wish the characters got more depth, because Blade, Whistler, and Dr Jenson have an interesting dynamic going on, but the movie does not care enough to explore it. It’s a good start for the first “modern” Marvel movie, especially in the comic book action department, but I’m really looking forward to seeing the characterization improve.

Blade II.title: Blade II
Blade II.blurb: Blade's follow-up is more Blade, but slightly worse. Blade the character is better, but the villains are worse. The side characters are less fleshed out, and the action is both better and worse.
Blade II.review:
Blade’s follow-up is more Blade, but slightly worse. I think Blade the character is better in this one, there’s slightly more stuff going on inside his head, but it still doesn’t really go anywhere. The villains are worse, although the side characters are better for the most part. The action is on par with the first one, but I think I like the first one’s action more; Blade’s various weapons are cooler than the fisticuffs he primarily uses in this movie, and it seems like he’s trying too hard to be flashy as opposed to just looking effortlessly cool in the first one. It’s like, in the original he’s very efficient, which makes him look cool since almost everything feels like it serves a purpose. In this one, he does a lot of overly fancy footwork and movements that feel like they were put in because they look cool, not because they’re actually useful in combat. Blade’s visual design is way better in this movie though. He looked awesome in the original, but the cape with the red interior and the hole in the back for his sword is incredible. Peak visual design, and the built-in sword hole is also very funny.

As for the plot and characters, this movie is definitely a step back from the first one. Whistler is back from the dead and Dr Jenson is nowhere to be seen. She’s not even mentioned, which is really disappointing because she seemed poised to take Whistler’s place at the end of the first movie. I was looking forward to seeing her further develop her relationship with Blade and her medically-focused combat against the vampire epidemic, but instead she’s just gone with her only legacy being the exploding anti-coagulant that doesn’t even work on this movie’s villains. With Dr Jenson gone and Whistler back, Blade II ends where Blade I begins, which is very disappointing.

As for the villains, we get a vampire parasite that kills vampires and basically turns them into smart zombies, which is pretty cool. They can only be killed by sunlight, and they’ve got awesome three-hinged jaws like the Predator. This means that Blade has to actually fight them instead of just mowing them down like the vampires in the first movie, which should make for better action scenes. However, the fights all feel more weightless as characters fly across the room and just get back up, versus the slaughtering of the vampires in the first movie. Basically, every bad guy in this movie is as strong as the superpowered Deacon Frost in the first movie. Classic powerscaling.

The zombies do turn out to be genetically engineered by the main vampire bad guy, which is a cool if somewhat predictable twist. This doesn’t really change the movie, though, as the main zombie still kills the main vampire and fights Blade as the final boss. This is super disappointing, since the entire movie has Blade working with a group of vampire elites to hunt the zombies, but little comes of it. Most of the elites die to the zombies, and although the vampires do turn on Blade, he kills like 2 guys before engaging in the final fight. This is really felt with Nyssa, the second-in-command of the vampires and the main vampire's daughter. She found out her father created the virus and was okay killing her to get rid of it, so she turns on him. This makes sense, I like this, but then she lets herself die too for some reason. I think it’s so she doesn’t have to fight Blade since she kinda likes him, but this is never really spelled out so it just feels like a waste of a good confrontation between her and Blade. I do like her death scene watching the sunset though.

The group of vampires is why Blade is better characterized in this movie too. We know he’s a one-track mind hardass with a good heart from the first movie, but here we get to see him forced to work with his enemies for the greater good. It’s cool seeing him try to outsmart them and assert dominance, while still not letting them get killed even though they want to kill him. They become his responsibility, and he takes that seriously. They still all die on mission though, except for the asshole who Blade gets to kill, and Nyssa who lets herself die when Blade is still captured.

I do generally like the squad, they’re all very cool and are unique enough to keep track of. They’re nothing special, just big hammer guy and cool sword guy and Ramona Flowers, but within the movie they’re unique and easy to identify. They don’t get much to do except for the resident asshole, but the scene of Ramona Flowers opening the manhole cover to burn herself and her zombified boyfriend to death is awesome.

Overall, I still had fun with it. It’s not as good as the first Blade, partly because it feels like a monster-of-the-week movie with nothing to really say. It tries to say some stuff about trust and allies, but never quite gets there. I do think bringing Whistler back and leaving Dr Jenson out was a mistake, since it really makes either this movie or the first movie feel pointless in the grand scheme of things. But it’s still a solid action movie, which is almost all it needs to be.

Blade Trinity.title: Blade Trinity
Blade Trinity.blurb: Ryan Reynolds is in this movie, playing Ryan Reynolds. Blade gets a team of young recruits for the final battle with the vampires. The action is awesome, the plot is decent, and the characters are very strong.
Blade Trinity.review:
Ryan Reynolds is in this movie, playing Ryan Reynolds. It is very jarring considering how serious and dramatic the rest of the movie is, while Ryan is over here spouting rough drafts of his Deadpool script. It almost works thematically since he’s part of a team - the Nightstalkers - that are supposed to be newbies who don’t understand the seriousness of what Blade is doing, so of course Ryan Reynolds is making quips. But he doesn’t stop making quips even when he’s been captured and all his friends are dead. Blade snarls, and Ryan makes dick jokes.

That said, I do like the idea of the Nightstalkers. Blade was given a team in Blade II, but they were never really fleshed out and almost all die before anything interesting happens. Here, the team is much more fleshed out, particularly Ryan Reynolds and Abby Whistler. Whistler having a daughter he’s never mentioned before is… a choice, but I do like her character and what she represents. She’s the future of vampire hunting, but also the inevitable tragedy that Whistler’s legacy will always be tied to killing vampires and neither he nor anyone he knows will have a normal life. This is made even more apparent by the Nightstalkers raising an actual 6-year-old - the daughter of one of their members - who is forced to live on their ship with them and already knows how to hide from vampires and keep her cool in emergencies. It’s a tragic life, but also the embodiment of why Blade and the Nightstalkers need to kill vampires: they’re doing it so Abby and this little girl can live in a future without fear or death.

There’s a lot going on in this movie, and while it isn’t all as fleshed out as it should be, it feels more full of life than II was. The vampires are no longer living the shadows, and are instead using their agents in the government to take full power. It’s the thematic culmination of Deacon Frost’s plan from the first movie, even if Deacon and his actions are never mentioned directly. Everything ties back to the vampires assuming total domination of Earth (or at least America), and so they need to be stopped right now.

If anything, the one part that’s out of place is Dracula, the ancient original vampire that created all others. If the rest of the plan is about moving forward, then Dracula is an instrument of the past, and doesn’t really fit thematically. He does get the best scenes in the movie though. His attack on the Nightstalkers is the scariest scene in the franchise, and giving him a sword so he can have a swordfight with Blade is an inspired decision. I also like that he has the tri-fold mouths of the zombie vampires from II. Since they were supposed to be advanced vampires with no weaknesses, it makes sense that they’d be closer to Dracula, the original vampire with no weaknesses. It’s a neat retcon.

Speaking of the swordfight, the action in this movie is way better than in II. Like the first, all of Blade’s actions feel deliberate, like everything is perfectly calculated to kill as many vampires as possible. This makes it look cool as fuck, and shows just how good Blade is at fighting. Meanwhile, Abby and Ryan Reynolds rely on their gadgets, which are also super cool, but each of their fights take longer. During the final confrontation, Blade kills like 7 vampires in the time it takes Abby to kill 1. It’s a perfect showcase of how good at this Blade is, while still letting Abby look really cool as she demonstrates her resourcefulness and grit instead of her experience.

Trinity still lacks the punch of the first movie, mostly due to slightly worse editing, music, and character arcs. Dr Jenson is still sorely missed, especially because the vampires are defeated with a “cure”: a virus that eats vampire blood. It’s something she would have made had her arc continued, and it would have been cool to give her a namedrop shout-out even if they didn’t get the actress back, especially since the Nightstalkers have friends everywhere. The characters are also very hurt by the ending. Blade gets to ride off into the city now that all the vampires are dead, but Abby, Ryan Reynolds, and the six-year-old get no closure, which is really disappointing since they’re the heart of the movie. The entire movie is about fighting for them, and we don’t even get to see them in the future Blade secured for them. It’s a big sour note to end the movie on that could have been remedied with like one scene of them at an ice cream shop, hurting what was otherwise a pretty good final movie in the trilogy.

It’s not perfect by any means, but the action is very good, which as I’ve said, is the most important part. The themes also work for the final movie, with Blade finally finding some peers and securing the future for them that he thought he’d never see for himself. I love that Dracula literally calls him the “next breed of vampires” that the vampires have been searching for throughout the trilogy. It’s so perfect, that he’s right there and yet they’re too scared of becoming human to truly work with him.

There’s also some fun stuff in terms of Marvel movies as a whole, like Ryan Reynolds playing proto-Deadpool and a Marvel comic making a physical appearance. Although they picked a book made after Blade debuted in the comics, which raises several questions. We also get a Marvel logo for the first time, and Ryan Reynolds and Abby feel like genderswapped Hawkeye and Black Widow in terms of powers (Ryan Reynolds even gets a “resist the interrogation” scene).

It’s not the best movie by any means, and it’s worse than the first movie, but I think it executes its ideas better than the second. It’s a good ending to the Blade trilogy, and to the first Marvel trilogy, and I’m excited to continue into a full ensemble with X-Men.

Nichijou.title: Nichijou
Nichijou.blurb: One of the funniest shows I’ve ever seen in my life. The show’s trademark brand of humor is taking something mundane and exaggerating it to maximum effect, treating it as the most important and impactful thing in the world, which it usually is to the characters on screen.
Nichijou.review:
One of the funniest shows I’ve ever seen in my life. The show’s trademark brand of humor is taking something mundane and exaggerating it to maximum effect, treating it as the most important and impactful thing in the world, which it usually is to the characters on screen. Mix that in with plenty of subtle gags and amazing non-sequiters, and the comedy almost never stops, aside from when the show slows down to set up the next bit. The show’s production values are also insanely high. Everything is animated incredibly well, with fully detailed characters moving around in the background as just one example of the show’s attention to detail.

The show does start a little weak because it takes some time to acclimate to the show’s characters. The show plays its character archetypes very well, and it takes an episode or two of getting used to their dynamics before the comedy really takes off. The show’s structure never really changes, being primarily a sequence of largely disconnected gags, but there are subtle character arcs and plots advancing over the course of the show. There are really only two moments where the show draws its continuity into focus (the middle and the end), but the continuity is there, and it’s hype as hell when it does come into focus.

My one big complaint is Hakase, who is just a dick. I think she’s supposed to be a small, selfish child, but she comes across as incredibly malicious. She created Nano with a key she hates, and never gives a good reason why she can’t remove the key when Nano asks, instead mocking her for doing so. It’d be so easy for the writers to just make the key a power source for Nano, but instead Hakase is just an asshole. She never learns any lessons, and frequently goes back on her word and then laughs at Nano for falling for the trick. She blames her cat Sakamoto for everything she does wrong, meaning that she knows that it’s wrong and refuses to take responsibility. It makes her incredibly obnoxious, even if some of her bits are still funny. You do need her to be somewhat antagonistic to Nano so there’s a conflict, but you could make her naive and unaware of the consequences of her actions to make her seem less malicious and improve her segments overall without losing the core conflict of “Nano tries to care for unwieldy child who can also control her body sometimes”.

As for the rest of the cast, they’re all great. The side characters get more development over time, but their gags are usually pretty good. The real stars of the show are Yuuko, Mio, and Mai, although Mai gets less to do as the show goes on. Yuuko is a bundle of chaos and misfortune who mostly brings it upon herself, and her exaggerated reactions both only make things worse and are incredibly funny. Mio is in a similar boat, but she presents herself as more reserved before breaking into the same heightened emotions as Yuuko when things go wrong. Their friendship works really well, and they feel like real friends while still having their antics be hilarious. Yuuko is also the first one to really befriend Nano, which is really sweet and paints her in a really good light. They don’t get a lot of scenes together, but they’re always wholesome because Yuuko straight up does not care about Nano being a robot and just treats her like a person.

Speaking of friendship, that’s kind of the underlying theme of the whole show, how people make friends and navigate the world together even if everything seems absurd and out of their control. And nothing speaks to this better than the second to last episode. Yuuko and Mio spell out the idea of you never know what will happen next, and Mio seeing her crush with someone else causes a high speed chase between Mio and Yuuko that accidentally results in Mio helping several people. And Mio is still sad, so to end things off, Yuuko, Mai, and Nano give her a friendship voucher to last for life, telling her that they’ll always have her back even if things go wrong.

And the last episode, while not nearly as funny, continues this with Yuuko throwing a birthday party for Nano. Even as the party devolves into a comedy of errors, everybody is still laughing and having fun, even Nano. It’s a really poignant ending to a chaotic and surreal show that nails home all of the themes and character arcs that have been developing in the background.

To just list some of my favorite bits for people who have seen the show: the Principal vs Deer scene; the camping bit where Yuuko and Mio ruin all of their food; the scene Yuuko, Mio, and Mai get stuck in an elevator; Yuuko losing her shoes; the Helvetica Standard segment with the gun in the book; the evil science professor trying to break into Nano’s house and getting scared shitless by random bullshit because she’s expecting something sinister where there is none; the reveal that Go+Soccer is a real sport; the Go+Soccer “match”; Yuuko and Mio’s argument that ends with them praising each other; and the whole sequence with Misato and Sasahara that ends with Yuuko chasing Mio across town.

It’s just such a heartfelt, hilarious show, and I really cannot recommend it enough.

Genocidal Organ.title: Genocidal Organ
Genocidal Organ.blurb: A movie that is essentially an exploration of the trade-offs between security and freedom. Unfortunately, it doesn't have any satisfying conclusions, instead opting for the doomerist mindset that society inevitably ends in genocide.
Genocidal Organ.review:
A movie that is essentially an exploration of the trade-offs between security and freedom. The plot goes that people felt unsafe after 9/11, so they implemented a security state, but people didn't feel free enough so some of them hid away from the security systems to be more free. Every human also has a "genocide organ", which certain words can trigger to make people want to do a genocide to protect their tribe (aka keep themselves secure). Some guy uses this to cause genocides in foreign countries to keep his own country secure and free, and then he dies and some other guy uses it on his country because his country also sucks. The rest of the plot is irrelevant (and also a generic action spy movie), the movie is about this thesis.

And the thesis is interesting. We get to see different characters react to this dilemma. The Genocide Guy, John, had his family die in a terrorist attack, so he causes genocide in other countries so the people in his don't think about their own troubles and feel safe. The main character is a soldier who suppresses his emotions to kill people better, sacrificing freedom for mental security, and he decides to throw away that security at the end for more freedom. Ya know, by causing a genocide. So he's taking away everyone's security by letting them kill each other, but he’s also taking their freedom because they're kinda being mind controlled. It is not a happy ending. Sure the government sucks, but that's not a reason to genocide people.

Some stories are improved by unhappy endings, where they feel like the natural conclusion to the story’s plot and themes. Unfortunately, this happy ending lacks that catharsis in favor of being doomerist. The movie says "genocide bad" and "security state bad", but doesn't really offer any alternatives. It kinda just goes "cry about it". Thinking metaphorically, it says that the security state will reach a tipping point where people violently choose freedom over security, and that the security state will cause this violence (the nation-wide genocide is triggered by being broadcasted on the news).

However, this is undercut by the people in-universe having no say in the matter thanks to the mind-control Genocide Organ, and the film doesn't provide any solutions to prevent this violence. It prevents a thesis with no conclusion, and leaves no options for the viewer to draw their own. Maybe that is the conclusion, that the genocide is inevitable, but that just feels overly doomerist. It’s a sour ending for a movie that could have easily taken a side, or even offered some character stating some solution to preventing genocide, but instead it offers nothing at all by deciding that none of it matters and we’ll all inevitably kill each other.

The Last of Us.title: The Last of Us
The Last of Us.blurb: Season 1 is one of the best live action shows I’ve ever seen, with incredible characters fueled by excellent acting and writing. Season 2 is also pretty good, but is half a story and ends on a pretty big cliffhanger.
The Last of Us.review:
For full context, I have not played The Last of Us games, but I knew the games’ general plots going into the show via cultural osmosis. As such, this review is focused primarily on the show as its own piece of media and not as an adaptation of the video games.

Season 1 is one of the best live action shows I’ve ever seen, with incredible characters fueled by excellent acting and writing. Even if the plot is a bit thin - it’s almost entirely “go from A to B without dying” - the characters are the focus of the show and absolutely carry it. The vibes are also immaculate, showing us a world on the brink of death that’s just trying to survive, and the direction is incredible, making it feel tense at every moment, and yet just relaxed enough when it needs to be.

Pedro Pascal and Bella Ramsey absolutely kill it as Joel and Ellie, delivering incredible nuance to the two characters. The supporting cast is also incredible, and you really feel for every character as they struggle to connect and survive. Shoutout to episode 3, a standalone episode about two largely unrelated characters that perfectly conveys what it’s like to live in this world. I do think it jars the pacing if you aren’t expecting a full-episode cutaway, but it works really well with the knowledge that it’s coming.

The second half of the show could use more Infected, but it does make the Fireflies look more evil at the end. Joel’s decision to save Ellie really works as the culmination of his character arc, where he finally learns to connect with another person and live for someone other than himself. Unfortunately, this also means that he’s depriving the world of a potential cure just to keep Ellie alive. Not that the Fireflies were being the friendliest in their treatment of him, but the show makes you feel like a cure is possible, especially because Ellie is willing to sacrifice herself to try. It’s the perfect storm that makes the ending tragic, since Joel spent the whole show learning a valuable lesson that makes his life better, and yet is the exact wrong lesson for the story he’s in. Season 1 works perfectly on its own, being a natural ending place for the story even if there are more places you could take the characters.

Season 2 is a solid follow-up to season 1, although my perception is definitely biased because I knew about Joel's death and the general plot going into it. Still, after a set-up episode, episode 2 is a certified banger, with a really good zombie fight tied in with the whole situation with Abby trying to avenge her family’s death at Joel’s hands. The scene is set up to make you think Joel will live, what with Ellie going to save him and then Joel and Ellie needing to save the town. But then Ellie isn't enough, and the town survives without Joel.

The rest of the season is fueled by this death, with Ellie becoming almost single-minded in getting revenge on Joel. And I do say almost. Ellie is so close at multiple points to abandoning Abby and going back home with Dinah and Jesse, but every time she sees something relating to Abby, she laser-focuses on that and forgets everything else. It's almost like a trigger, something the rest of her life can almost make her forget about until it comes back into focus. It makes for a tragic character arc, especially since the season effectively ends with Ellie's death.

The rest of the cast is also very good, particularly Dinah, Jesse, and Tommy. The Scars aren't great, but they set the scene for how fraught the world is outside of Ellie’s town. The infected also get a much more even screen presence this season, having major roles in several episodes.

The ending is a bit rough, as this season and the next really should be one season, but at least the show tells you that things aren't over and that next season will be at least partly about Abby. If we don't get another season, though, the show ends with Ellie's death, which is thematically poignant if a bit depressing. Ellie could not be saved from her vengeance, and took her friends down with her. Season 1 is definitely better than season 2, but season 2 is still very strong aside from obviously being half a season.

12 Angry Men.title: 12 Angry Men
12 Angry Men.blurb: Despite being so old it's in black and white, this movie holds up incredibly well. The most standout part is the direction, but the writing is super tight and every juror gets their time in the spotlight.
12 Angry Men.review:
Despite being so old it's in black and white, 12 Angry Men holds up incredibly well. The most standout part of the movie is the direction; you can almost never tell that cuts are being made, yet the camera is always focused right where it needs to be to convey the exact information and intensity the scene needs. The acting is also incredibly good, with every character being filled with subtle emotion in the way they talk and move.

The writing is also super tight, with almost every piece of the case being thoroughly examined from every angle, and every "hole" that is poked in it being something that has been around from the case's beginning. There are a few exceptions, which can make the arguments feel a little "gotcha-y" for anyone trying to draw their own conclusions about what happened, but it never fully takes you out of the movie. This is mostly because the film doesn't really follow any character's perspective. The guy who first goes "I vote not guilty" is obviously the main guy, but it's not really from his perspective, so you feel like an outside observer listening in rather than someone who is having info withheld from them.

Additionally, despite the large cast, every single juror gets at least one moment in the spotlight, usually more than one. Some jurors are more important than others, but everybody has a scene that's about them, either their morals or their contribution to the argument. It's very impressive when it'd be so easy to make 2 or 3 of the jurors irrelevant to focus on another 2 or 3, and while some jurors clearly have the spotlight more than others, it feels incredibly balanced overall. The movie also does a great job dissecting almost every character, being almost as much about their arcs and ideals and morals as it is about the case, as the case and arguments around it draw out their deepest ideas about the world. It's a very impressive, tightly-written, amazingly-directed film that stands the test of time.

Murder Drones.title: Murder Drones
Murder Drones.blurb: A fun little indie series that picks up its pace and technique very quickly. The first episode is rough, being plagued with annoying teen characters doing annoying teen things, but the show quickly transforms into a frenetic action show with intriguing lore and fun, interesting characters.
Murder Drones.review:
A fun little indie series that picks up its pace and technique very quickly. The first episode is rough, being plagued with annoying teen characters doing annoying teen things, but the show quickly transforms into a frenetic action show with intriguing lore and fun, interesting characters. Episode 3, “The Promening”, is probably the first real good episode of the show, thanks to the more consistent character work and Doll's really intriguing powers and backstory. The voice acting and animation are also really rough early on, but the entire cast and crew seem to learn as they go and both aspects are very good by the time the show ends.

I broadly like the story of Murder Drones, uncovering the mystery of what's up with the telekinetic Doll and the titular Murder Drones. Things do ramp up very quickly, going from very episodic for the first few episodes to being one long story by episode 5. The stakes also skyrocket in a way that almost doesn't feel earned, but is still really cool regardless. Really, it's not that Cyn doesn't work as a world-ending threat, it's that the stakes are so low in episodes 1-3 and escalate so fast that it feels unhinged. The rest of the plot is like that too though, moving really fast as Uzi gets her powers and befriends V (or J? Side tangent complaint: I can never remember which of the other drones is V and which is J, they just look too similar and their names are too similar. I only remember N because I knew his name before I started watching) and then Tess shows up and then the world ends.

It does make Cyn feel terrifying in her speed, but it also feels like some of the ideas from the first few episodes are left behind. Like, how long have the robots actually been on this world? How are they living in a world without humanity, isolated from the rest of the system? How do robots have kids? So I really like the Cyn stuff, she's terrifying and a great antagonist, but I feel like the show transforms radically to the point the first few episodes feel disconnected from the rest of the stuff. If the intent was to portray this change from Uzi’s perspective, like she's just tossed into this world-ending scenario, it doesn't really feel like it. We never even learn how the Absolute Solver gives people telekinesis, which seems like it'd be important, but whatever its sick as fuck so who cares.

As I said before, Cyn is a great antagonist. She's creepy and terrifying while still being very funny and sounding exactly like Glados (voice-wise, not dialogue-wise). Her design is incredible, and the slow reveal of her origin, powers, and plan is really good. Uzi and N are the main characters, and they both start really annoying before getting better over time. I like their relationship of two outsiders finding love in one another, and N's politeness and Uzi's recklessness complement each other well. Neither are super great on their own, but I really like them together, and their parallel arcs of fighting for their friends and finding their backbone are well done enough. J (or V?) is also here. She's fun, I like her fakeout death scene, and her slow arc of coming around on the robots and being more open about caring for N is well done. My favorite character is definitely Doll. She's just really mysterious with enigmatic motivations, and once they get revealed, they're still completely understandable. I'm not opposed to her death scene being used to up the stakes, but I wish she got a better resolution with Uzi, or at least V/J.

The rest of the robots are also here, and I'm not really sure what I'm supposed to make of their blase attitude towards death. It is kinda funny, but it also makes it feel like the robots don't care about each other. And maybe they don't and that's why Uzi is different, or maybe the robots just expect to be rebuilt but we don't spend enough time exploring their society to explain that? Not sure, it is funny in the moment but confusing from a worldbuilding perspective. Not like the robots are relevant past the first half anyways.

Lastly, the character design is peak. I love how expressive the robots are with their LED faces, and I've mentioned before how terrifying Cyn's design is. The worldbuilding could use some work, but I totally get how people vibe with the show's aesthetic and tone. It feels like it was made for teenagers in the best way, and teenagers will definitely enjoy it. Overally, it's a pretty fun show once it gets going, as long as you don't mind going with the excellent vibes and not thinking about the smaller details that often get left in the dust.

The Adventures of Tintin.title: The Adventures of Tintin
The Adventures of Tintin.blurb: A mocap animated movie that looks surprisingly great. It feels almost live action in its script and world, using the mocap just for heightened reality in the action sequences.
The Adventures of Tintin.review:
A mocap animated movie that looks surprisingly great. It feels almost live action in its script and world, using the mocap just for heightened reality in the action sequences. The crane fight and the chase through Bagghar stand out as really only working in the animated medium, but are still heightened by the 3d mocap making them feel more real. The incredible transitions similarly only really work in this style, as you can physically overlay the 3d objects on top of each other instead of just using drawings or janky practical cuts. The film's style is nearly flawless, which is a huge compliment for a fully animated mocap movie.

The plot is also very good, with an engaging mystery centered around Haddock's treasure and Sakharine's motivations. The character arcs are simple for both Tintin and Haddock, but that doesn't mean they aren't thought out or impactful in the moment. Tintin in particular is almost a static character, serving primarily as motivation for Haddock, the one with real emotional connection to the plot. He learns to stop wallowing in the past and live up to his full potential to reclaim his family’s legacy, while the villain refuses to give up a generations-old grudge.

The pickpocket at the beginning is a bit underutilized, but he serves to flesh out Tintin's world as one where this stuff just happens, and helps justify Tintin's connection to the (also underutilized but hilarious) Interpol officers. Everything flows really well from one plot beat and setpiece into the next, making it feel like the movie and characters are constantly on the move and getting closer to their goal. It’s immensely satisfying, even if the movie is simple on the surface.

X-Men.title: X-Men
X-Men.blurb: A banger superhero movie. While it does take itself very seriously, it still clearly loves the source material. A true ensemble, where everyone gets a chance to shine, even if Magneto steals the show.
X-Men.review:
A banger superhero movie. While it does take itself very seriously, it still clearly loves the source material, openly using everybody’s codenames and having goofy gadgets like Cerebro and Magneto’s whirring mutant machine. All the characters get a chance to shine with their powers, and the movie even manages to make Toad look threatening. They don’t all get an equal chance to shine as characters, though, with the supporting cast having much smaller emotional roles as opposed to feeling like a true ensemble. It doesn’t hurt the movie too much though, especially since the main cast is very strong.

For the supporting characters, Storm gets very little in the way of characterization aside from believing strongly in her cause, and Cyclops really just gets one scene where he promises to take care of Xavier’s school if Xavier dies. He at least gets a bit more characterization in his interactions with Wolverine, as does Jean Grey, but the stars of the show are Wolverine, Rogue, and Magneto.

Magneto gets the award for Most Aura Farming, and he definitely deserves it. He’s the opening scene of the movie and driving force of the plot. He gets to show his full power several times while the X-Men play catch-up trying to stop him. Shoutouts to the scene where he rips open a train car and the scene where he points the guns at the police officers. His cause is just - trying to prevent mutants from becoming the victims of a second Holocaust - but his plan is questionable, especially considering he decides to go through with it even knowing that it will kill the world leaders and not convert them into mutants. He also clearly detests humans, and comes across like he’s less interested in preventing a Holocaust and more interested in assuring that the mutants are the Germans in his analogy.

Rogue is our POV character for the beginning of the film, and her power shows us how dangerous mutants can be while not meaning any harm at all, and why this makes their lives miserable. She gets less focus as the movie progresses, but her desire for a place to belong permeates the film. Mostly because the sentiment infects Wolverine, who becomes our POV character in the second half. His arc of learning to let people in and finding a place to settle down instead of wandering alone is really good. He’s characterized early on as caring about people since he begrudgingly takes Rogue in, but his moment at the end to let Rogue steal his healing power is still a really strong moment of vulnerability, sacrifice, and character growth.

The plot is also solid, as the X-Men run around to try and stop Magneto and his gang while they manipulate world leaders for their own benefit. Senator Kelly’s death scene is really good as he realizes that mutants and humans aren’t so different. There are a few teases for the sequel, mostly revolving around Wolverine’s backstory, but they don’t feel too intrusive, especially since he promises Rogue that he’ll return to the School. It makes the ending feel like “and the adventures continue” while still concluding Wolverine’s and Rogue’s character arcs, versus feeling like a cliffhanger. It’s well done, and fits the movie’s quiet, deliberate, almost contemplative tone.

It’s a really good superhero movie, especially for 2000. The special effects are well done, and the ensemble is balanced well enough. The plot and themes are substantive enough to carry the movie, and the fight scenes are well done if very short. There are hints of a wider world that makes the world feel lived in, while also lending more weight to Kelly’s, Magneto’s, and Xavier’s arguments. They aren’t just fighting for the X-Men, or for Rogue, but for all the students at Xavier’s school that get brief moments in the spotlight, and the myriad more in the world that are implied to exist because of said school. It all feels deliberately crafted as a complete package with room to expand without ruining what makes this movie great.

X2: X-Men United.title: X2: X-Men United
X2: X-Men United.blurb: A significant improvement over the first movie, and an excellent example of how to do a superhero ensemble. Despite having a clear protagonist in Wolverine, everybody gets a chance to shine (except Cyclops). They all have excellent scenes for both their powers and personalities, and the fight scenes are actually good this time.
X2: X-Men United.review:
A significant improvement over the first movie, and an excellent example of how to do a superhero ensemble. Despite having a clear protagonist in Wolverine, everybody gets a chance to shine (except Cyclops). They all have excellent scenes for both their powers and personalities, and the fight scenes are actually good this time. The opening scene with Nightcrawler attacking the White House blows everything from the first movie out of the water, and the slow reveal that he can teleport is awesome. It shows just how dangerous mutants are, and the fights only get better from there.

The character interplay is really good in this one too. The X-Men team logically splits up at the start of the movie, putting them in place for where they need to be for the plot. It’s a fantastic plot too, with every scene flowing into the next. Motivations and actions impact each other across a weave of storylines, without anything feeling extraneous or coincidental. It’s fantastic, and the way everything culminates with an assault on Stryker’s base is awesome.

Everyone in this story is so well characterized with a clear time to shine. I love that the X-Men team up with Magneto. Major Stryker is just that much of a danger that the two enemies’ goals align. I like that Stryker himself isn’t really a danger, just his capability to take advantage of mutants. He uses his son’s mind control powers to enslave Yuriko and coerce Magneto into giving up the X-Mansion, then uses him again to get Xavier to nearly kill all mutants. This takes advantage not only of Xavier’s power, but also Cerebro, the machine Xavier built that only he can really use. It subtly hammers home just how much of a danger mutants are, since Stryker is only so dangerous because he can control other mutants. Without his son, Stryker is just a guy that Wolverine and Magneto easily overpower.

Magneto is great again in this movie, still being an evil prick while also proving to a degree while he’s right. Magneto is bad, but Stryker is just as bad, and it makes sense why Magneto would work with the X-Men to stop him. His manipulation of Pyro is also great, showing how someone could reasonably join Magneto’s side. I mean, Pyro watches his teacher get shot to death in front of his face. Wolverine comes back five seconds later, sure, but the cop did not know that. He shot to kill, and Pyro knows they’ll kill him too. It makes sense why he joins Magneto, even if we don’t see the ramifications of that this film.

Reducing Magneto’s squad to just Mystique is also great. She gets a lot of time to shine in this film, and acquires an actual personality in the process. She feels like her own character now instead of just another one of Magneto’s lackeys. Her helping Magneto order Xavier to kill all humans is also fucking peak. It’s such a dick move, basically betraying their whole alliance with the X-Men, but so in-character for both of them. They see an opportunity to win the war, and they take it, even if they don’t stay to ensure their wish is fulfilled. They are the exact same as Stryker, even if they’re on opposite sides.

As for the X-Men, Storm gets a redemption this film after her poor showing in the last one. She still cares very deeply about the mutant cause, but gets to use that to actually help people by bonding with Nightcrawler. She also gets to aura farm the fuck out of this movie, both in her scene where she captures Nightcrawler and the scene where she freezes Jason Stryker out of hypnotizing Xavier. Every time she starts charging up, you know something awesome is going to happen, and she always delivers.

Jean somehow feels like she gets less to do than Storm, but I think that’s just because she’s less flashy. Her whole arc is about gaining more control and confidence over her powers, and she uses them to sacrifice herself to save the X-Men. It’s obviously her biggest character moment, although I almost feel like her defining moment is turning Wolverine down. Like Wolverine says, she made a choice, and she chose Cyclops. I just wish we got a bit more of her actually feeling unable to make choices, but I think it’s more about her lack of self-confidence in using her powers than it is a lack of agency. It’s too bad Jean doesn’t have a history of resurrecting out of a deep body of water in the comics, or else I’d believe she could come back somehow to express that newfound self-confidence.

Wolverine is our POV character, but he’s really not the hero of this story. He saves all the mutant children at the beginning, but then he mostly focuses on trying to sleep with Jean and hunting down Stryker. He does catch and effectively kill Stryker, but it’s Magneto, Storm, and Jean who save the day. Rogue also doesn’t get to do a lot this film, aside from maybe helping turn Pyro to the dark side by preventing him from killing all those cops. She does fly the jet, but it’s not really a “her” moment, just a thing she does. Like, it doesn’t really showcase her character or powers. Bobby could have done it and it’d be the same. Still, though, she, Bobby, and Pyro are the embodiment of the children the X-Men are fighting for.

Xavier and Cyclops get the short end of the stick, being mind-controlled, but Xavier at least feels like he’s driving the plot since he’s instrumental to Stryker’s plan. His school and motivations are also what’s under threat, so he feels more integral to the story than poor Cyclops. Cyclops does get some good characterization at the end, but it’s almost all after Jean dies, so he still has no agency even if he does have a personality. The scene of him and Wolverine crying as they hug each other is fantastic though.

Everything works together to show again and again why mutants hide, even if most mutants mean no harm. The X-Men go out of their way not to hurt people and save humanity from Magneto/Stryker/Xavier, but Pyro blows up a whole bunch of cops. The cops also shoot Wolverine just for being a potential threat, and schoolchildren are kidnapped just for existing at a private school. They’re already isolated and yet still aren’t safe. You believe that mutants are real and exist all over the world, thanks both to the excellent showcase of quirky little powers at Xavier’s school and Bobby’s family’s reaction, and fully believe how dangerous they can be while still knowing that how society treats mutants is awful. The movie offers no easy solution, while giving the hard answer that fighting between the two groups is wrong. Magneto is evil, and so is Stryker, on the exact same level. Only by working together can we create a world where nobody has to live in fear.

X-Men: The Last Stand.title: X-Men: The Last Stand
X-Men: The Last Stand.blurb: This is not a good movie, and not just because it’s a significant downgrade from X2. It's also the unfocused plotline with messy themes, uninteresting characters, bad acting, and lame fight scenes.
X-Men: The Last Stand.review:
This is not a good movie, and not just because it’s a significant downgrade from X2. Most movies would be a significant downgrade from X2. Rather, it’s that this movie has an unfocused plotline with messy themes, uninteresting characters, bad acting, and lame fight scenes.

The movie only has two good fight scenes. The first is Jean’s obliteration of Xavier, which is good for its sheer intensity. The second is Kitty’s fight against Juggernaut. Iconic for its hilariously stupid “I’m the Juggernaut, bitch” line, this is the best power v power fight in the movie. Kitty finds the power nullification kid, immediately realizes that he nullifies the powers of those nearby, and tricks Juggernaut into rushing the kid so Juggernaut’s powers vanish and he knocks himself out on a wall. It’s a brilliant play from Kitty that uses Juggernaut’s power and stupidity against him. Despite its short length, this would be a good fight in the other movies too. It’s just that here it’s a standout.

The worst fight is the rest of the final battle. Iceman v Pyro is somehow just a beam clash, and the rest of the fight is worse. Magneto has an army of mutants, and yet none of them display any powers outside the three that showed them off earlier in the movie. This should be a chaotic mess of a fight, but it just comes down to nondescript guys running at Wolverine and Beast and getting mauled. There is absolutely no tension at all. Magneto’s grunts could be humans and the fight wouldn’t change.

The place where the movie dropped the ball the most is easily it’s mutant cure storyline. Should there be a “cure” for mutants is a fascinating question in a world where mutants can potentially be an active danger to themselves and those around them. Like, Rogue kills whoever she touches, it makes sense she’d want a cure. Unfortunately, the movie never asks these questions, instead settling pretty hard on “cure bad”. Magneto assumes that the government is going to force it on all mutants, and he may be right, but that’s a whole different question of whether something dangerous in the wrong hands should exist in the right hands.

Admittedly, there aren’t too many mutants whose powers are actively detrimental. The big two and Rogue and Cyclops, and Rogue does take the cure while Cyclops dies before it gets introduced. So while other mutants might want a cure, we never really see them. A big part of this too is that the movie doesn’t have enough mutants that don’t look human to weigh in on that obvious aspect of the cure. Almost every mutant extra looks human, even the large swathes in the streets and Magneto’s army needed more visual makeup. They should be all different colors with all manners of horns, tails, and the like. Not every mutant, but enough to go “yeah, these are mutants who are ostracized based on their looks”. Regardless of what side of the debate they’re on, it would add to the movie’s messaging and impact.

The only two non-human mutants in the movie are Angel and Beast. Angel very clearly doesn’t want the cure, and his mutation doesn’t negatively impact him outside of his dad hating him. Beast doesn’t seem to have any personal opinion at all, instead focusing on the political ramifications of the whole thing. It leaves that whole argument feeling ignored, especially when Nightcrawler’s whole backstory in the last movie is that he was only at home in the circus due to his looks making him a pariah elsewhere. And he is just not in this one.

Don’t get me wrong, I get why the movie comes down on the cure so hard, even if the X-Men still settle on protecting the pharmaceutical lab from Magneto. The cure is a metaphor for gay conversion therapy and the like, and in the real world, that stuff is unambiguously awful. While the X-Men are actually occasionally dangerous, only Rogue “needs” the cure, so her viewpoint and character arc comes across as half-baked. Regardless of whether Magneto is right about the government or not, most mutants like being mutants, so of course they wouldn’t want a “cure”, especially not one marketed with such antagonist language.

On top of that, this movie has a whole second plotline, that of Jean as Phoenix. Jean comes back from the dead as an emotionless psycho who kills anyone who gets close to her. This plotline sucks. Xavier turns out to be an asshole when he blocked Jean’s powers off to give her a split personality, totally ruining Xavier’s whole vibe and Jean’s whole arc in the last movie. Then Jean kills Cyclops 20 minutes in so he can go be Jimmy Olsen in Superman Returns, and then she kills Xavier at the halfway mark. After that, she does nothing until the last 5 minutes when Wolverine kills her. Her death scene is pretty good though.

I think the two plotlines are supposed to sync because Jean is an example of a mutant who is too powerful to control, so Xavier gave her his own version of the cure. So the “cure” made her controllable for a time, but then it also turned her into a psycho killer that she maybe wouldn’t have become if Xavier just taught her to control her powers from the start. It’s another dimension to the cure - should we use it on living nukes - that is never fully addressed.

This movie does have some things I like. Kelsey Grammer does do a good job as Beast, despite getting introduced randomly and not having a lot to do. He’s a pretty good voice of reason, exploring the whole cure angle from a somewhat neutral political perspective instead of being emotionally involved, but he doesn’t really contribute much, plotwise or thematically. I do like that the X-Men have graduates who do leave Xavier’s school, but it’s weird that this never comes up in the first two movies.

I like stopping Magneto by using the cure on him, it’s such a fitting ending to turn him into the very thing he hates most. A fate worse than death, but a deserved one. I like Wolverine’s line to Rogue about making sure she takes the cure because she wants to rather than because society wants her to. I also like Rogue’s follow-up about asking Logan to call her Marie, showing that she’s going back to society and is no longer isolated and on the run. Xavier’s death scene, the Kitty/Juggernaut fight, and Wolverine killing Jean are all pretty good. Magneto lifting the Golden Gate Bridge is awesome. The cure coming from a mutant parallels nicely how Stryker’s control last movie came from a mutant, showing again that only mutants can fight mutants. You get why the government may want to cure them, and why Magneto thinks they would. The intro with the X-Men comics is also cool.

This movie just has way more bad than good, to the point that the good gets lost in the tangled mess of unexplored themes and poor characterization. This movie had a troubled development cycle, and you can tell. It’s a sad ending to the first X-Men trilogy, especially considering how poised for greatness it was after X2.

Spider-Man.title: Spider-Man
Spider-Man.blurb: I did not like this movie, although I imagine that the reasons lots of people like it are the same reasons I didn't like it. The movie is not really a superhero movie in the traditional sense; it's not an aspirational story about people with power using their power to do good and change the world in a way that helps others. It's basically a tragedy, as the responsibility that comes with aging into adulthood hurts Peter and everyone around him.
Spider-Man.review:
I did not like this movie, although I imagine that the reasons lots of people like it are the same reasons I didn't like it. The movie is not really a superhero movie in the traditional sense; it's not an aspirational story about people with power using their power to do good and change the world in a way that helps others. Peter Parker gets powers, sure, and he uses them to stop the Green Goblin from murdering people, sure, but "with great power comes great responsibility" permeates the film. It's basically a tragedy.

Ben Parker tries to connect with his adopted son, and gets killed by a carjacker. Peter tries to stop Green Goblin, and it puts his aunt in the hospital and nearly kills the woman he loves, whom he can't even be with because of his powers. Not only that, but he has to kill his best friend's dad, and his best friend makes it clear that if he learns who killed him, there will be hell to pay. You want to be an X-Man, you want to be Blade, but you don't want to be Spider-Man. Peter is heroic obviously, but he isn't aspirational. In some ways he's the most heroic of all, doing the right thing even if it really hurts, with no chance of reward. But he deeply hurts the people around him too. Even if Harry might be better off without his neglectful, insane father, or MJ might be better off not dating a superhero, you don't see that in the film, so you're left with everyone ending in a worse place than when they started.

If X-Men is about treating people as equals regardless of their differences, Spider-Man is about how growing up forces you to take responsibility for your actions as you lose that idealism of youth. Peter's uncle dies randomly when Peter lets an unrelated criminal rob someone that slighted him, and he makes an enemy of his best friend's father when he tries to stop him from murdering his board of directors during a festival. Harry learns just how awful his father is, and yet is still enraged at his sudden death. Peter starts to see MJ as a real person instead of an idealized angel, and yet can't be with her because his power and responsibilities will get her killed. MJ falls for the first man who treats her well, and yet is rejected because he can't take care of her.

The superhero stuff is all tangential to this coming of age story, and in my opinion is worse for it. That's mostly because the movie is so cynical underneath the slow, dreamy direction, and neither Peter, Harry, nor MJ really engage me with their fucked-up three-way toxic relationships. Maybe they should, but the only relationship we actually see develop is Peter/MJ, so we miss all the good drama of the three relationships never letting each other reach a happy medium. Harry telling Peter that “[he's] the only family [he] has left” should hit hard, but it misses because we don't spend enough time on their actual friendship or why they're even friends.

As I alluded to, I'm not really a big fan of the directorial style. Most of the film is very slow, almost like it's in a dream. Shots take forever, and dialogue is slow and breathy. I get that neither Peter, MJ, nor Harry are very personable, and Peter at least gets better at talking as the film goes, but it just makes most of the movie feel like it's in a weird haze. I’m pretty sure the choice is intentional given that Willem Dafoe and JK Simmons are incredibly expressive, but I'm still not a big fan.

JK Simmons has way less screen-time than I remember, but Willem Dafoe is awesome as Norman. You can tell that Norman is unhinged even before he becomes the Goblin, and the way he switches between the Goblin voice and the Norman voice is awesome. His standout scenes are those where he talks to himself, either acting against himself in the mirror or bowing before the helmet. You feel like the Goblin is Norman's inner psyche being let loose, freeing him from the shackles of morality and letting him take all the power he wants for himself, without having to rely on the goodwill of those like the general or his board of directors.

One thing I will give the movie for in the superhero department is the costumes. The Spider-Man costume looks great, and I like the visualization of Peter's powers like wallcrawling and webslinging. Lots of people don't like the Green Goblin outfit, but I think it looks incredible. It feels like real metal body armor that could be worn in the field to fight people, not a cheap Spirit Halloween cloth costume. The fact that you can see Norman's eyes and mouth through the mask ups the creep factor while allowing him to be more expressive. It's somewhat realistic while still being terrifying, which does exactly what it needs to do.

It’s a film that just doesn’t land for me, thanks primarily to the movie’s underlying cynicism, but there’s a lot of other stuff I don’t vibe with either. It obviously works for a lot of other people, though, and I wonder if Spider-Man being so different from other superhero projects is the reason. It does have the most accurate costumes from the time and some decent fight scenes, but for me it doesn’t hold a candle to its Marvel predecessor (X-Men) in terms of story and characters. That said, it probably is better than Daredevil is going to be.

Iron Lung.title: Iron Lung
Iron Lung.blurb: Markiplier continues to prove that he knows how to make a movie. Iron Lung is a clear passion project, and its production value is incredibly high for something made by a Youtuber based on an hour-long indie game. The entire movie takes place inside a one-room submarine, and it somehow works.
Iron Lung.review:
Markiplier continues to prove that he knows how to make a movie. Iron Lung is a clear passion project, and its production value is incredibly high for something made by a Youtuber based on an hour-long indie game. The entire movie takes place inside a one-room submarine, and it somehow works. The first half is incredibly tense as everything that could break starts slowly reaching their breaking point. The movie spends plenty of time letting tension ramp and setting up signs of disaster, making sure that you never know what will go wrong next, or when. It’s incredibly effective buildup, delivering on the promise of “Markiplier in a deathtrap submarine” without ever feeling dull.

The film then switches genres at the half-way point to cosmic horror, as it gets revealed that the blood ocean is sentient, or at least inhabited by a god-like being of unimaginable power. It's never explained what this being is or what it wants, only that it kills all those who enter it. The rest of the movie is trying to retrieve the data that could save humanity while this horror tries to prevent it from being got, for one reason or another.

Things are intentionally left vague, but I think it hurts the horror in this instance. The blood magic is ambiguous enough that I don't know what danger Markiplier is actually in, so I'm not as scared as I was in the first half when the danger was mechanical and mental failure. Mix this in with a fairly ambiguous backstory and unclear motivations for Blood Chthulhu, and you're left with a lot of unanswered questions. The computer log seems to imply that the blood ocean holds no solutions and will kill those who try to use it, but it left me feeling unsatisfied due to just how ambiguous it is.

I think this near-universal ambiguity is intentional, playing on Markiplier’s insignificance to the rest of humanity and humanity’s insignificance in the face of the cosmic unknown, but it didn't quite land for me. You're supposed to wonder what will happen, but in my opinion it's the movie's job to give enough context to make that question answerable. Still, that doesn't detract from all the love and care that Markiplier clearly put into this film, and if you like cosmic horror, this movie will land really well.

Spider-Man 2.title: Spider-Man 2
Spider-Man 2.blurb: An improvement over the first film thanks to the acting not being awful, making the characters feel more like real people in this one. The plot is somehow more disconnected than last time, with Doc Ock and the MJ plots really having nothing to do with each other, but they managed to get tied together thematically at the end.
Spider-Man 2.review:
An improvement over the first film thanks to the acting not being awful. Characters feel more like real people in this one, even if there are still moments of weird dreamlike goofiness. The plot is somehow more disconnected than last time, with Doc Ock and the MJ plots really having nothing to do with each other, but they managed to get tied together thematically at the end.

Almost every conflict in the movie is solved by Peter being Peter and not Spider-Man. Harry stops trying to kill Spider-Man for killing his father when he learns that Spider-Man is actually Peter, and consequently learns that his father was the Green Goblin. Doc Ock realizes that he’s become a monster when Peter unmasks himself and uses Ock’s own words against him, and MJ finally understands Peter and can willingly be with him once she knows he’s Spider-Man. Spider-Man is straight up a burden on Peter this movie, and he can only help people when he’s being himself.

All that said, Peter kinda sucks in this movie. Admittedly, he has a lot on his plate, juggling school, friends, a job, and Spider-Man, and the world just also hates him in small ways like not letting him get a drink at the party. But man is he still kinda stupid. Peter keeps showing up to things late despite doing Spider-Man things and just expects to be on time. Sure he has a good reason why he’s late, but he can’t tell anybody so he comes across as entitled. Like if he just carried a watch he’d know he’s late instead of being surprised all the time, and then he could realize that he’s missed an entire school lecture instead of trying to go for no reason.

Plus, almost all his social problems are caused by him being Spider-Man. Harry hates him for hiding Spider-Man’s identity, and Peter has no good excuse. And why doesn’t he tell Harry the truth about Norman being the Green Goblin? Oh yeah, because the Green Goblin asked him to. It at least makes sense why Peter doesn’t tell MJ because she did get nearly murdered because she was connected to him, and she gets kidnapped this movie due to her connection to him again. She just accepts that she’s willing to be in danger to be with him, which is a nice way to resolve the plotline.

I do wish she didn’t leave her fiance at the altar though, that’s kind of a dick move on her part, especially since her fiance seems like an actually good guy this time. She needs to do what she needs to do to be happy, that’s kind of the whole theme of the movie, but it’s still rude as fuck. And she immediately looks like she regrets her decision when Peter runs off to be Spider-Man with her blessing, so surely this is a relationship destined for success.

I didn’t mention her in my Spider-Man 1 review, but Aunt May continues to be really good in this movie. She has such a strong emotional awareness of what’s going on, and her reaction to learning the truth of Uncle Ben’s death is great. She needs space from Peter in the moment, but doesn’t hold it against him. She unreasonably blamed herself, and he did the same thing, so she forgives him. I also fully believe she knows he’s Spider-Man, which is why she gives such a good speech about heroism. I like that she admits that sacrifice will be involved, but being a hero will still make the world better, and that heroism will be paid back in turn. Then, we see this over and over with the train scene and the kid grabbing Peter in the firefighter scene and every plot being solved by Spider-Man revealing himself.

As for the villain, Doc Ock is a fun one. He’s not as good as Green Goblin, but I like that he’s more set in his ways than insane. I do wish he wasn’t being mind controlled by the arms and just decided that he needed to do his experiment at all costs. I think it’d play into the “great power, great responsibility” thing better since he’d be powerful enough to destroy NY but not responsible enough to realize not to do it, and his heart-to-heart with Peter at the end would mean more. But I still like him overall.

The action scenes are also way more dynamic in this movie, which definitely helps sell Ock’s physical threat and ruthless determination. The scene on the clocktower is my favorite, but I also fully understand the love for the train scene. Ock letting Spider-Man stop the train and then effortlessly getting past the civilians to kidnap him is great.

Some other miscellaneous things: JK Simmons is still great as J Jonah Jameson, striking the right balance between unscrupulous and fair; John Jameson does not get enough to do, and he seems like an actually decent guy unlike MJ’s last two boyfriends, which makes MJ ditching him reflect worse on her; so many women scream in fear in this movie, especially compared to the very few men that do it, so it’s honestly kind of distracting; the scene where Doc Ock murders all the scientists with his arms is awesome; this is the first Marvel movie to imply a wider Marvel universe, with a reference to Doctor Strange.

It’s still not the greatest superhero movie ever, but I like its emphasis on heroism and how good things do come of it. I feel like the theme of this movie is telling the truth and not keeping your secrets, and I like that Peter’s life becomes so much better when he stops hiding who he is from those he cares about. Heroism is a good, inspirational thing, but you can’t be a hero if you’re miserable and alone.

Spider-Man 3.title: Spider-Man 3
Spider-Man 3.blurb: A poorly paced, overly-stuffed movie united by a theme of Peter, MJ, and Harry destroying their relationships with each other because they can’t empathize with anyone around them. The thematic and narrative tissue is there to make this movie interesting, it’s just that it fumbles magnificently in execution as things happen for seemingly no reason and plots jump from point to point with almost no buildup or connective tissue.
Spider-Man 3.review:
A poorly paced, overly-stuffed movie united by a theme of Peter, MJ, and Harry destroying their relationships with each other because they can’t empathize with anyone around them. The thematic and narrative tissue is there to make this movie interesting, it’s just that it fumbles magnificently in execution as things happen for seemingly no reason and plots jump from point to point with almost no buildup or connective tissue. For example: Harry gets amnesia and then gets un-amnesia-ed; Flint Marko becomes the Sandman by falling into a particle accelerator; the entire Peter-MJ-Gwen conflict is caused by a crane malfunction; and it’s this pacing that makes the whole movie feel haphazard.

The big focus of this movie is Peter’s imploding relationships with MJ and Harry. It’s not even a tragedy at this point: these people’s lives aren’t falling apart around them because everything is their fault. Peter and MJ cannot communicate with each other to save their lives, ultimately devolving into both of them cheating because why have an honest conversation when you can get your fulfillment elsewhere. Harry learns the exact wrong lesson from the reveal in the last movie and decides to continue his father’s murderous rampage by killing Peter. I assume this is due to the sunk cost fallacy at this point because it’s blatantly obvious that Harry’s dad is the psycho murderer who tried to kill him. So, bonus points to Harry for being evil on purpose. It’s honestly entertaining because you no longer feel sad for these people, so you can revel in watching their friendships explode due to their own egos.

Harry’s arc at least seems like it ends where it should, with him finally forgiving Peter. MJ’s arc ends with her having not changed at all since movie one. She cheats on Peter and leaves him as soon as she’s unsatisfied, just like all her other boyfriends. Having your main female lead not grow as a person at all in three films is certainly a choice. Peter does grow a little bit, realizing that he can’t let ego go to his head and that he has other people’s feelings to consider too. It’s just hard to see his growth because Harry and MJ refuse to let it have any effect on them until Harry’s realization in the final act.

There are also two other villains in this movie on top of Harry. Sandman is to give Peter someone to try and murder basically. It’s why he’s effectively immortal I think, so Peter can have a change of heart when his murder attempt fails instead of Sandman just fucking dying. And the reason Peter wants to kill him is because Sandman is actually the guy who killed Uncle Ben and the guy from the first movie is just an accomplice. It’s such a stupid retcon because it seems to come out of nowhere just to make Peter’s life worse. Even making Sandman the accomplice would be better, because it wouldn’t diminish the first movie and Peter is so angry in this movie that I believe he’d want to kill him anyways. Sandman seems to have some thematic resonance because he seems to want to help his daughter, but hurts so many people to get there. It’s clearly “great power, great responsibility”, and there’s some clear tension there between trying to help one person at the expense of others, but it never really goes anywhere. His realization that he’s done wrong comes after he’s defeated, so doesn’t challenge Peter or make him reflect in any way.

The other villain is Eddie Brock, played as a slimy, egotistic conman by Topher Grace. He thinks that one date means that he’s dating Gwen Stacy even though she openly rejects him, and fakes his photo submission to the Daily Bugle even though its his last shot at his job. And instead of reflecting on his actions, he instead prays to god to kill Peter for exposing him, which is admittedly pretty funny. He was designed to be Peter if Peter had no moral compass, and he does a pretty good job, especially considering how much of an ass Peter is in this movie. Him getting the symbiote and gaining superpowers is just the cherry on top, literally making him an Evil Peter.

The Venom symbiote is also in this movie, although it’s never called Venom so I’m just gonna call it the symbiote. First thought: why is there an alien in this movie? This plot point literally comes from space, when it’d fit this universe so much better if the symbiote was made in a lab or something. Whatever, there are aliens now, moving on.

The movie almost doesn’t change if you remove the symbiote, aside from Eddie getting powers. Peter’s descent into egocentrism works without the symbiote amplifying his anger, although I do like it as a physical metaphor for Peter’s ego. Plus, it feels like a metaphor for substance abuse with how Peter struggles to get rid of it. Despite not being necessary for the drama, the symbiote works in the same way that Green Goblin works as a physical metaphor for imperfect parents in the first movie.

In some ways, this is the perfect ending to the trilogy, re-focusing the original’s theme that growing up is miserable. Peter’s best friend is dead, the girl of his dreams turned out to be shallow and awful under the surface, and all he has left is a cushy position at a job that barely appreciates him. Does that make this a good trilogy? Depends if you treat this as a drama or a superhero series. As a drama about people getting older and yet not outgrowing their flaws? Perfect. As a superhero series about responsibility, heroism, and hope? Awful.

Oh yeah, the Bully Maguire scenes are peak. They’re so ridiculous it wraps around to being hilarious. The scene where he dances in the jazz club with Gwen just to piss off MJ is awesome, even if it is Peter at his worst. The memes are fully warranted.

Hulk.title: Hulk
Hulk.blurb: If your definition of "artsy film" is "uses split screen effects from Windows Movie Maker", then this is an artsy film for sure. Just as prominent as the movie’s relatively simple take on Hulk’s origin as a monster movie from the monster’s perspective is all the split screen.
Hulk.review:
If your definition of "artsy film" is "uses split screen effects from Windows Movie Maker", then this is an artsy film for sure. Just as prominent as the movie’s relatively simple take on Hulk’s origin as a monster movie from the monster’s perspective is all the split screen.

The movie uses split screen frequently, usually featuring events happening at the same time, like five angles of the military bringing Bruce into a prison, or three characters talking to each other. It makes everything hard to follow, and would probably be better served in a single shot. Although I do respect the commitment to the bit, and it’s clear the director and editor had fun using this brand-new split screen technology. The only times it really works is when someone is talking over the phone or radio, as you can see the person talking as well as the main action taking place, such as when Ross is ordering his troops around while Hulk escapes. You wouldn't normally get those two perspectives in one shot, so the splitting works.

Unrelated and yet very related, there are a lot of weirdly edited montages of animals in this movie, particularly reptiles and also moss (not an animal but close enough). They go away as the movie goes, but they just make the entire first half of the film feel so bizarre. Bruce's powers come from reptiles, I get it, please stop showing me a lizard for no reason.

I also need to shout out Talbot’s death scene. He gets hit by an explosion and just gets encased in this white outline and hovers on screen for a good half-second before the explosion overtakes him. It’s like he was selected by the Magic Select tool and his png is just held there. It’s utterly hilarious with how bizarre it is, and you fully understand why directors don’t reuse this technique.

Direction aside, the plot and characters are just okay. The intro where we follow Bruce's dad is very long, but it turns out to be Bruce’s dream so it works. I do like the setup and context it gives to Bruce's Hulk transformation, it just takes forever. The rest of the first third is setting up character relationships, which is important so you care about these characters when the action starts, but it does take a long time.

When Hulk first appears, paying off that tension established in the intro, he feels like a horror monster, being filmed in darkness and destroying everything around him. It's only when Hulk fights off the mutant dogs (love the mutant dogs by the way; they’re so hilariously stupid) that it stops feeling like a horror film. And yet the similarities continue, with the military bringing Hulk in, then him escaping due to the military's stupidity/hubris, before making his way to a populated area. However, Hulk is not a monster, merely a misunderstood depressed man, so instead of rooting for the military to kill this unstoppable beast, you're rooting for Hulk to escape and live his best life free from captivity. It works well in a thematic way.

It unfortunately never gets past “just okay” in any other way. The directing does make the film feel off, but I never got too invested in any of the relationships or arcs. I wanted Bruce to be free, but I was never interested in him getting back with Betty, or Betty reconciling and/or rejecting her father, or Talbot going behind Ross' back to try and replicate the Hulk. Bruce's dad is kind of interesting, but it becomes clear that all of his apparent nuance is a front and he's grown to hate everyone who's ever threatened his work, including his own son.
