The plot is very simple aside from the monster movie inversion, so it's riding on its characters (and direction I guess). The characters work in the moment, but they never really grabbed me in the long run to make the film more than the sum of its parts. Ironic for a film with so much split screen.

Being a monster movie with inspiration in superhero comics, there are of course some action scenes. They're also just okay. The big fight is very anticlimactic, with Bruce's Absorbing Man dad just becoming a bunch of rocks and the fight basically being a short, generic slugfest before Bruce overwhelms him with emotion. The idea of his power is cool, but it never manifests for me. Which is kind of how I feel about the whole movie honestly. Some good ideas, but just okay execution, marred by the bizarre dedication to split screen and lizards.

Daredevil.title: Daredevil
Daredevil.blurb: They play Wake Me Up Inside in this movie 10/10. I think this movie is meant to be serious, and it largely fails at that. However, it is also the most 2003 movie ever made and wraps back around from being bad to being very entertaining. A "so bad it's good" movie.
Daredevil.review:
They play Wake Me Up Inside in this movie 10/10. I think this movie is meant to be serious, and it largely fails at that. However, it is also the most 2003 movie ever made and wraps back around from being bad to being very entertaining. A "so bad it's good" movie, thanks to the music choice, weirdly spinning camera, and slightly goofy writing and acting. Daredevil and Elektra are played completely straight by their actors, to the point of being almost wooden, but Bullseye and Kingpin are hamming it up and having the time of their lives.

There's a point where Bullseye kills a guy, then points to the bullseye burned into his forehead and goes "Bullseye" in the most hilarious voice. His intro scene is that he plays darts while not looking, then kills a guy with paperclips for making fun of his ethnicity. Which, you shouldn't be racist, but also Bullseye kills a woman on an airplane for talking too much so he’s just like this. Bullseye would be right at home in a Blade movie, and I say that as a compliment.

Kingpin is played by Michael Clarke Duncan, who does an absolutely excellent job as an imposing businessman who delights in killing his competition. It is weird making Kingpin black, since he's supposed to be a rich man who exploits the poor, but he does come across more like a rich mafia boss in this movie, so it works. Honestly if he wasn't literally the only black person, I'd have no notes, since Michael Clarke Duncan is so good at his role.

Daredevil and Elektra did not get the memo that this movie is a stupid action comedy, but Daredevil does get some pretty good one-liners. Aside from that, the two really don't have a lot going on. They fall in love immediately, go on two dates, have one fight, then Elektra has a mental breakdown about learning Matt Murdock is Daredevil, and then Bullseye kills her. She’s really underdeveloped, despite being the catalyst for the main plot. Daredevil has a little arc about trusting in the legal system, but it's mostly in the background. The rest of the plot is also pretty lackluster. Daredevil is hunting down Kingpin for running the city's crime and eventually killing Elektra's dad, but that’s pretty much it. This simplicity does work for this movie because it lets the action come into focus, there's just not a lot to talk about there.

The fight scenes are really good though. Some of the stunts are clearly CGI, but the choreography is still very good. The characters have their own styles and the fights are very kinetic. Bullseye especially is really fun to watch, but I like that you can tell that Daredevil isn't trying against Elektra just from the choreography. One part of the CGI that is really good is Daredevil's sonar vision. It's consistently portrayed excellently, with everything appearing in these light blue silhouettes that ebb and flow with the sound of the world. The scenes where he sees in the rain are beautiful, but I think my favorite scene is young Daredevil's panic attack when he first gets his powers. There are so many sounds and so many visualizations that blend together and yet are clearly distinct. It's probably my favorite scene in the movie.

Aside from that one excellent scene, it's an okay movie that you can have a lot of fun with if you don’t analyze it too hard. I think some of the comedy is intentional, namely Bullseye and Kingpin, but most of it is just the early-2000s edge being retroactively funny. All of the side characters being named after Daredevil writers is also very funny, especially the rapist being named after Marvel's then-Editor-in-Chief Joe Quesada. This movie is also a proto-Batman movie, given that Ben Affleck plays Daredevil, all his lines about vengeance, and the literal bats that fly out of the pipe organ. Not intentional, but it adds to this movie's charm, 20 years later.

Elektra.title: Elektra
Elektra.blurb: The best way I can describe this movie is "generic". It's the most cookie-cutter "assassin develops a conscience over a child" plot, and executed in a way that makes it seem like nobody making the movie cared at all. It feels like it was just created from the pitch "Jennifer Garner sexily fights people in skimpy clothes", and yet she barely fights people and her clothes are barely skimpy.
Elektra.review:
The best way I can describe this movie is "generic". It's the most cookie-cutter "assassin develops a conscience over a child" plot, and executed in a way that makes it seem like nobody making the movie cared at all. Elektra is hyped up in the intro as one of the world's best assassins who can kill anyone and nearly teleport with her speed, but she has dinner with her target one time and immediately decides not to kill them. If she had put more thought into figuring out why someone wants this family killed, or if she had spent more than two days getting to know them before the hit was put on them, it'd be more believable. But as it stands, she has dinner with people once and immediately decides to throw away the life she's built as an assassin despite not even knowing if they’re innocent. After that, she just goes through the motions of learning to care about someone and trying to protect them, and realizing that that means teaching them how to protect themself. It’s a generic plot that starts with a weak foundation and is given no emotional weight.

The people Elektra’s protecting aren't that interesting either. The daughter Abby is a snarky teen with a headstrong streak who remains a snarky teen with a headstrong streak, and her dad is also there. They also have the most obvious secret, being that they are hunted by the Hand for having the Treasure that will turn the tide of the Hand’s eternal war. Or, in this case, they are hiding that Abby is the Treasure. Decent twist, but she's the Treasure not because she’s special, but because she's a prodigy at combat. At least make her a prodigy at the cool powers the ninja have.

Oh yeah, the cool powers. Elektra can see briefly into the future, which is used for some good action a few times, but mostly feels like it's used to handwave how Elektra always knows where the fighting is. People who are good at future sight can also resurrect people from the dead for unexplained reasons. I’m genuinely unsure what the explanation is, which is bad because peering into the timeline in no way implies resurrection powers. The bad guys also have some fun unique abilities, namely Tattoo. He has animal tattoos on his body that summons into animal spirits that he can control, and the visual effects for this are honestly pretty good.

Other than that, the fight scenes are just okay. They're all really short with mediocre choreography that never really gets you hooked. The final battle is underwhelming, with Elektra just blowing up the mooks with a bomb and then beats the main villain - a speedster - by catching him off-guard with no fanfare. She does use her future sight to throw her sai through like ten bushes though, which is cool.

This movie is also technically a spin-off of 2003’s Daredevil, but you'd never know it. Elektra's mentor is blind, and she tells Abby that "they'll find each other" to parallel her goodbye in Daredevil, and that’s it. I don't know if the movie is better or worse for it, but it is weird they got Jennifer Garner back and then didn't make use of that continuity at all.

Really, the movie just left me bored. Nothing in it hooked me at all, or even unhooked me enough that it became hilariously bad. My biggest complaints are the stuff they didn't do - good action scenes, good characterization, interesting plot - versus stuff they did do, which is far less interesting to analyze for me. I'm not sure anyone had fun making this movie. It feels like it was just created from the pitch "Jennifer Garner sexily fights people in skimpy clothes", and yet she barely fights people and her clothes are barely skimpy, so I don't even know what we're doing here.

The Punisher.title: The Punisher
The Punisher.blurb: An okay action movie with okay characters, a straightforward plot, and decent action sequences. That said, it is even worse as a Punisher movie than an action-gang movie.
The Punisher.review:
An okay action movie with okay characters, a straightforward plot, and decent action sequences. Frank Castle's family is killed by the Saint crime family after he kills one of their sons during his last job as an FBI agent, so Castle makes it his mission to humiliate and kill the head of the family. He does this by recruiting an inside man to help emotionally and professionally destroy Mr Saint, then kills him. He also befriends some kindly poor people in the building he's staying in, and they help protect him when the crime family shows up.

That's about the extent of the plot, minus the details of how Castle destroys Mr Saint. He convinces him that his wife is sleeping with his right-hand man, which is cool but not complex, especially since we only see the plan get executed and not developed. I do respect the movie killing Frank Castle's kid since kids are usually safe in these types of movies, but there isn't really a lot else going on plot-wise.

As for the characters, they are also fairly boring. I like Castle's intense determination and how he exploits Mr Saint's insecurities, but there isn't much else going on there. Everybody is fairly flat on purpose, but that style just isn’t doing it for me. I do like that the poor people recognize Castle as one of them and befriend him after he protects Rebecca Romijin’s character - oh yeah, Rebecca Romijin of X-Men fame is in this movie - from her abusive ex, and yet Castle still can't form any meaningful bond because he's too traumatized. The opening has some religious symbolism with the big bad being named Saint, Castle's wife saying they've been blessed with each other, and Castle's kid buying him the Punisher shirt to ward off evil spirits, but then there’s no more religious motifs for the remaining hour-and-a-half. It's an okay action-gang movie, but that's about it.

That said, it is even worse as a Punisher movie than an action-gang movie. It's Frank Castle's origin story as the Punisher, and he develops an intense anger and loneliness, but it never fully manifests as brutal violence. He's incredibly methodical with lots of forethought as opposed to just murdering Mr Saint and his family outright. His family's death was so targeted that his motive feels like a vendetta as opposed to something that will become a crusade. The Saints killed his family, not the idea of organized crime, so it feels out of place that he decides to eradicate all violent criminals. He has to because this is supposed to be a Punisher movie, but this version of Frank Castle does not feel like he'd become that character. I get the movie’s idea that he's too detached to ever live a normal life and that violence is all he has left, but I feel like he’d run into the woods to mourn his family in peace instead of becoming a rampaging vigilante. I think the movie is better if you pretend it isn't a Punisher movie, and even then it's still not great.

Fantastic Four.title: Fantastic Four
Fantastic Four.blurb: A fun adaptation of the Fantastic Four’s origin story that’s light on the action but strong on the characterization and drama. There’s also a decent bit of humor, almost all of which comes from the character interactions.
Fantastic Four.review:
A fun adaptation of the Fantastic Four’s origin story that’s light on the action but strong on the characterization and drama. There’s also a decent bit of humor, almost all of which comes from the character interactions or tongue-in-cheek references to the powers the characters will get later.

The characters are all very well written, with everyone having well-defined personalities that organically clash with each other while never making any of the main four come across as assholes (aside from Johnny, and that’s on purpose). Making the characters old friends from university before splitting into two groups due to Reed and Sue breaking up is also brilliant, as it lends some believable tension to the drama. There aren’t just current grievances, but old grievances resurfacing as the characters are reminded of why they broke up in the first place.

While everyone is characterized pretty evenly, the heart of the film is 100% Ben Grimm. He’s the one with the most clear arc of learning to accept his condition, and the one who makes the big decision to sacrifice his normal life and return to being The Thing in order save Reed and Sue from Dr Doom. None of the other three feel left out, but Ben drives much of the emotional beats, even being the one to cause the car accident that makes the Fantastic Four heroes in the eyes of the public. The move is essentially “character drama with superpowers for good measure”, and Ben is the one hit by this the hardest.

Reed also ties into the superpowered drama theme well, as his keeping the team in isolation to try and cure their transformations matches the fact that he never acts, only plans. Reed finally acting is what makes Sue agree to be with him again, although Sue doesn’t get much of an arc of her own. She leaves Doom once she realizes he’s an asshole, but it’s still Reed that changes to make their relationship work. Johnny doesn’t change much either, but he has the most fun with his powers and acts as a foil to Ben and Reed, showing what they could be if they embraced their changes instead of rejecting them. He’s also pretty funny despite his hotheadedness, which helps his scenes stand out.

The film does have a sense of humor, both through Johnny’s devil-may-care attitude and the lighter nature of some of its character drama, like Sue turning invisible at inopportune times or Johnny teasing Ben. However, the drama still hits when it needs to, the biggest example being Johnny mocking his teammates on national television and the subsequent fight between him and Ben that culminates with both of them striking it out on their own.

Doom is the weakest part of the movie, yet he still works for what this movie is. He basically goes through Norman Osborn’s plotline from Spider-Man 1: he gets superpowers from a science experiment that causes his shareholders to oust him from his company, and then he kills them using said powers. This time it’s even more personal than in Spider-Man, since Reed was involved in Doom getting his powers instead of Spider-Man simply interfering after the fact. Doom mostly just slowly descends into power-hunger until he snaps at the end of the film, but his manipulative presence is still felt in nearly all the character conflicts between the Fantastic Four.

Doom isn’t a very comic accurate adaptation, but he still feels like an adaptation as opposed to a new character with the name slapped on. He slots into this movie perfectly as Reed’s old arch-rival, and I like how they gave him his suit’s energy beams from the comics by making him channel and shoot electric lasers. The core comic elements like Doom being Reed’s extremely rich and intelligent rival are still there, they just made him a businessman instead of a ruler to keep him physically close to Reed’s office. The rest of the movie also feels like it's adapting the comics as best it can, exemplified by the lighthearted tone punctuated by interpersonal drama that climaxes with a big fight. It’s a great origin for the Fantastic Four, which should help make Doom’s changes land better even for those who want an extremely comic accurate version.

The whole movie is a very fun time, and while it isn’t a masterpiece, it’s not nearly as bad as people say it is. Sure there aren’t a lot of superheroics, but the movie is so focused around what it is doing - the character drama enhanced by superpowers - that you only barely notice. It’s a well-rounded dramedy, and a great origin for the team on top of that, leaving the audience primed for more stories with this now-established cast.

Fantastic Four: Rise of the Silver Surfe.title: Fantastic Four: Rise of the Silver Surfer
Fantastic Four: Rise of the Silver Surfe.blurb: Some pretty stupid character conflicts mix with an interesting yet underbaked plot to create a movie that's lacking real substance. The Fantastic Four have no clue how to handle wedding conflicts, and their arcs have nothing to do with the plot at all.
Fantastic Four: Rise of the Silver Surfe.review:
Some pretty stupid character conflicts mix with an interesting yet underbaked plot to create a movie that's lacking real substance. The Fantastic Four are all acting like immature idiots because of changes brought about in their lives by Reed and Sue’s upcoming wedding, but it is unclear how much time has passed since the last movie so I have no idea how justified this infighting is. The movie probably should have opened with some superheroing before Reed and Sue’s wedding to establish the new status quo to understand why the shift in their lives matters. It would also help frame this movie’s threat as something new the FF don’t know how to handle (physically and emotionally), but we’ll get to that later. First, the character conflicts.

Sue wants to have a big wedding, but it keeps getting interrupted by superhero stuff, although we are only told that and not shown it. Reed wants to focus on the superhero stuff (again told and not shown), and when this movie’s big crisis pops up, he goes behind Sue's back to do it. So she's mad at him for lying to her and seemingly not caring about the wedding, and he’s apologetic that he can’t give her the wedding she wants, but obviously the world comes first. Sue comes across as self-absorbed here, even if Reed shouldn’t be lying to her about what he’s doing. Either way, he decides to stop being superheroes to raise a family with her, which Ben and Johnny overhear so now they're mad that they're getting left behind and aren’t being told about it, despite none of them giving Reed and Sue a chance to explain. Y’know, in the middle of the big crisis. On top of that, Johnny swaps powers with whoever he touches, so nobody wants to touch him and he feels lonely.

None of the characters handle any of these conflicts well at all. Johnny shows that he hasn't developed at all by getting passive-aggressively angry and acting on his own instead of following the team's plan, on top of his continuous showboating. Reed can't have an honest conversation with Sue about his priorities, so while Sue rightfully feels betrayed, she also can’t put the wants of others (read: the Earth) above her own. She also doesn't seem to like the big ceremony because of all the paparazzi, which makes it worse. Nobody handles these conflicts well at all, despite them learning to get along in the first movie. The conflicts are different this time around, but I feel like we needed a movie with the status quo of the FF getting along for these "we want different things out of life" conflicts to really work.

None of them get resolved well either. Sue just realizes at some point that she likes superheroing and decides to keep being a hero with Reed, even if she doesn't get her wedding or her nuclear family. The movie isn't really about this character arc, mind you, the change just kinda happens at the end of the movie, magically resolving everything. Having a brief, paparazzi-less wedding in China is a nice way to solve the conflict physically, but it still doesn’t feel earned.

Johnny's power switching is also never used for dramatic potential, just to make Johnny more upset and drive another rift between the team. There’s the very obvious opportunity to do something with Johnny being able to let Ben be himself again instead of The Thing while Johnny becomes a rock monster for a bit, but this is never even discussed, and Ben willingly swaps back to being The Thing after the initial exposure. Admittedly, that does mean that his character development from the first movie stuck, so maybe it’s a good thing that this isn’t mined for drama.

Secondly, the plot. Silver Surfer shows up from space and starts burrowing holes in the Earth so Galactus can show up and eat it. The FF have to work with the military, who have also hired a resurrected Dr Doom, to help save the Earth from Silver Surfer and Galactus. Doom's sole contribution is to antagonize Reed and then steal the Surfer's magic surfboard for one fight scene before getting knocked into the ocean. I get that they had to bring Doom back after the teaser last movie, but he really does not need to be here.

The Silver Surfer also doesn't really do a lot outside of burrowing holes and running away. The plot is mostly the FF running around trying to stop him, and then he gets like 10 lines of dialogue about how he serves Galactus to save his homeworld. Then he realizes that Sue reminds him of his wife so he kills Galactus. He doesn't even need a power-up or anything, he just kills the world eater. It nearly kills him too, sure, but it really comes across like he could have killed Galactus this whole time and just decided not to until now. I get that the idea is that the FF make him realize that all life is precious or whatever, but it doesn't tie into any of the other character conflicts in this movie so it feels like the writers pulling something out of their ass to end the conflict.

The movie kinda feels like an episode of a TV show, where there's a simple plot that vaguely ties into the character conflict of the week, which itself is only part of the character's development overall. As a movie though, it feels rushed and unfocused, leaving a story that doesn't do or say a lot. The special effects look cool though, and the actors are acting well, it's just that there is absolutely no substance to elevate these things beyond “A For Effort”.

Ghost Rider.title: Ghost Rider
Ghost Rider.blurb: An okay movie with one major high point: the Ghost Rider special effects look awesome. Even if the mouth is a little stiff, it feels like Ghost Rider is really there on set, which is pretty impressive. This was a big challenge, and they nailed it. That said, he's mostly wasted.
Ghost Rider.review:
An okay movie with one major high point: the Ghost Rider special effects look awesome. Even if the mouth is a little stiff, it feels like Ghost Rider is really there on set, which is pretty impressive. This was a big challenge, and they nailed it. That said, he's mostly wasted.

The fight scenes are underwhelming and really short, which is sad for four interesting villains. Big bad Blackheart’s three stooges all get defeated in their first fight, and only Air Demon (I forgot his name) causes any trouble. That said, there are two fights I like. The action scene where Ghost Rider runs from the cops while chasing Air Demon through the city is really fun and actually lengthy, and Ghost Rider riding on water and up the sides of buildings is awesome. The final fight against Darkheart isn't great, but I like that Johnny Blaze's backup plan is to let Blackheart absorb all 1000 souls from the contract and then kill them all with the Penance Stare. It's a fun use of power limitations that makes for a good "aha" moment to round out the movie's climax. The Penance Stare effects look good too, giving you just enough visual and audio information to understand that bad stuff is happening without actually showing you each atrocity.

As I said, though, the action scenes are relatively short, and the movie does not have a lot going on in terms of characters or plot. The best character is fortunately our protagonist Johnny Blaze. I like Blaze's motivation of trying to prove to himself that he's a good stunt rider and it isn't just Mephistopheles keeping him alive so he can use Blaze later. Blaze ending the movie by choosing to remain Ghost Rider so nobody else makes deals with the devil honestly works for me as the end to his arc. Nic Cage is weird and off-kilter, but it feels intentional for a man who has nothing but fame and is basically trying to kill himself to prove that he's earned that fame. I also like his intense research of Christian mythology, since it subtly gives him a lot more depth by characterizing him as intelligent and resourceful instead of just an idiot out to get himself killed. His arc isn’t great, but it's better than some of the Marvel movie protagonists I’ve seen so far.

The supporting characters don't have a lot going on though. Blaze's best friend basically disappears partway through the movie only to get killed by Blackheart. Blackheart is very one-note, although at least he seems like he's having fun. His three stooges have no personality, aside from Water Demon (I forgot his name) realizing that Blackheart is sending him on a suicide mission to stall Ghost Rider since he’s the last stooge standing. Roxanne feels like a love interest for the sake of being a love interest. Blaze left her behind at 17, and yet she finds him all these years later and reveals that she never lost her feelings for him. Honestly, if they had rekindled their friendship but not their romance after she realizes what Blaze has been going through, I would have liked her a lot better.

The one cool supporting cast member is the Caretaker, the guy who runs the graveyard. There’s clearly something weird about him since he knows so much about Ghost Rider, but the reveal that he's the previous Ghost Rider is still really cool. We don't know that Ghost Riders get extended lifespans, so the reveal isn’t obvious, but it makes so much about his character make sense. That and his demon horse is freaking awesome. He unfortunately just rides Blaze to the final fight but doesn’t have enough energy to participate, but his character still works regardless. He’s also played by Sam Elliot, the same guy who played General Ross in the 2003 Hulk movie, which is very funny.

The plot is straightforward: Blaze makes a deal with the devil, gets cursed to inherit sick-ass fire powers he can’t control, learns to harness those powers, and fights bad guys to become a hero. It mostly works though, or at least it would if I liked the characters better. The serviceable plot isn’t inherently a bad thing, but the lack of interesting characters and action scenes means that the movie is mostly this generic plot.

As for my other assorted thoughts; calling the devil Mephistopheles like in mythology instead of Mephisto like in the comics is a funny choice. Blaze dropping blood on the contract’s signature line after pricking his hand on the contract and Mephistopheles going "good enough" and the taking the contract before Blaze can read it is very devil-like, but it does absolve Blaze of some wrongdoing since he never agreed to sign the contract in the first place. The frequent one-liners during fight scenes are also out of place since they clash so heavily with the rest of the film's serious tone. It's still an okay movie, but it needs a more well-rounded cast and more Ghost Rider.

Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance.title: Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance
Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance.blurb: A big dumb action movie with the world's worst camera work of all time. It is so shaky man. The characters are very one-note and the plot has just enough going on to be interesting, but the action is on-point. It's bombastic, over-the-top, and frankly just delightful to watch.
Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance.review:
A big dumb action movie with the world's worst camera work of all time. It is so shaky man. The characters are very one-note and the plot has just enough going on to be interesting, but the action is on-point. It's bombastic, over-the-top, and frankly just delightful to watch. Ghost Rider possesses a giant mining machine and uses it to maul people. He tanks a bunker buster. Some guy gets the power to disintegrate anything he touches and disintegrates all the food he tries to eat, like a fucked up version of King Midas. Ghost Rider pisses fire like a flame-thrower. A 12-year-old breathes fire on Nic Cage to turn him back into Ghost Rider. It's awesome.

Ghost Rider also looks very good in this movie, with him and his jacket looking all grimy and burnt up. I don't think I like it as much as the more clean version from the last movie, but his fire does turn to smoke when he gets injured in this one which is a really cool touch. The actors are also having the time of their lives just hamming it up, especially Nic Cage as Johnny Blaze and Ciaran Hinds as Roarke. Idris Elba is also in this movie, which surprised me, although he’s playing his role straight. But the hammy acting from our main hero and villain matches the action scenes perfectly.

The plot isn't super interesting, but at least there's enough going on to keep you invested. Between Ghost Rider tracking down Danny Ketch, Danny trying to escape Roarke's minions, and then the deceptive safety of the sanctuary, the plot actually has some twists and turns. It's nothing to write home about, but I think it is more involved than the first film. The best part is when Danny gives Johnny Blaze his Ghost Rider powers back, delivering on the bond they built up (even if it was built up very quickly) and making use of the fact that Danny does have Roarke's powers. It's awesome, even if you know it's coming. The special effects help too, which is really most of the movie. It's like 75% Ghost Rider action scenes, and they really do make the film. It's highly entertaining watching everything explode and just be generally over-the-top, even if there isn't much to write home about in terms of storytelling.

This movie does make some weird changes from the first one. It makes Blaze way more complicit in signing Mephistopholes' contract, with him smashing a beer bottle to generate the blood instead of accidentally pricking his hand. They also changed Mephistopholes' name to Roarke for some reason, which is just weird. I don't know why they did this. None of these changes hurt the movie any, and I think the first helps the film work, but why did they change Mephistopholes' name, and why did they decide not to do Mephisto again? Why???

I do think this movie is better standalone than as a sequel, because the tone is so different and they're really unrelated plotwise. We get a recap of Blaze's backstory in this cool and slightly goofy mural sequence, so you don't even need to watch the first one. These movies are similar in rank, but I would not recommend them to the same people, or for the same purposes. This movie is an unhinged action flick, while the first is a slow character drama. Both do have cool flaming skull people though, so they get bonus points for that.

Punisher: War Zone.title: Punisher: War Zone
Punisher: War Zone.blurb: A slightly gory action movie that gets right into the action and doesn't slow down. The characters and plot aren't very deep, but they don't need to be. This movie is all about the larger-than-life personalities and intense gun violence, and it absolutely works.
Punisher: War Zone.review:
A slightly gory action movie that gets right into the action and doesn't slow down. The characters and plot aren't very deep, but they don't need to be. This movie is all about the larger-than-life personalities and intense gun violence, and it absolutely works. The main villain Jigsaw and his psychopathic brother are unhinged delights to watch as they murder anyone who crosses Jigsaw even slightly. His main goal is to extort a widow and her daughter for money all out of petty revenge because her husband was a mole in his organization. Punisher, by contrast, has an intense, silent fury within him that almost never breaks, making him perfect for the crazy action scenes where he mows down highly expressive villains. Shoutout to the guys on meth who do backflips; they're just minor villains but they're very fun. I don't quite have the words to describe the action, but it's highly entertaining. It's very kinetic, with characters constantly on the move and using the environment to their advantage. Punisher is almost always on top, but it's fun to see what explosive weapon he pulls out next. Things explode all the time, including people's heads, but the gore is never too much, being just enough to sell you on the intense violence. The film is action almost all the way through, and it almost always hits.

The movie is not a sequel to the previous Punisher movie, and is in fact a reboot. If you asked me which Marvel character would get a theatrical reboot first, my guess would not have been the Punisher, but here we are. In contrast to the first film being an origin story, this film assumes you already know Punisher's origin and launches right into the action. We get a brief flashback to Frank cradling his dead family and some expository dialogue from some cops, but that's it. And it's really all you need, because Punisher’s origin is important to the film but doesn’t need the detail to get the gist of “likes kids, hates mobsters”. I like this version a lot better.

Punisher himself is a decent lead. I like how warmly he treats the little girl and how far he goes to save them. It really makes it feel like Punisher isn't just doing this to kill criminals, but to ensure that nobody suffers what he suffered. It makes him a lot more sympathetic, which a guy like Punisher really needs to lead a story. He's intense when he needs it, but it's these quiet moments with the girl and her mom that really make you root for him. The mom is boring, but I like how aware her daughter is of people. She knows Punisher is nice immediately upon meeting him, and her stepping outside to prevent her mom from grappling with whether or not to kill Punisher any more than she has to is really perceptive and brave of her. Based 6-year-old. Despite not being super interesting characters, you care about them just enough to stay invested in the fight scenes for the plot as much as the action, which is really all they needed to do.

Punisher’s guy in the chair Micro is a good if minor addition. I like how willing he is to sacrifice himself to save people when it comes down to it, despite him not being in the field most of the time. There's also the ex-con that Micro takes in and sends to watch over the girl and widow while Punisher murders Jigsaw’s men. There's some hints that he might be secretly working for Jigsaw, but I like that they don’t do that. He did actually repent, and does everything he can to buy time for the girls to escape. It's not enough to matter, but I'm happy he's not evil. It helps land the idea that rehabilitation can work on criminals, but people like Jigsaw are too far gone and they’re the reason the Punisher exists.

The plot is also decent enough. It’s constantly moving forward, and actions Punisher and Jigsaw take constantly play into the next scene. This is best shown when the FBI agent recruits the Russian guys to attack Jigsaw because Jigsaw threw their kid to the cops earlier in the film. The cops in this movie are not as fleshed out as they could be, but they help sell the idea that Punisher lives in the real world and not fantasy murder-land. Most of the cops like him, and the one requisite hater comes around in the end, which is definitely a decision.

I understand why cops are okay with Punisher murdering people like Jigsaw, but because we never see where Punisher draws the line between people who can be rehabilitated and those who can’t, it definitely comes across like the cops are okay with murder. The movie ends with a cop talking about how he doesn’t support the death penalty when he’s accosted by a homeless man trying to mug him, and Punisher has to save him. This scene is played for a joke in an otherwise very serious movie. It leans the movie too strongly into justifying extralegal murder for me, since the rest of the villains in the film are psycho murderers and meth dealers. The murder comes with the territory of the Punisher, and I can mostly ignore it when the bad guys are as sadistic as Jigsaw, but that last scene rubs me the wrong way.

Implicit advocacy for vigilante murder aside, it's a surprisingly solid action movie all the way through, with enough plot and characters to keep you invested in the awesome action. If you don’t care about the moral politics, you’ll probably have a blast hopping from one action setpiece to the next.

Gaslight District Pilot.title: Gaslight District Pilot
Gaslight District Pilot.blurb: An eclectic, fast-paced pilot that really keeps you on your toes. The stylization and animation is immaculate, with everything from the title card to the action scenes to the character design having such strong visual flair that it sucks you right into the win. Despite not being a full series, I’d recommend this pilot for the animation alone.
Gaslight District Pilot.review:
An eclectic, fast-paced pilot that really keeps you on your toes. It's almost too fast-paced though, with it hard to follow all the details of the scenes. The general plot is easy enough to understand, but the details of the character actions can definitely get lost. On the other hand, it also gives the pilot its own vibe, that of a world that moves too fast for its own good where nobody ever slows down to think, which is ironic given that everyone in the world is immortal. The stylization and animation is immaculate, with everything from the title card to the action scenes to the character design having such strong visual flair that it sucks you right into the win. Despite not being a full series, I’d recommend this pilot for the animation alone.

The plot itself is also interesting, and is sure to offer up lots of twists and turns as it goes. Making the main character Mel the only vulnerable person in the world is a good choice that should add a lot of tension to the series since she’s actually in danger. The relationship between her and her dad is really good and grounds you in their batshit insane world. I'm sure the angels and human egg will have fascinating lore revealed about them, and the dual cliffhanger of Mel’s plan failing and someone fishing up Jack to unveil her secret identity has me excited for future episodes. I want Mel to have a fulfilling character arc, whether that means destroying the world or upholding it, which is a strong start to a show.

Some other fun details I like: Breadhead being made of actual bread somehow; people can’t die so they’re trapped at the bottom of the ocean, which is horrifying; the shot of Ken eating that Virtue’s brain goes crazy hard; the opening and closing narration actually work to establish the tone going forward and aren’t boring; the cliffhanger being Mel’s lie about the egg being exposed and not her identity is a good threat while still keeping the tension of her secret identity; the Virtues look like Ultrakill enemies, which isn’t really a plus but it is funny since they’re both angels. It's a solid pilot, and if the rest of the series follows suit, it'll be another banger for GLITCH.

Knights of Guinevere Pilot.title: Knights of Guinevere Pilot
Knights of Guinevere Pilot.blurb: Another intriguing pilot from GLITCH that takes itself more seriously than its other works, presenting a run-down dystopia that has lost almost all sense of joy and whimsy. The story seems to be about rediscovering the whimsy in the ashes, but only time will tell.
Knights of Guinevere Pilot.review:
Another intriguing pilot from GLITCH. This one takes itself way more seriously than Amazing Digital Circus or Gaslight District, presenting a run-down dystopia that has lost almost all sense of joy and whimsy. The story seems to be about rediscovering the whimsy in the ashes given the magic Princess Guinevere android Frankie and Andi find in the trash, but only time will tell.

The pilot just drops you into the world with little explanation, and I wish we knew more about the general setting to really understand our protagonists’ situation. Stuff like Guinevere's origins and deal is obviously intended to be a mystery, but I would love to know how much of the world is poor, how much is controlled by the evil princess lady, how much is there to actually salvage, stuff like that.

I do really like our main characters and how they contrast personality-wise, yet still feel like they’d be friends. Their character designs are really solid and convey their personalities while giving them unique silhouettes, which is always a good thing. The old man that Frankie worked for seemed like a cool boss for the situation he’s in, and I’m curious to see how strong the old Guinevere android is, both in terms of physical strength and in terms of how many secrets she knows about the world.

As it stands, I'm interested to see where the show goes, as there's clearly a lot of mysteries and worldbuilding planned and I know that Dana Terrace knows what she’s doing. However, I'm not fully invested at this point, and I think that is due to the lack of understanding about the basic premises of the setting. Lots of people seem excited, though, so the dystopian mystery may just not be my thing. The animation is really pretty and well-done, and I'm curious to see where the story goes, but it didn’t hook me the way it did a lot of other people.

Super Mario Bros Movie.title: Super Mario Bros Movie
Super Mario Bros Movie.blurb: An okay adventure movie that is nonetheless a delightful adaptation of the Mario games. It is clear that the people making this movie love the games, as they crammed in so many fun details and references that help make the world feel alive. If you like Mario, I highly recommend this movie, but if you don’t, you can probably skip it.
Super Mario Bros Movie.review:
An okay adventure movie that is nonetheless a delightful adaptation of the Mario games. It is clear that the people making this movie love the games, as they crammed in so many fun details and references that help make the world feel alive. There's a fun collection of enemies serving as the wildlife, like the plants with long thorny legs from New Super Mario Bros; all kinds of floating blocks that match the vibe of the Mario levels; almost all of the action scenes taking place in 2D like Mario parkouring through NY, the training course, and the battle against Donkey Kong; the frequent use of Mario songs as background music; the karts being game-accurate; and the Banzai Bill blowing up Peach's Castle being a Smash Melee reference.

Opening with Mario and Luigi in their classic Italian accents for the commercial is a great touch, as it proves that Chris Pratt (and Charlie Day) can do the Mario voice, but are using more normal voices for the movie so you can actually understand what they're saying. All of the voice actors do a pretty good job - you forget that Chris Pratt of all people is voicing Mario - which is impressive considering nearly every character in the film has a famous voice.

The whole movie is gorgeous, having fluid and expressive animation that manages to make background enemies like Bloopers look cute. The fight scenes are easy to follow despite all the action going on, which makes them a delight to watch. The backgrounds are beautiful, especially the landscape shots depicting the various kingdoms. It helps make the movie a joy to watch, especially since the plot and characters are very simple.

The plot only just has enough going on to be interesting, but it helps that things never slow down. Mario's home life sucks, so he goes to the Mushroom Kingdom, trains, fights Donkey Kong, has the big race on Rainbow Road, and then fights Bowser in the climax. The movie does have problems of plot elements just randomly being introduced, mainly all the various power-ups, The only one that is ever meaningfully used twice is the Mini Mushroom that is used to imprison Bowser at the end, while the Super Mushroom and Fire Flower don’t do anything meaningful in their second appearance aside from spicing up the action a bit. I wish the Tanooki got foreshadowed at least, because letting Mario fly feels like an asspull. The climax also basically happens because Bowser randomly learns Mario’s location through unexplained means, and the Banzai Bill comes out of nowhere. It blowing up the Pipe and sending everybody back to Earth is cool, though.

As for the characters, Mario’s character arc of fulfilling his potential and getting people to like him is simple, yet effective. I like that Luigi gets the Super Star at the same time as Mario since they are the Mario Brothers, and it helps complete his little character arc of becoming more brave, even if he does spend most of the movie as a male damsel in distress. Peach is great in this movie, having the qualities of a strong ruler that cares for their people and puts themself in harm’s way to help them, which is nice because it's like she's paying the Toads back for raising her. I like that she is canonically one of, if not the only, human in the Mushroom Kingdom, giving a reason for her to implicitly feel connected to Mario. Bowser is fun in this movie, being scary while occasionally funny with how dorky he is about Peach. It's a mostly serious Bowser, but they are planting the seeds for him to be a funnier character later. The funniest part of this movie is that nihilist Luma though, holy shit. The movie has a bunch of jokes, but almost none of them outside the Luma gave me anything more than a smirk.

It really is just an okay movie, but has a clear passion for Mario as a franchise. If you like Mario, I highly recommend this movie just because of how much it loves the source material, but if you don’t, you can probably skip it.

Iron Man.title: Iron Man
Iron Man.blurb: A banger movie that holds up really well. As the first movie in the MCU, it feels really standalone, which is perfect for an introduction film. It’s absolutely character-focused, being based around Tony’s character arc, yet that doesn’t stop the plot from being engaging, the action from being thrilling, and the character banter from being hilarious.
Iron Man.review:
A banger movie that holds up really well. As the first movie in the MCU, it feels really standalone, which is perfect for an introduction film. You feel like there is sequel potential, as opposed to this just being half of a movie. It also helps that the movie is really good, which makes you want to see that potential fulfilled. It’s absolutely character-focused, being based around Tony’s character arc, yet that doesn’t stop the plot from being engaging, the action from being thrilling, and the character banter from being hilarious.

The film hits the ground running, immediately establishing Tony’s character as a charismatic arms dealer asshole before blowing him up with his own missile. The 36 hours earlier sequence serves to establish Tony’s daily life and supporting cast - Pepper, Rhodey, and Obadiah Stane - before we spend the next chunk of the movie with Tony by himself in a cave with Yinsen and a box of scraps. It’s a really good chunk of movie too, as we slowly see Tony come to rely on someone else (Yinsen) and actually make friends with them. Tony asking Yinsen about his family is the first time he ever shows an interest in anybody else for something other than their body, and it starts his transition towards becoming a hero. Yinsen sacrificing himself seals the deal, leaving Tony as the lone survivor of a terrorist attack that used his own weapons. This opening act is incredibly important, showing us Tony’s normal life of arrogant, dismissive excess before taking that all away and forcing him to live in the cruel reality that he’s creating.

Despite all that, Tony doesn’t completely transform into a selfless guy, which is honestly more realistic than if he had. He wants to rid the world of his weapons, but it’s just as much because he realizes that the weapons can hurt him versus him realizing that they are hurting other people. His solution is to tank his company, hurting all the employees that rely on him for income (although it’s implied that he will pivot to energy and the like since he does have non-weapons divisions, so the employees aren’t completely screwed), and give himself the ultimate weapon: flying power armor. He refuses to share this with anyone else for obvious reasons (it's even more dangerous than the missiles), but it means that he and he alone has ultimate power. He doesn’t deal weapons anymore, but he still controls the war.

Even without giving up that power, it’s clear that Tony is becoming a better person and shutting down his weapons division isn’t just him soothing his ego. He goes out of his way to save refugees in Afghanistan before destroying the missiles, and he comes to rely on Pepper more instead of just blowing her off. Maybe he hasn’t earned her help considering how he treats her, but it shows he trusts her, which is enough growth for someone who was originally completely self-absorbed. He also stops trying to sleep with her when she expresses that she’s uncomfortable with it, which is honestly the bare minimum but still feels like a big deal for a playboy who’s used to sleeping with whoever he wants.

Across from Tony, Obadiah is a really fun villain. He comes across at first like he’s just trying to keep the business running and simply doesn’t care about the casualties of war like Tony, which makes the reveal that he tried to kill Tony hit really hard. Kicking Tony out to sell weapons to terrorists would be one thing, but trying to kill Tony even before Tony shuts down the weapons division kicks him into full on villain territory. The seeds are planted almost immediately with Obadiah having taken over the company after Howard’s death and then Tony coming back and taking things in his own direction, so of course Obadaiah wants him gone. The Iron Monger suit is also really cool, absolutely looking like a version of the Iron Man armor made by someone who wants a hulking weapon and not a practical piece of gear.

Speaking of Tony’s armor, it looks really good, and nothing shows this more than the suit-up sequences. You believe that this is a thing made of metal with mechanical parts that precisely fit together with how beautifully detailed the first big suit-up scene is. It’s honestly one of my favorites in the movie from a purely visual standpoint. The suit is just sci-fi tech magic at the end of the day, but the movie makes you feel like the Iron Man suit is a machine that Tony really built. Him flight-testing and fucking up repeatedly certainly helps, as does Tony’s other pieces of sci-fi bullshit like semi-autonomous robots that respond to voice and interactive holograms that help him build his suit. It makes the armor seem more plausible because this other future-tech already casually exists. And yet Obadaiah still rides a Segway because this movie was made in 2008. Love it.

As opposed to Tony and Obadiah, Pepper and Rhodey aren’t really fleshed out, especially Rhodey. They both have Tony’s back when it counts, but they’re primarily there to show Tony’s character and the consequences of him making the power armor. That said, I actually really like Pepper’s involvement in the movie’s climax, and it pretty much saves her character for me. The fight between Tony and Obadaiah in their armors is very visceral as both suits get ripped to shreds, but Pepper’s involvement elevates this fight to great. It solves the age-old problem of the supporting cast being worthless in the MCU’s first outing, and Tony trusting Pepper to destroy Obadiah using a beam that might kill him too is the natural endpoint of his character arc in this movie. She’s still there to highlight Tony’s arc, but it still has to be her doing it, and the movie would not work nearly as well if Tony defeats Obadiah by himself.

Of course, speaking of the end, the last minute change to have Tony reveal himself to be Iron Man is perfect. Aside from the fact that it irreversibly changed the MCU, I can’t really imagine this movie ending any other way. Tony is too egotistical to stay hidden, but it also hammers home that he is no longer dealing weapons and is committed to stopping them. It’s not some guy who destroyed those weapons and stopped those terrorists, it was him. He’s a super hero now, if an egotistical one, and he’s going to continue to trust everyone to do right by him as he does right by them.

That’s my review of the movie as a standalone, but I would be remiss to not talk about the parts that do set up the future MCU. That said, there aren’t a lot, with only Phil Coulson’s SHIELD references and Nick Fury’s post-credits cameo hinting at a wider world. Even then, SHIELD’s acronym isn’t established and Fury invites Tony to the Avengers Initiative instead of the actual Avengers, implying that the Avengers don’t exist yet. Tony has drawn the attention of something bigger, but this isn’t a massive superhero world yet: anything that exists is in the shadows. Coulson is mostly there just to set up SHIELD, but he does have a very minor role in the climax and then gives Tony his alibi at the end (even if Tony doesn’t use it), so he avoids being a character that’s purely there for set-up. The post-credits scene is a novel idea, although I’m surprised it's at the end of the normal credits and not the fancy credits. You’d think Marvel would want it earlier so people will actually see it, but I guess not.

Iron Man is a perfect start to the MCU, establishing a grounded world that still has room for some sci-fi bullshit like the Jarvis AI, paving the way for more fantastical stuff like the Super Soldier Serum, Extremis, and Thor. It’s also almost perfect as a self-contained movie about Tony turning from an amoral guy who sells weapons into one who will put himself in great harm to stop weapons from being used. Does he do this by making a bigger weapon? Yes. Does it show how he’s putting his talents and privilege towards a better cause? Also yes. I don’t know if it's the perfect superhero movie, but it’s the perfect start for the MCU. I really have no complaints.

Super Mario Galaxy Movie.title: Super Mario Galaxy Movie
Super Mario Galaxy Movie.blurb: A fun movie with no substance. The film is still visually gorgeous, with beautiful landscape shots and bustling travel hubs that feel lived in. However, there are no character arcs and a disconnected plot, so the film is nothing but action setpiece after action setpiece.
Super Mario Galaxy Movie.review:
A fun movie with no substance. The film is still visually gorgeous, with beautiful landscape shots and bustling travel hubs that feel lived in. They got a bunch of different Mario species to serve as aliens, and it makes the Gateway Galaxy feel diverse and the universe feel vast. The action scenes are also well choreographed, with each one being easy to follow while still intense and having a good flow of back-and-forth between our heroes and villains that keeps you guessing. I also like that nearly all the fights are in 3D this time because it's the Mario Galaxy movie and Galaxy is in 3D, versus the 2D fights from the first film. The only exception is the awesome Bowser bossfight recreation from Super Mario Bros for the NES.

The film is really all over the place though, and nowhere is this shown better than the power-ups. Every power in the movie is used once, which is really disappointing because it means we have no idea what our heroes can do in any battle, including the final one. Seriously, we get three new power-ups at once for the finale and then a fourth to finish it off. Yoshi's power-up works because it's a gag, but the Red Star that lets Mario fly does literally the exact same thing as the Tanooki Suit from the first movie, complete with the big spinning attack. I get that the Red Star is a Galaxy reference, but the power-up still comes out of nowhere when it just lets Mario do something we already have a power-up for.

Don't get me wrong, the choreography is good for each power once you know what they do, but for someone who doesn't, they must be incredibly confusing. I think the idea is that you're getting new powers like in a video game, but you still gotta do each power twice: one introduction and then one return at a crucial moment. I will add that Bowser Jr's paint power means that anything he draws up is fair game, including Mr Game & Watch. The random powers do give the universe a sense of wonder since you never know what’s coming next, but they are a mess in terms of plot structure.

The rest of the movie is structured the same way, introducing new characters and then discarding them. Again, they do help the world feel expansive but also means that nothing connects. Queen Bee and the T-Rex show up once and then never again, and the same goes for Wart and the Ninjis despite Wart being plot relevant. The Lumas do get their big moment at the end, and I do like that we get several Bowser Jr fights that each up the ante, but aside from that the most recurring character is Star Fox of all people. It's weird that we have Star Fox in a supporting role in the Mario movie, but if you don't know that he's Not A Mario Character, he works well enough as washed-down Han Solo. The gag where he recounts his backstory at lightning speed in a different artstyle is funny, especially because said backstory is totally irrelevant. Rosalina is also reduced to a MacGuffin in this movie, which is really funny because she has so much power and then spends it all in a cage.

I mentioned that the film has no substance, and aside from the film being scattershot, that's mostly because the only person with a character arc is Bowser. Plus, his arc is deciding to stay evil to be with his kid, which means he ends this movie where he started the last movie except less alone. I actually like this decision and respect them for keeping Bowser evil to be a good dad, especially because it would have felt weird if he betrayed Bowser Jr for the Mario Bros after being imprisoned by them for years, but literally nobody else changes in this movie. It’s just action setpiece after action setpiece, more like a TV show with 10 10-minute episodes than a movie. Which is fine - the characters are fun as is - but there's less to analyze here for people looking for something other than Mario references.

I do think this film does some things better than the first movie though. The film still clearly loves its source material (there are so many Galaxy references in this movie), and the fight scenes are better. The soundtrack is also banging, replacing all the pop songs with Mario music. Bowser coming back as Dry Bowser is awesome, because you know it's coming due to the Koopa Getting Melted Into Dry Bones gags, but Mario and Peach still clearly feel awful that they probably killed him. It’s probably the only moment of any actual emotion or plot payoff in the whole movie.

That said, I do wish the film cut back on undercutting its hype moments with gags though. They aren't even emotional moments that might make you feel sad, it's the film actively stopping its characters from aurafarming to make jokes, over and over again, which is so bizarre. The final battle plays itself straight at least, and it is the best part of the movie.

Overall, I think Galaxy is more fun than the first film, but less well put together from a writing standpoint. If you liked the first one, you'll probably like this one, and if you didn't like the first one, you probably won't like this one.

Iron Man 2.title: Iron Man 2
Iron Man 2.blurb: A downgrade from the first movie for sure, but still good in its own right. The film’s biggest flaw is how disjointed stuff feels while watching. There are three main plots that barely interact, as they mostly happen in parallel, but they come together in the end for an explosive and mostly thematically coherent finale.
Iron Man 2.review:
A downgrade from the first movie for sure, but still good in its own right. The film’s biggest flaw is how disjointed stuff feels while watching. There are three main plots: Tony self-destructing due to his Arc Reactor killing him slowly; Justin Hammer recruiting supervillain Ivan Vanko to recreate the Iron Man armor; and the military trying to prove that Tony is too irresponsible to have the armor and that he should give it to the military. The three storylines barely interact, as they mostly happen in parallel, but they come together in the end for an explosive and mostly thematically coherent finale.

Vanko hacks the military drones to prove that the military shouldn’t have them and Tony comes out of his funk to save the city to prove that he should have them. The movie ends with Rhodey getting the War Machine armor because he is trustworthy, giving the military one suit and setting the baseline for who can and can’t use the armor. This does align with Tony’s arc of facing consequences for being an asshole, with him only getting his act together right before the climax so he can save New York, so the themes do come together even if Vanko’s takeover makes things muddy. That said, the three arcs are not treated equally by the film at all in terms of characters or screen-time.

Of the three arcs, Tony’s Self-Destruct arc is my favorite, as you can really see all the signs that he knows he’s dying. He starts doing stupid shit like driving a racecar with no practice, and he starts giving his stuff away, including promoting Pepper to the head of his company. She’s qualified in theory, but it really comes across like Tony is assuring that she and the people under him are well off when he dies of heart poisoning. His self-destructing primarily tarnishes his reputation, because the whole movie is about whether Tony is responsible enough to have the suit. That said, Rhodey is the one who picks the fight with him at his birthday party when he hasn’t hurt anybody yet, so Rhodey is kinda responsible for that one.

Speaking of Rhodey, he’s interesting in this movie. He’s the heart of the Military Arc, but that arc has so little happening that it almost doesn’t matter. He still gets to do more than in the last film, being constantly torn between being Tony’s friend and being a military colonel. It’s an interesting dynamic as those two desires are clearly at odds, but we never see much of his inner turmoil, partially because the military plot is so tertiary to everything else. It gets hijacked by Vanko in the last act when he takes control of the drones, so Rhodey’s arc is solved by Tony’s and the military’s goals briefly aligning.

The third plot is the Vanko/Hammer Arc, which is mostly interesting but loses its luster because it doesn’t interact with Tony as much as it should. After the first Tony/Vanko fight on the racetrack, they don’t interact with Tony until the finale. The arc is carried by Vanko, who is basically a scheming mastermind. I love how smart, driven, and manipulative he is, willing to hurt who knows how many people just to kill Tony, even if it isn’t Tony’s fault at all. He contrasts nicely to Hammer, who has no motivation beyond getting rich and recognized. I do like Hammer, who is Tony’s charismatic playboy side but evil and if nobody liked him. He’s definitely the weaker of the two villains, but he makes Tony look better and Vanko look more intimidating by comparison.

SHIELD and Fury are also here a little bit. Coulson does almost nothing, but I like that Fury’s role is to just point Tony in the right direction and let him figure out the rest. Black Widow is cool here, especially as we slowly learn that she’s not just a secretary. She does get to kick ass, and her ass-kicking scene is cool, but she never overshadows the Tony/Rhodey dynamic at the heart of the film. They’re a bit distracting since Fury just shows up half-way into the movie, but I think their role is fine overall.

Pepper has a much less prominent role in this movie, becoming CEO of Stark Industries and then doing that in the background while Tony self-destructs. She still works, but Rhodey is the supporting cast member with the spotlight this time. I do like her taking charge of the situation when Vanko attacks Stark Expo though.

Despite the movie’s themes and plots being held together by string and dreams, there are some things I really liked: this movie is funny, way funnier than the first one; the scene where Tony watches his dad record the Expo and then finds the new element in the blueprints is heartwarming and awesome at once; the final fight in the biodome is really good, showing off Tony’s and Rhodey’s powers and teamwork, complete with a callback to earlier in the film; Vanko’s scene in prison where he tells Tony that he will destroy Tony’s legacy is chilling; the whole Monaco scene is excellent, and the suitcase armor is incredibly cool; Tony’s favor he wants from Fury being that the senator who hates him has to award him the medal is very funny.

It’s definitely not as good as the first movie and has a lot of flaws, but I still like Iron Man 2. It was a fun watch all the way through, and the movie does fit together if you think about it really hard. There’s a few bits to set up future MCU projects, namely Captain America’s shield and the Thor post-credits scene, but they’re actually less intrusive than the first movie’s. SHIELD was established before, so of course they’re in this movie too. It’s a nice expansion of the world and continuation of Tony’s development into being a good person, even if it can’t match the highs of the first movie.

The Incredible Hulk.title: The Incredible Hulk
The Incredible Hulk.blurb: This movie assumes you’ve already seen Hulk (2003), showing us the Hulk transformation in the opening credits and starting with Banner in hiding after running for years. Unfortunately, this movie then proceeds to do the exact same plot as Hulk (2003) but with worse characters and worse CGI. To refresh, the plot of Hulk (2003) is also not very good.
The Incredible Hulk.review:
This movie assumes you’ve already seen Hulk (2003), showing us the Hulk transformation in the opening credits and starting with Banner in hiding after running for years. Unfortunately, this movie then proceeds to do the exact same plot as Hulk (2003) but with worse characters and worse CGI. To refresh, the plot of Hulk (2003) is also not very good.

Banner peaks in the opening act when he tries to save that lady and we see both his heroism and resourcefulness, but then he spends the rest of the movie just trying to cure himself. There's no conflict between him and Betty, he doesn't try to hide anymore so there’s no tension there, and Bruce seems to have no opinions of General Ross at all. Bruce jumping down to stop Blonsky and save New York is heroic, but there's just nothing else going on under the hood. Betty is similarly boring, being willing to drop everything just to help Bruce. Again, it’s heroic, especially because she has to stand up to her father, but she has no arc at all. Also Liv Tyler really sounds like she needs an inhaler. Get this woman some oxygen.

As for our villains, Ross is a lying, evil asshole with no redeeming qualities. He kind of had a point in the 2003 movie since the Hulk is such an unknown factor, but here he’s just evil because he;s trying to make a weapon and still only cares about capturing Hulk to make said weapon. He lies to Bruce about it to create Hulk in the first place, is too stupid to stop putting his men in danger when they clearly can't do anything, and is the reason Bruce turns into the Hulk every single time. The only exception is the Blonsky fight at the end, which is also his fault because trying to recreate the Hulk is what turned Blonsky into Abomination in the first place. Blonsky at least starts interesting as a guy who stands up to authority and seems to want to stop Hulk for national security reasons instead of bioweapon reasons, but then he just turns into a revenge-driven psycho with no morals.

So all the characters suck, and the plot is only slightly better. I do like that it's about Bruce trying to find a cure as he dodges the military. That said, it's really silly in hindsight because we know he can't find a cure: he has to be in Avengers. Even aside from that, he's too big of a comic character to only have one movie. Maybe if this was an indie film I'd be more invested in the plot, but I know he’ll never cure himself, and the movie opens by showing that Bruce knows how to survive on his own, so I'm not invested in anything at all because there is literally no tension. There is no moral or message here except that Ross is a fucking idiot, which I knew from the half-hour mark.

Now you may be thinking that a movie with no message and boring characters can be good if the action is good. And you’d be correct, except the action sucks. I hate Hulk’s design in this movie - I think it’s the horizontal lines on his chest and washed out color - and Abomination isn’t much better. The fights look like video game cutscenes, and the choreography isn’t creative or character-driven. Even Hulk (2003) had interesting powers for the villain despite them being underutilized.

In further contrast to the 2003 movie, there is no intrusive split-screen. Honestly thank god, but also, this movie is so fucking boring that I think the split-screen would have helped. At least the 2003 movie is memorable because of it, even if it makes the movie a headache to watch. This movie has nothing memorable at all.

There are a few references to the wider MCU, namely that Ross was trying to recreate the Super Soldier Serum, which really means nothing if you haven't seen Captain America yet. Ross is also able to access SHIELD databases somehow, and then Tony Stark shows up to recruit Ross of all people to the Avengers. For reasons??? Honestly, Blonsky having a working Super Soldier Serum is a cool idea since it's basically the bioweapon Ross wanted, but no he's too stupid to stop there and really really needs another Hulk. And of course a Super Soldier can’t fight the Hulk so Blonsky does nothing with it anyways. That’s truly the movie in a nutshell: a remake of an older project that does absolutely everything worse.

Captain America: The First Avenger.title: Captain America: The First Avenger
Captain America: The First Avenger.blurb: A decent action movie with a very strong focus on what type of person it takes to become a symbol of hope and justice. The movie spends a lot of time hammering in who Steve Rogers is before he becomes Captain America, and it pretty much works as the heart of the film. A hero isn't someone strong, but someone who does the right thing regardless of how strong they are.
Captain America: The First Avenger.review:
A decent action movie with a very strong focus on what type of person it takes to become a symbol of hope and justice. The movie spends a lot of time hammering in who Steve Rogers is before he becomes Captain America, and it pretty much works as the heart of the film. It both shows that Steve is proving himself in-universe and shows the audience why this is the guy who becomes Captain America. A hero isn't someone strong, but someone who does the right thing regardless of how strong they are.

That sense of responsibility and justice is exactly why Steve has to sacrifice himself at the end, and it’s exactly why Peggy Carter is so drawn to him even before Steve becomes Captain America. I like that about their romance, that despite each other finding the other hot, they’re really drawn together by how much they admire each other in terms of personality. Like Peggy says, they both understand what it’s like to have doors barred because of what they are, with only their personalities allowing them to get where they are. The only part of the romance arc I don’t like is the scene where Cap gets sexually assaulted by one of the other women in the office is stupid. Steve is clearly not into it, and of course Peggy freaks out about it because why wouldn't a man be into it, and then she gets over it they just resume their slow-burn romance like nothing happened. I don’t like it. That said, Cap crashing into the ocean while on call with Peggy is appropriately tragic, and it doesn’t work if you don’t believe that Steve and Peggy like each other.

As for the rest of the supporting cast, they’re just okay. Howard Stark is funny without taking away from the seriousness of the movie, and serves well as the military’s requisite genius. Bucky is underutilized though, basically disappearing for half the movie until he gets saved by Steve and then dies two scenes later. He's the reason why Cap jumps into the field, but he almost has a bigger impact in the first half of the movie than the second, which is funny. It feels like they're setting up Winter Soldier as opposed to establishing him as Cap's partner, which is both cool in hindsight and disappointing for this movie as a standalone.

I do like Red Skull. He's very threatening and the Red Skull makeup looks very good. He doesn't have a lot going on, but I do like him as Evil Captain America. Not in that he's Captain Nazi, but in the sense that he believes the power makes him great while Steve knows that he has the power because he's great. I do like that he writes the name of each city on his super bombs, it's very goofy in a petty, self-obsessed way.

The plot is fun, if not very deep. I like Cap's history in the MCU, with him being a figurehead before becoming a war hero. It makes perfect sense that you can't just send one guy into war, but a symbol can still help the war in other ways. The Tesseract power is scary, but it just manifests here very very deadly bullets since we don't see it used for anything except lasers. Presumably the bombs are Tesseract-powered, but we never see one go off. It also opens a portal into space when Red Skull touches it for reasons, although I do like symbolically that he thinks he’s above humanity and then touching something actually superhuman just fucking kills him. The fight scenes are pretty good, and I like the Cap choreography with the shield.

I also think it's funny that the movie avoids featuring the actual American military or actual Nazis by having the two main sides be the American Secret Science Team and the Nazi Secret Science Team. It's so clearly pro-American and anti-Nazi that I don't even think this serves a purpose aside from explaining the sci-fantasy tech in the movie.

As for the movie’s connections to the established MCU, they’re pretty irrelevant. Yeah they mention Odin and yeah Howard Stark is Tony's dad, but that connection isn't relevant, instead just being easter eggs for the fans. Even SHIELD only shows up at the end once Cap wakes in the present, which is the only real connection. Well, that and the literal trailer for Avengers as the post-credits scene. It's so 2000s, it's very funny. The film does open with the government finding Cap's shield in the present day, which is really weird. It doesn't really add anything, and I think the film would work better without it to be honest. Cap waking up in the present works really well as an "oh shit" moment, and it doesn’t hit as hard because we know they find Cap’s shield in the present. That said, his "I had a date" line really humanizes him as it shows you what he lost: not his old life, but his future plans too. Everything is gone.

I watched this film before Thor to get a Loki duology with Thor & Avengers, but on rewatch, it might be this movie that leads into Avengers better, and I am hyped for Avengers. Steve is the anti-Tony: a good person without power gaining power to do good, versus a bad person with power realizing how to be a good person. Tony is the exact person that Dr Erskine doesn’t want to have the Super Soldier Serum, and Steve waking up in the present day sets him up to be the real hero of Avengers. Him waking up is a metaphor for the hope and justice he symbolizes returning to Tony’s world of black and light gray.

Honestly, my only real complaint is that nothing really grabbed me and drew me in. Aside from Cap crashing into the ocean while on call with Peggy, I think the most impactful scene in the movie is Cap waking up to find himself in the 21st century. Y'know, the tease for the crossover movie. It’s still a good movie, and a lot better than Incredible Hulk, it’s just not special. Fortunately, at this point, good with an excellent Captain America is all the MCU needs it to be.

Thor.title: Thor
Thor.blurb: A fun film in the vein of a Shakespearean play, but with a mostly happy ending. Thor develops from an arrogant warrior into a selfless hero, his evil brother is forced off the throne, and he and his lover are working to reunite across realms. The real standout though is the characters, as almost every character is well-defined with clear chances to let their personality shine through.
Thor.review:
A fun film in the vein of a Shakespearean play, but with a mostly happy ending. Thor develops from an arrogant warrior into a selfless hero, his evil brother is forced off the throne, and he and his lover are working to reunite across realms. The plot is pretty good, with the politicking of the Asgardian royal family and the Frost Giants matching perfectly with Thor’s and Loki’s character arcs. The real standout though is the characters, as almost every character is well-defined with clear chances to let their personality shine through.

Loki gets to go full manipulative mastermind in this movie, using Thor's ignorance to lock him on Earth and Laufey's arrogance to eliminate him from the equation and make Loki a public hero. Truly his only mistake is leaving Heimdall alive on the Bifrost as a warning, as if he had died then Thor would be stranded on Earth. Heimdall gets a really good showing for being a supporting character, standing up for his beliefs while still following the oaths of loyalty he is bound by.

Jane is great, being strongly motivated by her desire to research and understand the unknown and willing to put herself at great risk to do it. She also has a kind heart, trusting Thor and helping him regain his power, even if that may be partly because she thinks he's really hot. Seriously, her lust for him is palpable. That said, Thor's and Jane's quiet scenes are the ones I remembered most going into this movie, and they still really work. The scene on the roof where Thor draws in Jane's notebook while explaining the Nine Realms is great for both of them. However, the scenes are really short, way shorter than I expected, to the point where I don't think their star-crossed lovers status is really earned. This is most felt when Thor nearly dies and Jane rushes to his side instead of his lifelong friends. That should be Sif holding Thor while he dies on the ground, not Jane.
