Obviously she's our POV character, but you'd think Sif would care far more.

That’s how Sif is treated the whole movie though, her and the Warriors Three. They basically do nothing aside from be Thor's friends and contribute to the action sequences. You could cut them in half and the only thing that would change is that Thor has less friends. The same goes for Jane's group. Darcy has some fun lines, but she mostly just exists to be there. Erik Selvig has more plot and character contributions, but I’m honestly not sure why he’s there in-universe aside from being friends with Jane’s late dad. He doesn’t seem like Jane’s professor, so did she just ask him along? I still like his character, but you don’t really need him and Darcy, aside from losing Darcy’s handful of comedic lines.

The star of the movie though is Thor, and the two scenes that encapsulate his excellent character arc are my two favorite scenes in the movie. The first is Thor failing to lift Mjolnir in the SHIELD base, and the second is his slow walk towards the Destroyer knowing he's about to die. It shows his ultimate despair and then how much he's grown, having been humbled by knowing what it's like to be powerless. Odin's plan worked, even if Loki made things worse. The scene where Thor gets his power back is also awesome.

Plus, I like that despite Thor’s arrogance, there are signs even early on that he’s an honorable person. He admits that Sif was her own greatest advocate when he’s hyping up his friends even before he’s cast to Earth, and once there he accepts without any fight that he must remain on Earth to maintain peace between Asgard and Jotunheim. Sure Loki is lying about it, but Thor doesn’t know that, meaning he fully accepts remaining exiled if it is the best for Asgard. His kindness with Jane only accentuates this, showing us that he is a good person once he realizes that he doesn’t have all the answers.

This plays into the relationship politics on Asgard and Thor’s clear care for Loki, even as Loki betrays him. I also love the scene where Loki confronts Odin about being a Frost Giant, showing just how broken Loki is over the real thing while showing how much Odin loves his adopted son. Odin is really good in this movie, truly being a wise ruler whose main mistake is not realizing how hurt Loki is by not becoming king, and the truth of his heritage just amplifies that. Odin shows nothing but love for Loki, and he does the same for Thor, despite it being tough love in Thor’s case. Loki's fall into evil is excellent, even if the seeds were always there when he ruins Thor's coronation and then manipulates him into attacking Jotunheim. I love their whole dynamic and all the politicking wrapped up in their relationships, even if it leaves Jane's half of the movie feeling weaker by comparison. She's not useless - she's a great POV - but we get enough POV from Thor and Loki that she's clearly the weaker half of the movie. Whenever she’s on-screen, I want more Thor, Loki, and Odin, which says just how good their dynamic is.

As for MCU connections, SHIELD plays their role well as a three-letter government agency. They could be the FBI and the movie wouldn't change, but it works well at both connecting the MCU while letting this movie feel self-contained. Also Hulk is mentioned, which is fun. The post-credits scene is also really good, hinting at what will come in Avengers with Loki’s survival. It is funny that the post-credits is the Tesseract, a completely unrelated glowing blue cube to the other glowing blue cube in this movie (the Casket of Ancient Winters), but if you’ve already seen Captain America then you know what’s up. It's a banger movie with great characters, pretty good special effects, and a strong plot that stands well on its own while building out the mystical world of the MCU only hinted at in Captain America.

Avengers.title: Avengers
Avengers.blurb: A near-perfect ensemble film that masterfully ties together the first phase of the MCU. Normally I save the MCU section for last, but there is no Avengers without the MCU. What makes this work is that every main character is given equal plot relevance and character arcs that make the film feel like a proper ensemble despite starring four main characters from other films.
Avengers.review:
A near-perfect ensemble film that masterfully ties together the first phase of the MCU. Normally I save the MCU section for last, but there is no Avengers without the MCU; everything of importance aside from Maria Hill and the Chithauri are from previous films. What makes this work is that every main character is given equal plot relevance and character arcs that make the film feel like a proper ensemble despite starring four main characters from other films, as well as upgrading Natasha to main cast.

What helps is that everyone is introduced with their own scene that characterizes what they do: Banner helps, Natasha spies, Steve fights, Tony fixes, and Barton sees everything. The character with the weakest intro is Thor, but he spawns on top of a helicopter and immediately starts interrogating Loki himself, so it still works. I do wish we got to see Hulk in some form before Banner transforms since Hulk is alluded to so much. I think you’re supposed to be like “what’s up with Banner” if you haven’t seen Hulk, but the initial transformation isn’t threatening enough to sell that for me.

I also love opening the movie with SHIELD. Plot-wise it makes sense because that’s where Loki first shows up, but it starts the film with the connective tissue of the MCU and uses them to pull in our big heroes, the ones that they’re implicitly connecting by their very presence. It gives us a starting point that isn’t one of our stars, preventing that first hero from feeling like a main character, while still giving us a set of POV characters to follow while our main cast is assembled.

From the excellent intros, things hit the ground running. No line of dialogue is wasted, with it either going towards progressing the plot or characterizing our expansive cast. Even the quips are characterization, showing what one character thinks of the other. The best scene for this is easily the bickering scene in the Helicarrier, with everyone’s larger than life personalities finally clashing. Even though their emotions are amplified by Loki’s sceptre, every jab feels real, with Fury revealing just how mistrustful he is, Thor looking down on humans, Natasha being terrified of Bruce, and Tony and Steve feeling that the other doesn’t live up to their vision of a hero. The characterization is strong enough that the requisite “heroes fight when they meet” thing works, since Thor feels like Loki is his responsibility and Tony refuses to talk things out.

Nobody has a major arc, but pretty much every main character gets an arc in some form. Tony has the conversation with Cap where Cap accuses him of refusing to lie on a metaphorical wire to let another man cross, and Tony asserts that he would just cut the wire. So when the chips are down and the metaphorical wire can’t be cut, Tony lays his life on the line and flies the nuke into the portal. Steve learns that even if he can’t trust the new government in this less black-and-white world, he still has a place among other living legends. Thor gets humbled in his last movie and learns that he doesn’t know all the answers, but here he learns to respect that there are humans as strong and influential as he is and that it’s okay to let them help fight. Natasha gains something to fight for, becoming a hero instead of just a spy who does what Fury asks of her. Bruce Banner makes a friend and finally finds a use for the Hulk.

Barton doesn’t really get an arc, but he also spends half the movie mind controlled, so the fact that he gets to be a badass hero at all is impressive. Really, he’s just an accessory to Natasha’s arc, being the person that helped motivate her to join SHIELD in the first place, and now motivating her to become a hero. Fury also doesn’t get an arc, but he gets to stand his ground against the World Security Council and support the Avengers. He’s still manipulative, like lying about the Tesseract weapons and later lying about Coulson’s trading cards being in his pocket instead of his locker, but Fury is clearly a good guy despite being incredibly distrustful. Like Cap, he’s put in a perfect place for Winter Soldier to finish his arc.

Coulson is also used very well. He gets more screentime here than ever before, fleshing out his deadpan characteristics to turn him into a pretty chill guy who loves heroes. It works to make his death poignant, since he’s the main one bonding with the Avengers while they all bicker. Him being one of our first POV characters also helps, since we’ve been following him since the start of the movie if not since Iron Man. Him getting the last laugh on Loki by telling him he’ll lose because he lacks conviction - correctly diagnosing his motive when even Thor can’t - is one last moment of awesome for the character who first expanded the MCU. Without his characterization here, Coulson never becomes the star of Agents of SHIELD, and he fully earns it.

Loki is used incredibly well in this movie. We already know who he is from Thor, but giving him the Tesseract and his mind control sceptre makes him feel dangerous despite the fact that he lost last time. He’s still a manipulative mastermind in this movie, but because everyone knows he’s evil, he uses more mind games and planning instead of just lying to people. He’s escalated from scheming liar in Thor to full-on supervillain here, which is a joy to watch. Even still, there are points where it seems like his heart isn’t really into conquest, like he’s made up some poor excuse just to get attention from Thor and maybe Odin.

Loki’s motive of world conquest gives us the movie’s main theme, with Fury opposing him thanks to being our initial POV character. Loki wants to rule with force by himself using an army of faceless goons, while Fury brings together good people to protect humanity together using their unique skills. Of course he does run a shadow government, which is why once he knows that the Avengers will work, he sends the Tesseract back to Asgard, because you can’t be the good guy while giving the shadow government laser guns. The Avengers are Fury’s answer to the Chithauri (literally “I have an army” vs “we have a Hulk”), and it’s that individualism that makes them heroes. They fight to give everyone the right to choose and be someone special, while Loki is the villain because he fights to take that away. It’s not the most present theme, but it is there, and it complements the characters really well.

There are so many iconic scenes in this movie, and by the end you understand why they’re iconic. Tony’s “I have a plan: attack” line summarizes him up so well, showing that he thinks he’s on top of the situation so much that he doesn't need to take it seriously. It makes him mourning Coulson’s death hit harder, because it’s his first real loss across 3 movies. His “we have a Hulk” line is then the other end of his arc: he’s still sure they’ll win, but now it's a “we” instead of an “I”. Hulk then pays this off with the hilarious “puny god” scene, humbling Loki completely after all his gloating. Barton being the one to capture Loki by pointing the arrow at his face also works similarly. Your first thought is probably “why Barton and not Thor”, but one, Barton was mind controlled by Loki for half the movie so he deserves it, and two, Loki thinks he’s so much better than humanity and yet is pinned down and defeated by the primitive bow and arrow. It’s the perfect capstone to his ideology being defeated along with his army. Nuking New York is a stupid-ass decision, and Fury elects to ignore it because despite being the shadow government, he personally does want to help people, which is why the Avengers exist in the first place. “That’s my secret, Cap: I’m always angry” is the culmination of a series of people asking Banner how he reins in the Hulk, and the answer shows that Banner has simply learned to control and direct his anger. He only ever loses control when he’s overwhelmed, which is a great interpretation of Hulk that lets his character arc from his solo movie stick while still letting the Hulk be a rampaging beast. Side note, The Incredible Hulk is clearly the least important MCU movie for Avengers, to the point of recasting Bruce Banner, but letting Bruce keep his arc from that movie shows that they do care, even if the rest of the movie isn’t referenced at all. Finally, shawarma is funny.

Oh yeah, the action is also fucking awesome. The final battle is obviously the standout with everyone working together, but almost every fight is really good. Natasha kicks ass, the Tony/Thor fight that ends with Cap’s shield tanking a hit from Mjolnir is awesome, and Hulk’s breakout on the Helicarrier is appropriately terrifying. I love that Tony’s job during the Helicarrier action sequence is to fix the propeller because he’s the inventor of the team, while Thor gets to be the bruiser and Natasha deals with the human spies. Barton blowing up Loki with a bow and arrow is funny, as is Tony’s Arc Reactor making him immune to Loki’s sceptre. Loki is intimidating, but really his best moments are when he’s being humiliated due to underestimating humanity’s technology. Also shoutout to Iron Man 1 ending with Tony blowing a big blue beam into the sky to stop Obadiah Stane, and this movie ends with Natasha shutting down a big blue beam in the sky to stop an invasion.

Other random things I like include the Stark logo on the tower collapsing to just leave the A for Avengers is funny; the World Security Council launching a nuke literally a minute before Natasha shuts down the portal; Banner being hired for his mind instead of for Hulk; Thor’s hammer crashing in the field in the same position as it crashed during Thor; and the initial portal for the Tesseract looking like Tony’s Arc Reactor.

The weakest part of the movie is the Chithauri, who really show up with no explanation and serve as Loki’s faceless grunts. There’s the one leader, but he’s not even in the final battle. That said, the Chithauri being faceless adds to the movie’s theme about choice and your unique contributions to society, so I can’t complain too much, especially because Loki is the real villain of the movie. The movie also really doesn’t need a teaser for the sequel, even if Thanos is cool, because it’s the perfect conclusion to the five-film long saga of the then-MCU.

There’s really nothing I would cut from this movie despite it being 2 and a half hours, and almost nothing I would add or change. It’s not as deep as something like 12 Angry Men, but it’s not trying to be. Even if it wasn’t a perfect crossover, it’d still be a masterful ensemble film that utilizes everyone super well. Everyone has a well defined character, and they all feel meaningful. It is everybody’s movie instead of nobody’s movie, and that’s hard to pull off. There’s really nothing else like it, except for maybe Infinity War and Endgame. Other crossovers exist, but none on this scale. Genuinely a masterpiece.

X-Men Origins: Wolverine.title: X-Men Origins: Wolverine
X-Men Origins: Wolverine.blurb: A big dumb action movie with a simple but serviceable plot until the last act when the plot gets really complicated and bad for no reason. The plot before the last act is still just connective tissue to get you from fight scene to fight scene, but the fight scenes are pretty good.
X-Men Origins: Wolverine.review:
A big dumb action movie with a simple but serviceable plot until the last act when the plot gets really complicated and bad for no reason. The plot before the last act is still just connective tissue to get you from fight scene to fight scene, but the fight scenes are pretty good. The CGI is surprisingly good for a movie with this bad of a reputation, and the simple revenge story is just enough motivation to make you root for Wolverine and hate Sabretooth with just a little bit of government conspiracy. 

The standout fight is the one where Wolverine uses a motorcycle to fight a sniper in a helicopter, but the Gambit fight, the scene where Team X storms the compound, and, dare I say it, the Deadpool fight, are all also pretty good. They’re big dumb action with entertaining choreography, and that's all they need to be. Wolverine launches himself out of a motorcycle into a helicopter and slashes the blades off, what more do you want. You wanted a character-driven plot like the other X-Men movies? Yeah we don’t got that, sorry.

Okay actually the first five minutes has that. The intro is short but sweet, giving you a strong impression of Wolverine's home life and setting up his dynamic with Sabretooth in just a few minutes. The war montage is similarly good, showing Sabretooth's deterioration and Wolverine’s reluctant caring for him. The intro climaxes (and the movie starts) with the aforementioned compound storming scene, featuring Ryan Reynolds’ excellent on-screen audition for the Deadpool movies (wait isn’t he playing Deadpool-). After that the plot devolves into generic military and revenge stuff for most of the movie, with the only real attempt at a twist being that Sabretooth works for their old boss Stryker.

Then the ending decides to ruin a good thing by getting all complicated and subsequently being really bad. Wolverine's dead love interest isn't dead and was actually blackmailed into dating him the whole time. Wolverine decides that this means he shouldn't kill Stryker for reasons, then Sabretooth tries to kill her anyways because he’s just like that, then Wolverine finally beats Sabretooth. Then after beating his arch rival, Stryker just throws Deadpool out, so Sabretooth teams up with Wolverine to fight Deadpool, also for reasons, and then Sabretooth just leaves without trying to kill Wolverine again. Both of their characters just make no sense at this point. And then to top it all off, Stryker shoots Wolverine with an adamantium bullet to give him amnesia. Because he needed to lose his memories for X-Men, and clearly this was the best way to do it. It's so anticlimactic after the rest of the movie, and just feels really tacked on. Like he won, but no, adamantium bullet be upon ye. Oh and the love interest dies anyways. It's just such a massive fumble to end off what has been so far a big dumb action movie, and proves that the writers were trying to take this seriously and just failed.

Slight Deadpool tangent: I kinda like this version of Deadpool. Is he comic accurate at all? No, not even close. But he’s a cool final boss for the movie since Sabretooth needed a redemption arc I guess. As I said, the final boss should have been Sabretooth, but I like Stryker’s plan to make a military-controlled supermutant by combining mutant powers, and it does make an epic final fight that manages to keep some emotions by kinda-sorta reconciling Wolverine and Sabretooth.

Really, what makes this movie worse is that this is not a good addition to the X-Men timeline. Aside from being a big dumb action movie (admittedly on accident) versus the character-driven original trilogy, this film and the originals do not gel well at all. The Sabretooth in this movie is so clearly a different character from Sabretooth in X-Men 1 that it's silly. Cyclops is here for some reason, yet he and Wolverine never interact so they can meet for the first time in X-Men. Xavier is also here and can walk, and yet he never even tries to free the mutants from Stryker's island. He only talks to Cyclops, and only shows up once Wolverine frees them. It makes him look incompetent when we know he's anything but, and it's not even necessary since Gambit literally came back just to get the mutants off the island. You could cut Xavier from this movie and both the movie and Xavier come out looking better. 

I also don't like this movie's version of Stryker. The timeline technically lines up, but the vibes are off. His plan seems to contradict his plan in X2, because here he wants to make supermutants for the military and there he wants to just kill all mutants. Maybe it's just character development (he got worse), but it feels wrong. He manipulated mutants in X2 as well so that’s consistent, but the vibes are off. We didn’t need this extra backstory. Also in X2, the implication is that the procedure gave Wolverine his amnesia, which is way more dramatic than adamantium bullet. Also the adamantium partially comes from space for some reason. All the X-Men connections just make this already middling movie worse, and the fact that they are most prevalent in the already stupid ending only compounds things. 

The fight scenes are probably pretty good on YouTube because the special effects are pretty good and Hugh Jackman is doing his best, but this movie is a waste of time outside that.

X-Men: First Class.title: X-Men: First Class
X-Men: First Class.blurb: A banger ensemble film that matches the vibe of the original X-Men trilogy by telling an interconnected story fueled by its characters. Xavier and Magneto are the stars of the movie, but Sebastian Shaw makes a good proto-Magneto and Mystique is a good tritagonist, caught between Xavier’s and Magneto’s philosophies.
X-Men: First Class.review:
A banger ensemble film that matches the vibe of the original X-Men trilogy by telling an interconnected story fueled by its characters. Xavier and Magneto are the stars of the movie, but Sebastian Shaw makes a good proto-Magneto and Mystique is a good tritagonist, caught between Xavier’s and Magneto’s philosophies.

Mystique has the biggest arc in the movie, going from hiding with Xavier to becoming a mutant supremacist with Magneto. Her “mutant and proud” line becomes more sinister as the movie goes on, especially once she says it to support Magneto trying to murder two whole military fleets (in her defense, they tried to kill him first). In contrast, Xavier’s and Magneto’s worldviews haven’t changed, only that they’re fighting harder to obtain them. Xavier still wants mutants to coexist with humans and Magneto still wants to get revenge on humanity, but now Xavier has the X-Men and Magneto has the Brotherhood. It makes them both excellent leads, spearheading the two sides of the mutant-human conflict while not being completely static characters, but it means that Mystique is the heart of the film.

That said, the Xavier/Magneto relationship is much better handled than the Xavier/Mystique relationship. You believe the growing friendship between Xavier and Magneto while fully understanding how it falls apart so spectacularly, and it makes it appropriately tragic. The Xavier/Mystique relationship deteriorating is also supposed to be tragic, but it comes across as slightly more stupid given that their last conversation before the finale is Mystique getting pissed at Xavier because he asks her to put some clothes on now that she’s 30 when he didn’t when she was 12. Yeah he’s clearly uncomfortable with her mutant form, but he’s hardly seen it after all these years because she keeps it hidden. Of course that’s because he asked her to hide it, but that’s so she can live in society instead of being locked in prison or executed. Her growing frustrations with Xavier are understandable, but she refuses to communicate her problems at all. On the other hand, despite repeatedly saying that he doesn’t understand what’s up with her, he’s really condescending about it and refuses to consider her point of view at all. It’s a failure of communication on both their sides that feels really weird given how long they’ve known each other, only amplified by their last conversation being so stupid. What mostly saves it for me is that they both still clearly care for each other when Mystique joins with Magneto at the end of the movie, showing that they still want the other to live their dream even if they don’t understand.

Outside of our core 3, the rest of the cast isn’t the most fleshed out. The best is Beast, being a foil to Mystique by becoming more visibly a mutant while still not wanting war, but we don’t really see that until Days of Future Past. Shaw isn’t that great of a villain, mostly using his powers to intimidate normal people. However, he works great as a proto-Magneto, becoming the type of villain that Magneto would become in the original trilogy, and serves well enough as an antagonist for this movie in terms of theme if not threat level. Havok and Banshee get bare minimum personalities, while Angel gets nearly no speaking lines after she joins Shaw halfway into the movie and Riptide and Azazel have no personality.

The best parts of the movie are the opening and final battle. The opening half-hour is a bunch of cuts between Xavier, Magneto, and Moira, and while Moira doesn’t really do anything except build up the big impending threat for us, we get to see how different Xavier’s and Magneto's upbringings are. Each scene is placed so intentionally, and it keeps you engaged despite the two plots being so disconnected aside from the themes of these two discovering their mutant powers. The fact that we know them from the original trilogy definitely helps keep us invested, but the structure is still really good. We learn back to back that Magneto had a good relationship with his mother but a terrible upbringing, and then used his powers to get revenge on the Nazis, while Xavier had a terrible relationship with his mother but a cushy upbringing, and used his powers to flirt with women. Despite neither wanting to be the only mutant, neither are situated to be the friend the other needs.

My other favorite scene is the scene where Magneto kills Shaw. Magneto counting down with the coin like Shaw did at the beginning shows how petty Magneto is, exemplifying that this isn’t about morals but revenge. And then Xavier screaming in Shaw’s brain as the camera pans with the coin, cutting back and forth between Xavier and Shaw as their heads remain aligned on the screen until the coin pops out of Shaw’s head. It’s so so good and shows symbolically that Magneto is committing to his path of violence and killing any chance of peace he had with Xavier. It’s such a perfectly written and edited scene.

With Mystique as the character with the most change, and the one caught between Xavier and Magneto, the movie is almost arguing for her point of view that mutants must fight, especially given that Magneto is right about the humans trying to kill the X-Men after they stopped WWIII. Even Xavier seems to agree that humans and mutants must remain partly separate, given that he sends Moira away at the end of the movie by mindwiping her.

I do think the mutant metaphor is handled a little goofily in this movie. By the final act, all the X-Men except for Beast and Mystique are white men, with Darwin dying and Angel joining Shaw, and then Mystique joins Magneto’s Brotherhood to end the movie. The implication is that Xavier’s dream is a pipe dream, one born from a place of security and privilege in being able to hide his powers, and that Magneto’s/Shaw’s dream is the only way for visible mutants (or minorities) to truly be themselves. This metaphor pretty much holds through the whole cast except for Beast, who does not want to be blue, except that Magneto and Shaw are both also white men. The implication there, then, is that even if Magneto and Shaw seem to care about mutants more directly than Xavier, they are still just using them to uphold their own superiority, which seems to hold for Former Nazi Shaw and Nazi Hunter Magneto. By the end of the movie, Xavier wants a better world for mutants while Magneto just uses that as an excuse to kill people who wronged him, putting them exactly where they are at the beginning of the first X-Men movie 35 years later. A pretty salient metaphor, leaving the mutants’ best chance with a nepo-baby who never has to deal with the downsides of being a mutant.

Narrative aside, the special effects are really good. Everyone’s powers are done really well; Havok’s lasers look incredible, Mystique’s effects still look amazing, Shaw’s abilities are weird but visually intuitive, and I’m so happy they let Banshee fly with his powers. The fight scenes aren’t the best, but the final scene on the beach is easy to follow and hits all the key beats well, even if Riptide goes out like a chump. Magneto breaking Xavier’s legs and immediately snapping out of villain mode to check on his friend is really good character work.

It’s not a perfect movie, but almost all of its pieces work together really well. The characters feel like they’ll become the characters they are in the original trilogy, and the mutant metaphor carries over from here to there as well. I don’t think it’s as perfect as X2, especially since some of the supporting cast is really underused, but it’s more thematically deep than the original, even if that depth is enhanced by being a prequel to that original trilogy. Even without that, this is still a really engaging film, and with that connection it’s must-watch for any fan of the original trilogy.

The Wolverine.title: The Wolverine
The Wolverine.blurb: A competent action movie where the bare minimum government conspiracy plot and character arcs are just there to get you to the excellent action sequences. The action takes a bit to get started, but once it starts it never stops, and almost all of it is really good.
The Wolverine.review:
A competent action movie where the bare minimum government conspiracy plot and character arcs are just there to get you to the excellent action sequences. The action takes a bit to get started, but once it starts it never stops, and almost all of it is really good.

The intro scene in Nagasaki is light on the action, but is an excellent re-introduction to Wolverine. The first real fight is the yakuza attack at the funeral, which is an explosion of tension after the slow, atmospheric first act of the movie. It’s a fun, frenetic battle with lots of moving pieces while people's motivations are still unclear, meaning you never quite know who’s on Wolverine’s side and who isn’t. After that is the excellent train fight, which is my favorite fight in the movie. It's such an excellently tense scene, made even more exciting by the high-speed train that threatens to eliminate anyone at the slightest mistake. Wolverine faking out the ninja and making him jump into a billboard is hilariously awesome.

Yukio gets her one big fight scene at the movie’s midpoint against an actual samurai, and it’s also really good, proving why she’s Mariko’s bodyguard. Wolverine has to finish the fight, but Yukio does her job of holding out long enough for Wolverine to fix his healing factor, so she doesn’t feel useless. I love that they let Wolverine fight an actual samurai before the mecha samurai battle in the finale. Is a giant mecha samurai goofy? Yes. Is it awesome? Also yes. Yukio hitting Viper with an elevator is hilarious, and Mariko throwing Wolverine's severed claws like knives is incredible, especially since she's standing up to her deranged grandfather. Her saying that "she buried her grandfather" is so good. It shows that she refuses to see her grandfather as the monster he's become, allowing her to honor his memory while still fighting him to save Wolverine and Yukio.

Aside from the action sequences, the movie does not have a lot going on. Starting with the plot, Mariko's grandfather Ichiro dies so she gets attacked by the yakuza, who were hired by her father so he could inherit Ichiro's company since he's giving it to Mariko. Also her ex and Viper are working for her grandfather to make him immortal. Wolverine gets dragged into this because Ichiro needs his mutant power to become immortal, and then he just gets involved. This is spelled out slowly, but never really holds a lot of weight because the movie knows that you don’t care. Ichiro coming back in a giant samurai mecha is a cool twist though, helped out significantly by Giant Samurai Mecha. Yukio is also in the movie.

As for the characters, they are all as flat as a board. Wolverine almost doesn't change throughout the movie, going from a guy with no life goals who's depressed to a guy with no life goals who's excited to find something new. This could be a big change, except this happens 30 minutes into the movie. Wolverine just immediately switches into hero mode when Mariko gets attacked. To be clear, though, Mariko is Wolverine’s old friend’s granddaughter who he doesn’t even know. It’s incredibly heroic of him, and this driven heroism is enough to carry you through the movie.

The other characters are similarly one-note, but fun. Mariko is a scared girl with some fire in her, Yukio cares about Mariko deeply but can't show her emotions (and never does), Viper is delightfully evil, and Mariko's dad is a selfish asshole. The most interesting character is probably Mariko's grandfather Ichiro, who used to be a good man before the inevitable spectre of death turned him into a manipulative bastard who will stop at nothing to become immortal like his hero Wolverine. Him trying to gaslight Wolverine into giving up his powers by convincing Wolverine that he truly desires death is diabolical.

There’s also Mariko’s ex, Kenuichio Harada. He’s the Silver Samurai from the comic, but here he's basically Hawkeye. His deal of loving Mariko enough that he goes along with Ichiro's plan because he believes it's in Mariko's best interest and then switching sides to help Mariko is cool. However, he has almost no presence, rendering his entire character arc almost meaningless. He does help ensure that Mariko lives, meaning both her and Yukio make it out of the movie alive, which is definitely a good thing.

As for X-Men connections, this movie is basically a good version of X-Men Origins: Wolverine, so we can forget that movie exists. Wolverine also shouldn’t remember meeting Ichiro because of the adamantium bullet-induced amnesia, so this movie also forgets that X-Men Origins: Wolverine exists (ignore the bone claws). I can't believe they got Famke Janssen back for this movie just so she can lie in silken pajamas and tell Wolverine to kill himself. I do like Wolverine being traumatized by Jean's death, but it’s wild to me that she's back. Also, the Days of Future Past teaser is very funny just because the movie both asks and refuses to answer how Xavier is back from the dead. “Just don’t worry about it.”

The movie isn't great, and really isn't super memorable outside of the train scene and samurai mecha, but it is both fun and competent, and sometimes that’s all a movie needs to be.

X-Men: Days of Future Past.title: X-Men: Days of Future Past
X-Men: Days of Future Past.blurb: The film concludes with a near-perfect ending for the X-Men film franchise, despite being rocky the rest of the time. We get a glimpse of a better future that builds on the previous four films, while showing us the second chances that got us there.
X-Men: Days of Future Past.review:
The film concludes with a near-perfect ending for the X-Men film franchise, despite being rocky the rest of the time. We get a glimpse of a better future that builds on the previous four films, while showing us the second chances that got us there. The film is all about second chances defining who you are, which is perfect for a time travel movie. Unfortunately, the film has some problems. Almost every scene is good on its own, but don’t become greater than the sum of their parts, and at the same time the overall plot is really good on paper but isn’t super compelling on a scene-by-scene basis.

The best and most important part is the ending, so we’ll start there. After the mutant population has been nearly wiped out by Sentinels the first time, we awaken to a new future where Storm, Wolverine, Cyclops, Jean, and Beast are all living at Xavier’s School, which is filled with happy students. The apocalypse has been averted and the timeline has been altered enough that Beast doesn’t feel the need to become a part of the president's cabinet and Jean doesn’t die under Alkali Lake fighting Stryker. That tells us everything we need to know, even if we never see a single shot outside the School: after trying and failing for four movies, mutants finally found respect and peace in a world that no longer hates and fears them. That’s the implication anyway, and it’s a perfect capstone to this quintology of X-Men films and also two Wolverine movies.

That’s literally the last 5 minutes though, and while a perfect ending certainly helps a movie, it can only do so much. The opening fight scene in the future is actually pretty good, showing off how powerful the Sentinels are by having them slaughter a bunch of X-Men and then introducing Kitty’s time travel gimmick. The future cast doesn’t do a lot after this fight scene except die, which I’m pretty much fine with because they’re here to nail home the hook and premise: in the future, humanity builds giant robots and wipes mutants to extinction. The idea sounds far-fetched if you don’t actually show the future, and this opening sells it. That said, it would’ve helped if we had more of the remaining X-Men from the original trilogy. They’re all there, they just don’t do anything except Kitty and Xavier. I’m not even sure that Colossus speaks, and Storm goes out like a chump. I wish Quicksilver were there to provide some connection between the past and future beyond Wolverine, Xavier, and Magneto. I think he’s the white-haired guy in the beginning who gets obliterated, but a bigger presence would have been nice. I also think he could solo the Sentinels, though, which is probably why he isn’t there. Instead the most prominent member of our future team is Blink for some reason, so shout out to all 20 Blink fans out there. Don’t get me wrong, the future team does their job, they just don’t do their job nearly as well as they could have.

The main character of the story is ostensibly Wolverine. He’s the one we follow back in time, the one who both tells Xavier and Magneto about the Sentinels and convinces them to stop them, the one who recruits Quicksilver, and the one who gives the big pep talk to Xavier in Cerebro. We get a lot of little moments with him reacting to stuff in the past, and they all seem pretty telling about his character, especially since this is movie 7 with him. However, his role in the climax is to get yeeted into a lake and accomplish nothing. He’s our POV character for everything except the climax, which is just weird. I get that his role is to be the mentor to Xavier, to give him the strength to do what needs to be done, and it is a cool role reversal in theory, but Xavier never felt like the protagonist of X-Men 1, so it still kinda falls flat for me.

Instead of Wolverine, the climax of the movie centers around Mystique choosing to follow Xavier or Magneto, just like First Class. This time, she chooses Xavier, shooting Magneto in the neck in order to save Richard Nixon of all people (do you think Watergate still happens in this universe?). It’s a cool moment that really solidifies the film’s theme of second chances. When faced with the finale of First Class again, Mystique chooses Xavier instead of Magneto, redefining herself. This gives the humans a second chance, allowing them to redefine themselves as mutantkind’s allies instead of committing genocide-by-robot. Mystique’s change of heart was in turn caused by Xavier’s, who got out of his depression spiral early to once again stand up for mutants. He failed before, but he won’t fail now. And that in turn was caused by Wolverine going back in time, creating a literal second chance for the whole universe. Wolverine redefines himself as well, being the mentor instead of the mentee, and he really is the perfect character to kick off this theme considering how many second chances he’s had, including that time he got amnesia (does he still have amnesia?). The only person who doesn’t change is Magneto, who is still on the same genocide route he was on in First Class, which is why he’s the villain of this story. Maybe he’ll change in the future, but with no Sentinels, maybe he won’t. Human villain Trask also doesn’t change, but he really has no character outside of hating mutants and putting his logo on everything.

Weirdly enough, outside of the climax, I think the weakest parts of the movie are Xavier, Magneto, and Mystique, despite being the best parts of First Class. They all have pretty good scenes in a vacuum (shoutout to the scene where Xavier snaps at Magneto on the plane), but it’s pretty much all rehashing character conflicts from First Class. Even the Xavier/Mystique scenes, which should be a new dynamic, feel the same as their scenes from the latter third of First Class. Xavier wants to save everybody, Magneto goes rogue to kill people, and Mystique is caught between the two. Magneto trying to kill Mystique at least makes logical sense because Trask uses her DNA to make the Sentinels, but then he does just decide to go full supervillain because he can’t stop trying to be a mutant Nazi.

The timeline is also bizarre. Instead of Magneto and Mystique having a long and storied history together, Magneto gets arrested like a year after First Class and Mystique is on her own for a literal decade. Then it takes four years for Xavier to open the school, only for his literal first semester to get ruined by the Vietnam War. Everything falls apart immediately, when the movie works way better if the characters actually have more grievances than just the Cuban Missile Crisis.

The best scene in the movie is hands-down the Time In A Bottle scene. It may have ruined Hollywood speedsters forever, but it’s so so good. The music, the pacing, the setpiece, the details, it’s just peak. And then Quicksilver leaves the movie never to contribute again, probably because he could solo the Sentinels and Magneto at the same time.

I still mostly like this movie, and it is the perfect ending to the X-Men franchise so far, but man is it not as good as it could be. I’d still recommend it for any X-Men fan, but it’s not nearly as well-put-together as something like X2 or First Class.

Amazing Spider-Man.title: Amazing Spider-Man
Amazing Spider-Man.blurb: This film is like two movies sandwiched together: the first half being a slow-burn sci-fi horror story about Peter getting bitten by a radioactive spider that's tied to his parents' mysterious disappearance, and the second half being a superhero story about a mad scientist trying to turn people into lizards and the sole hero who can stop him.
Amazing Spider-Man.review:
This film is like two movies sandwiched together: the first half being a slow-burn sci-fi horror story about Peter getting bitten by a radioactive spider that's tied to his parents' mysterious disappearance, and the second half being a superhero story about a mad scientist trying to turn people into lizards and the sole hero who can stop him. Despite having some pretty good elements, like Andrew Garfield’s Peter Parker and excellent action sequences, the two halves do not blend together well.

The first third of the movie is actually pretty good, slowly building up the characters of Peter, Gwen, Curt Conners, and Uncle Ben while having Peter look into the mystery of his parents and grapple with the effects of the spider. The fact that none of the other test subjects survived and the vibes that Dr Conners is hiding something help give this part of the movie some horror-like tension, which is fun. Peter feels like a good man who’s trapped in his own head because he feels like he can’t do anything about his missing parents or the school bully. He really has no friends, and yet is still willing to fight, which makes him the perfect character to be corrupted by an evil spider virus. Ignoring the horror movie vibes that don’t manifest, I like that Peter’s skateboarding gives him some athletic experience before becoming Spider-Man, and that his love of photography means that he’s always watching the world, but never changing it.

The second half of the movie kicks off with Uncle Ben dying, and it’s so stupid. Peter barely knows how his powers work, so while he doesn’t try to stop the guy robbing the convenience store he’s at, it makes sense because the robber has a gun. The cashier asks Peter to go after the guy and Peter refuses, but like yeah he has a gun. Sure Peter is doing it to be an asshole, but at this point, he can’t reasonably be expected to stop a mad gunman. I do not like this scene.

Peter then goes on a rage and starts hunting down criminals to avenge Uncle Ben's death like he's Batman, which is how the Spider-Man half of Spider-Man kicks off. Peter tracks down a few false leads before he gets distracted by the Lizard, and then Uncle Ben’s killer is never brought up again. Normally dropping a plotline would be annoying, but here it ties so well into Peter's character arc. He stops seeking revenge on Uncle Ben's killer and starts using his powers to help people by stopping the Lizard, transitioning from a vigilante to a hero. The bully plot and Peter’s parents plot do go nowhere though, which I am annoyed about.

Speaking of the Lizard, he’s serviceable. The lizard serum makes Dr Conners insane like the Green Goblin for some reason, which is annoying because he's actually a very reasonable character before that. He literally gets fired for refusing to do human testing before he's sure it's safe, and turns out not to be responsible for Peter’s parents’ disappearance. His only flaw is that he's strongly motivated to get the serum working, but then he turns into a psychopath who wants to turn people into lizards because that will cure cancer erase weakness. Like, he gets cured at the end of the movie and immediately reverts back to his previous characterization. I wish he was just unhinged from the start, since it would help make the two halves feel more connected by leaning into the horror angle.

The fight scenes are all very good though, especially the fight in the school. It’s just super creative and fun. The Spider-Man suit is also very good, even if I don’t like the Lizard’s design. My favorite action scene - and scene in general - is Spider-Man saving that kid from the falling car by taking his mask off and inspiring the kid to be strong since he can be strong too. It’s the incident that causes Peter to become a hero, and it’s so good. The dad paying Spider-Man back by aligning the cranes for him to reach Lizard is the cherry on top.

I don’t have much to say about Gwen or her dad. I like that Gwen gets to participate in the plot by making the lizard antidote, but her and Peter become ride or die for each other so fast for basically no reason. Gwen’s dad is a pretty typical cop, but I do like that he cares for his daughter enough to ask Peter to stay away from her even after he protects Peter’s secret identity. Peter not telling Gwen about her dad's wish and just blowing her off is just stupid, but it's implied they'll get together anyways so whatever.

If the Sam Raimi trilogy felt like daydreams, this film feels like an actual movie. Not a very good movie, but an actual movie, with competent directing, lighting, acting, and pacing. Andrew Garfield is good as both Peter and Spider-Man, and he feels like an actual good person with flaws instead of an egotistical idiot like Tobey’s Peter. That said, the Raimi films do have more directorial flair and stronger intentionality, but I still think I like this film more. I know that’s a piping hot take, but the Raimi movies feel like the world’s most boring fever dream where you want to scream at everyone in it but can’t because you’re moving in slow motion. Even as far as “bad” superhero movies go, you could do a lot worse than Amazing Spider-Man.

Amazing Spider-Man 2.title: Amazing Spider-Man 2
Amazing Spider-Man 2.blurb: A set of really fun action sequences strung together by a frustrating plot with an obnoxious lead. Peter had his rough edges in the first film, but here he cannot communicate anything of importance and frequently makes things worse for himself and those around him by giving into his paranoia instead of talking things through with people.
Amazing Spider-Man 2.review:
A set of really fun action sequences strung together by a frustrating plot with an obnoxious lead. Peter had his rough edges in the first film, but here he cannot communicate anything of importance and frequently makes things worse for himself and those around him by giving into his paranoia instead of talking things through with people. The villains also don’t tie into the story or the themes very well, but Electro is very cool once the fighting starts.

Peter’s self-sabotaging paranoia rears its head in two major ways. Firstly, he refuses to actually be with Gwen because her dead father asked him not to since she could get hurt because he's Spider-Man, and he never manages to have an intelligent conversation with her about this. Nevermind that she wants to be with him, he makes the decision for her and then can't even commit to the bit since he takes the slightest invitation from her to flirt with her. He literally makes out with her in a security closet. The second thing is refusing to explain to Harry why his spider-infused DNA will probably kill him when Harry asks to take it to cure his disease. Peter just says shit like "it'll kill you" instead of explaining the whole situation with Curt Conners becoming a lizard and all the dead test animals. He then shows up as Spider-Man just to tell Harry the same thing, which predictably just pisses him off more. Spider-Man showing up is an implicit “yes”, and it makes Peter look like a dumbass.

The worst part is that this paranoia is justified. Harry takes the serum and becomes a psycho-murderer, although he's admittedly a psycho-murderer already, so I'm not sure the spider serum does anything except give him jaundice. On Gwen’s side, Peter finally decides to be with her, leading to her helping him on a mission and immediately dying. Sure Peter didn't want her on the mission, but she wouldn't have come if he didn't declare his love for her in giant webbing, so the fact is that him getting with her caused her death, meaning the paranoia was right. The film’s message is in fact "don't tell people anything or try to connect with them because the worst will happen", which is such a fun message for a movie

The other big theme is to cherish what you have before it’s gone, centered around Peter’s relationship with Gwen and her inevitable (read: comic-mandated) death. The idea is that time always runs out, and that Peter should have been with Gwen while he had the chance. Except there’s nothing to cherish, because they were doing stupid will-they-won’t-they bullshit the whole movie instead of actively dating. And more importantly, Peter having Gwen is why she fucking died. If they had been dating the whole movie, her death would hurt more, and it would give Peter something to actually cherish. If the writers really wanted to will-they-won’t-they, then Gwen should have left for England while Peter fought Electro alone. He’d still lose her, but it wouldn’t be his fault so the lesson would actually work. Her death just does not work with this theme because their relationship is too broken by their inanity. At least she hits the ground this time instead of the web snapping her neck like in the comic.

The tertiary plot of this movie is Peter learning about his parents, and he learns that they died. Big wahoo. They made the spider serum and then died trying to escape the Oscorp mafia. This is nothing that wasn’t implied last movie; why are we revisiting this. The villains aren’t much better. Max Dillon is pitiable but really annoying before he becomes Electro, and Harry is a snarky asshole whose past relationship with Peter adds almost nothing. They both have a theme of being downtrodden, albeit in very different ways, but this doesn’t connect to Peter or Gwen or Peter’s parents at all so they both feel very disconnected. Also Harry becomes Green Goblin just long enough to kill Gwen and then gets arrested. At least they both get fun one-liners.

That said, there are some things I actually like in this movie. Gwen herself is awesome, taking none of Peter’s bullshit while always trying to help when she can without sacrificing her social life. Spider-Man is easily the best we’ve ever seen in this movie. He’s always so compassionate when he’s in-costume, helping and reassuring random civilians that are in danger and walking bullied kids to school so they’re safe. Him trying to talk down Electro before the fight breaks out is a really good showing for him, and he can still be snarky against the irredeemable assholes when it matters. He really feels like Spider-Man.

The fight scenes are also really good. Like, top-tier Marvel fight scenes. They’re all very intense and creative, with both Spider-Man and his foes doing fun stuff with their powers and the environment to create fights where you never know what’s going to happen next while still feeling plausible in-universe. The film also makes frequent use of slow-mo for emphasis and detail, and it’s only occasionally too much. My favorite scene in the movie is actually slow-mo, being the scene during the first Electro fight where Electro electrocutes Times Square. We see electricity running up the railings and jumping off towards people’s hands before we snap back to real time and see Spider-Man save everyone. It’s not just a great showcase for Electro’s powers, but the best showcase of Spidey-Sense so far. Delectable scene.

As far as Raimi comparisons, this movie is basically just Spider-Man 3 but with better fight scenes and less dancing, so take your pick. Overall, just watch the fight scenes on YouTube. This movie would be a higher recommendation if the plot and characters were even just mid instead of a fucking mess, since they really do bog down the moments of excellence.

Thor: The Dark World.title: Thor: The Dark World
Thor: The Dark World.blurb: A serviceable film that's really nothing more than a bridge. It's the first MCU movie that really feels like an episode of a TV show instead of a film, at least in terms of story. The characters still go through arcs, and I like where most of them end up, but their journeys to get there mostly aren't very interesting.
Thor: The Dark World.review:
A serviceable film that's really nothing more than a bridge. It's the first MCU movie that really feels like an episode of a TV show instead of a film, at least in terms of story. The characters still go through arcs, and I like where most of them end up, but their journeys to get there mostly aren't very interesting. The same goes for the reality-bending aspects of the film’s plot, which are cool but aren’t explored very well. Even during the finale when they’re at full effect, it’s mostly set-dressing as Thor fights a forgettable main villain. The episode-style format isn’t inherently bad, it’s just that this film feels underbaked across every aspect.

Let’s start with the characters. Thor decides to become Protector of the Realms instead of King of Asgard, but we don't really see why he decides to do this. It works for him, but this film is not about him reaching that conclusion. He also reunites with Jane, but it’s unceremonious without any real build-up at all. Jane herself is less of a character than in the first movie, being mostly a plot device to house the Aether, which is disappointing. She’s still a determined genius, but the film isn’t really about her character, either. Erik Selvig is insane, which in theory makes sense because he was mind controlled, but it comes out of nowhere since he seemed fine at the end of Avengers. Darcy is back as comic relief, and does her job pretty well, while Thor's friends have even less presence than last time, making this the first time the cast feels bloated with side characters. At least they are pushed to the side instead of taking up unnecessary screen time, though.

The only character with an arc that's properly explored is Loki. We see him actually work with Thor to get revenge for his mother's death, proving that he does still love his family. Even then, he's still self-serving, and somehow manages to pretend to be Odin in the epilogue. Admittedly, he does by actually giving Thor praise and encouraging him to be his best self when he could be a dick. Yeah it means that Thor isn't contending for the throne, but Loki still treats Thor as he’d want Odin to treat himself. Odin himself is way less of a wise king in this movie than in the first one, but that's partly because he's grieving his wife's death. His presence is also diminished because we never see his reaction to Thor’s victory due to Loki replacing him. It’s kinda weird, but if this were a TV show, you know there’d be some big Odin scene next arc. Instead, he’s just gone.

Moving onto the plot, it has the same problems of being present but barely explored. The gravity reality-bending stuff and other realms are used minimally, and the cool ideas are let down by poor strength of execution. Malekith is as boring as everybody says he is, having no real motivation aside from revenge and no interesting backstory. You could argue that the ancient Asgardians were overzealous since we've now gotten two films where the prologue is them crushing foreign countries, but both of these nations also seemed to be invaders so it's up in the air if the Asgardians were actually defenders or conquerors. Either way, aside from Thor becoming Protector of the Realms, the movie doesn't care. Frigga's death is a cool motivator for Loki and the film tries to explore her character in the first half, but doesn't really pull it off since she dies so fast and had no character from the first film. Props on trying to make her relevant, but they did do it by killing her.

The fight scenes are pretty fun, and I like how much use they get out of Thor's hammer. The spaceship scene is cool, and it’s awesome how the other realms have this futuristic tech since "magic is just science you don't understand". The same goes for Thor making use of Erik's stabilizer machines; Thor could easily think human tech is primitive, but he understands how and why it works and uses it. It's a good scene. The scene where Loki fake betrays Thor to destroy the Aether is also really good. The film is also surprisingly funny between Loki's sardonic wit and Darcy's eager naivety, which somehow makes them the best characters.

In terms of MCU continuity, I like Loki's arc here. After warmongering in Avengers, here he gets what he wants through trickery instead, while learning that he does still belong in Asgard. Plus, the final scene of Loki posing as Odin on the throne is perfect setup, and in hindsight it feels like the whole film is building towards it. We also get our first hints at the Infinity Stones, which is a fun start to Phase 2, even if all we know is that the Tesseract is involved. However, since we know it has a lot of untapped power, it's still a fun hook.

I don't hate this movie like a lot of people do, but it really feels like an episode instead of a complete package. Characters are mostly static with changes happening instead of developing, and the villain makes some cool setpieces but is uninteresting outside of that. We're set up for a good sequel, but this is a stepping stone that leaves a lot to be desired as a standalone film and standalone sequel.

Iron Man 3.title: Iron Man 3
Iron Man 3.blurb: A fun movie with a messy conclusion. The whole movie is about how Tony Stark isn't Iron Man because he has the suit, but he has the suit because he is Iron Man. It's excellent at this, and shows it with some banger fight scenes. The villain doesn’t really contribute to this, but they’re once more a fun mirror to Tony with a twist that I really like.
Iron Man 3.review:
A fun movie with a messy conclusion. The whole movie is about how Tony Stark isn't Iron Man because he has the suit, but he has the suit because he is Iron Man. It's excellent at this, and shows it with some banger fight scenes. The villain doesn’t really contribute to this, but they’re once more a fun mirror to Tony with a twist that I really like. The supporting cast unfortunately doesn’t get a lot to do, and the plot is a bit all over the place, but the film manages to hold its own despite that.

The best part of the film is seeing Tony Stark operate without the Iron Man armor. Not only does he get to jury-rig a whole bunch of tech to break into a secure mansion, but he even gets to fight off some superhumans with just the environment around him, including breaking handcuffs on superheated skin and blowing someone up by putting metal in a microwave. Most of his investigations are usually done with the help of Jarvis, but he manages to figure out what's going on with Extremis and the Mandarin without Jarvis' help at all. It's an excellent showing for Tony Stark the man, with even his personal relationships focused on him as a man and not as a CEO.

However, he is still Iron Man, and the only reason he and his friends survive the final fight is because he has 30 Iron Man suits buried in a secret vault under his house, which is where things get messy. When he blows all the suits up, it feels less like he's starting from a clean slate and accepting that he is the hero, and more like he's quitting being a hero. That's probably not the writers’ intent, but that's what it feels like since we never see the next project he starts. It muddles the ending to what is otherwise a very good character showcase for Tony Stark.

As for the rest of the film, it's got some problems but is still pretty good. I like Killian as a villain, even if he’s not great as a character. Instead, he’s a great embodiment of Tony Stark's past, turning people into literal living weapons after being spurned by Stark the CEO. This is made better by Killian being a superhuman and not a guy in armor because this movie is about Tony Stark, not Iron Man. Pepper nails this home, since she chooses Tony Stark the man and rejects Killian, who's become the same evil CEO that Tony Stark was when we spurned Killian in the first place. Also, I like the Mandarin twist. We already know that Mandarin and Killian are connected somehow, but revealing Mandarin to be entirely an act for Killian to hide behind is very fun, and is foreshadowed enough without being obvious. It's also a fun escalation of Obadiah Stane, with Stane using real terrorists to further his military goals while Killian just fucking invents his own. While Killian is treading old ground by being another mirror to who Tony used to be, he takes things further and in new directions, which makes him feel fresh after Stane and Hammer.

The biggest flaw is definitely the supporting cast, especially Rhodey. He's barely in the movie and then his War Machine armor (now the Iron Patriot armor) gets hacked for the second movie in a row. He does get to help fight as a normal soldier, but reusing the hacking plot from the previous film makes Rhodey feel like he’s here just to be here. Killian's lead biologist Maya getting killed off unceremoniously also sucks after she finally decides to turn on him, particularly since we already know Killian is super evil and spiteful. Pepper has a minimal role in this movie, but I like that she gets to kill Killian after he infected her with Extremis. Harley is also very fun, sue me. Tony is still an ass to him, but you can see him doing his best to dial back the assholeishness because Harley is a kid who's trying to help. Tony giving Harley a bunch of new tech as thanks is awesome. Plus, despite the letter being typed, the signature is handwritten, meaning it's technically Tony's signature despite being anonymous.

I've alluded to this, but the action scenes are awesome, and are definitely the highlights of the film. The best ones are the scenes where Tony fights on his own with no armor, but the airplane scene where he saves all the civilians is really cool. I love to see a hero save people, and he does it in a way that only Iron Man can. The part where Killian blows up Tony's house is crazy because you really don't expect Tony to just lose everything in a sneak attack. In that same scene, Tony saving Pepper with the suit after it nearly kills her in his paranoia is such a good showcase for why he built it. And then as much as I don't like Tony blowing up the suits, the finale is awesome. The suits are just distinct enough to feel different while still being interchangeable, and the action is hype, frenetic, and very pretty. Rhodey swinging on cables like Nathan Drake to save the president is cool, and Tony Stark trapping Killian in the suit to blow him up is freaking awesome. The movie really makes the most of the detachable, telekinetic suit, which is very impressive. It getting hit by a car to reveal that Tony isn’t even inside is very funny.

The movie does have some flaws, as mentioned. Like, Tony Stark is apparently believed dead after his house got bombed and nobody seems to comment on this at all. It means nothing, even after New York. Tony's anxiety/PTSD is never fully addressed, but I do like the implication that Harley's speech about building something new instead of relying on Iron Man broke Tony out of his spiral for good. It also means that Harley indirectly created Ultron, but that's a future movie's problem. There really aren't any MCU connections here outside of Tony's anxiety/PTSD, which I think is fine. Plus, unlike Erik Selvig's insanity in The Dark World, it feels like a more natural continuation of flying a nuke into a black hole. Instead of building out the MCU, it's an Iron Man movie through and though, and a pretty good one at that. It never hits the highs of the first film, but I think it's more focused in terms of both plot and characters than the second, even if the ending is messy. That can't fully drag the movie down though, and it's still a fun ride all the way through.

Gameoverse Pilot.title: Gameoverse Pilot
Gameoverse Pilot.blurb: An interesting premise that doesn't fully explore the implications of its world. As a pilot I think it works pretty well, showing us what a typical episode would be like. Our characters try to save a game world by helping the villain while the antagonists help the hero, and they learn some lessons and deal with PTSD along the way.
Gameoverse Pilot.review:
An interesting premise that doesn't fully explore the implications of its world. As a pilot I think it works pretty well, showing us what a typical episode would be like. Our characters try to save a game world by helping the villain while the antagonists help the hero, and they learn some lessons and deal with PTSD along the way. The animation is decent but not spectacular, although I think all the budget was saved for the action-packed finale fight. There are several things happening at once, it's very cool.

I personally found most of the cast very annoying, which does not inspire confidence. Every time they introduced a new character, I went "oh great, this guy's annoying too". I think some of the characters (like Flappers) are annoying on purpose, but I don't think the rest are meant to be. I'm not sure how to describe it, but it's like the characters are constantly taking pauses during their dialogue even when they don't need to. Plus most of the dialogue sounds like it’s trying too hard to be edgy in that late-2010s kinda way, and it made the show kinda grating to watch. Kit's voice sounds fine, as do the two main villains, but everyone else feels off. Like, Gobbles’ voice does not fit a kids' entertainment character. The only great parts writing-wise are Gobbles' learning speech and Kit's PTSD moments, and Kit’s moments are carried almost entirely by the animation.

One thing I am concerned about is the lore and how the world works. Worlds explode when a hero beats their game, but that leaves several unanswered questions. What about games that get restarted, or stuff like New Game+; are those worlds destroyed and then reborn, or are they gone forever? Are these "game worlds" tied to actual physical video games like Wreck-it-Ralph, or are they more a manifestation of the game developers' original creation? Like, is there a Kit&Kaboodle for every person who bought Kit&Kaboodle, or just one game world representing the source code of that game?

I think the first question is more important to the context of the story, mostly because a key facet of video game worlds is that they don’t end and can be replayed and explored infinitely. Even once Mario beats Bowser, you can still play Mario Odyssey. Maybe these are questions that will get answered later, but they feel important for establishing the stakes. Like, the protagonists are trying to keep the heroes from winning, meaning they're dooming each world to the villain's control. Is this an intentional idea that a shitty life is better than no life, or are the protagonists preventing the worlds from cycling like normal every time a game is restarted? We don't really know what's going on, and maybe the characters don't either, but I think it makes the stakes feel more confusing as opposed to being an interesting mystery.

Also, a minor complaint, but I wish the fight scenes felt more like video game fights. Flappers has some good moments and so does the finale, but the opening fight with Kit&Kaboodle should feel like a video game immediately. You should just see the animation and go "yeah, this is Ratchet&Clank", instead of needing it exposited that every world is a "game world". Also, Gobbles’ deal makes no sense without the trailer, but that’s fine for a pilot instead of a first episode. I do like that all the characters feel like video game characters, and all of the designs are very good. Overall, the pilot did its job in giving me a good idea of what to expect from each episode, but didn't really hook me on the show as a whole. I would watch the next episode, but it's more cautious optimism than enthusiasm.

The Suicide Squad.title: The Suicide Squad
The Suicide Squad.blurb: An incredible movie, with a delightful cast of lovable characters, insane action sequences, strong direction, and an uplifting message about overcoming the limits placed on us by society to do the right thing.
The Suicide Squad.review:
A banger off-beat superhero movie. The main cast is all incredible and very likeable, even Peacemaker. He’s so unhinged in his pursuit of peace through violence that he so clearly enjoys that he’s a delight to watch. My favorite is Ratcatcher II for being the loveable heart of the film and the most heroic one, but Bloodsport, Polka-Dot Man, Harley Quinn and King Shark are all also incredible. Bloodsport really grows on you throughout the film, contrasting nicely against Rick Flagg as the stereotypical hero with a sense of justice even if he works for the wrong people. Harley Quinn is so clearly not all there while obviously having a blast and being arguably the most competent of them all. She also gets some of the best scenes in the movie, but we’ll get back to those later.

The thing that really makes this film stand out ahead of the characters and action is the direction. You get fully engrossed in this off-beat world of B-team heroes and villains that still participate in world events, because that's just what kind of world this is. The music helps set the tone - even if it is a bit overused at times - and the in-universe title cards are incredibly fun. The intro really sets the tone, introducing all these quirky characters and then violently killing them almost all off. It's such a great scene, pulling the rug out from under you and establishing that anyone can die, while still being relevant throughout the whole film thanks to the survival of Flagg and Harley Quinn.

The action in the movie is also top notch. The Peacemaker/Flagg fight is visceral and brutal, while Peacemaker and Bloodsport tearing through a military camp is hilariously dark, especially with the reveal that it’s an ally camp. Harley Quinn gets the standout scene with her solo escape from the prison, and the shot of her diving into Starro's eye is beautiful. Ratcatcher II gets my other favorite scene, summoning a swarm of rats to overthrow Starro. You just watch the streets get covered in rats as Ratcatcher calls out the smallest inhabitants of the city to take out the biggest one with this look of intense determination and satisfaction on her face. It’s genuinely awe-inspiring.

Other things I really like include Harley's romance scene with the dictator. It's so very Harley Quinn, and you feel like she might just go along with his affections until she shoots him unceremoniously. It's such a good character moment while still being incredibly funny. Javelin's javelin being completely useless is an underrated bit. Harley carries it the whole film, trying to figure out what Javelin wanted her to do with it, and in the end she uses it to kill like five guys while the rats are the ones who kill Starro. Starro is an understandable villain who just wanted to drift in space until he was kidnapped and experimented on for years, and yet he's still a terrifying threat that needs to be stopped before he mind controls the whole world in revenge. Amanda Waller getting knocked out by her own underlings because she's willing to sacrifice the whole world is awesome, and really solidifies that the message of the movie is helping the little people, even if it means overthrowing your own government.

When this movie first came out, we were knee deep into the DCEU, and this movie makes perfect sense in that context. We already have the background for superheroes and supervillains and the somewhat realistic politics of this world. Now, it's technically the first movie in the DCU, and I don't think it's quite as good a movie for that. It's mostly stand-alone aside from one mention of Superman to establish Bloodsport's abilities, which is weird now because we don't know who Superman is yet. We're also thrown right into this world of weird-ass supers, which does kind of work. I don't think it's quite as good as the DCU’s first entry as it was as the DCEU’s 11th, but the intro squad has a lot of weird powers that somewhat establishes what world we're in. Even after that, the movie takes itself seriously enough that you can just lean into the absurdity. While Starro is ridiculous and comes kind of out of nowhere, he debuts early enough to get used to him, and all the characters take him super seriously, so the audience starts to as well. Besides, over half the DCU at this point is The Suicide Squad spin-offs anyway.

It's an incredible movie, with a delightful cast of characters, insane action sequences, and an uplifting message about overcoming the limits placed on us by society to do the right thing: Bloodsport was raised to be an assassin from birth, Ratcatcher II was homeless, and Rick Flagg works for the US government, but they all do what they can to save the world anyways. Compared to the rest of the DCEU, it’s a world full of hope, and that message is a much better fit for the start of the new DCU.

Captain America: The Winter Soldier.title: Captain America: The Winter Soldier
Captain America: The Winter Soldier.blurb: A very tight film that makes great use of its ensemble cast for some excellent action sequences and its strong theme of knowing who you can trust. The entire film revolves around trust, from Hydra hiding inside SHIELD to Bucky hiding inside the Winter Soldier to Black Widow’s checkered past to Nick Fury’s espionage tactics to the budding friendship between Steve and Sam Wilson.
Captain America: The Winter Soldier.review:
A very tight film that makes great use of its ensemble cast for some excellent action sequences and its strong theme of knowing who you can trust. The entire film revolves around trust, from Hydra hiding inside SHIELD to Bucky hiding inside the Winter Soldier to Black Widow’s checkered past to Nick Fury’s espionage tactics to the budding friendship between Steve and Sam Wilson. The Hydra twist is brilliant, and the subsequent Bucky twist adds an interesting wrinkle to what would otherwise be a straightforward climax: SHIELD can’t be saved, but can Bucky?

Speaking of Bucky, he has so much aura in this movie, starting immediately with his excellent character introduction. Fury spends like 10 minutes showing off how prepared he is by escaping a bunch of Hydra agents while they attack his car, and then Bucky just appears in the middle of the road and effortlessly flips Fury’s car with a bomb before ripping the door off the car. Not 5 minutes later, he snipes Fury through an apartment window and catches Captain America’s shield. Bucky is instantly established as a threat through not only his power and competence, but also how nonchalant he is about the whole thing. Despite being evil, it makes him cool as fuck. His intro to the highway fight scene is equally incredible, with Bucky just ripping Jasper Sitwell right through the car window before our heroes even know that he’s landed on top of them. It’s an excellent fight scene too, as Bucky fights off Captain America, Black Widow, and Falcon all at once. What helps make him cooler is that he falls for tricks and takes hits, but still keeps going. It makes him feel actually powerful instead of just being propped up by the writers.

Honestly, aside from Bucky’s incredible aura, the characters aren’t that great in this movie. They’re all likeable, and they have some good moments, but none of them really stand out for me like some of Marvel’s other characters do. I like the banter between Steve and Sam at the beginning of the film and how their friendship develops naturally. I also like how Steve slowly comes to trust Natasha as the film goes on, exemplified by her asking him if he’d trust her to save his life, and him saying that “[he] would now.” Nick Fury is badass as always, but I’m not really in love with any of these characters. They’re all pieces in the complex narrative more than characters, which is fine since they play their parts well. Cap argues for freedom over security and oversight, Nat learns to become a person instead of a SHIELD agent, Sam is the normal guy, and Fury learns that he needs friends and trust if he wants to protect the world.

The whole film is about trust, both how you need it to do the right thing and how it can be exploited by the wrong people. The only reason the team even suspects anything about Hydra is because Fury doesn’t trust those around him and hired Batroc to hijack the SHIELD ship so he could steal the data on it. But then, the reason things go sideways is because Fury trusts his old friend and Secretary of the World Security Council, Alexander Pierce, who turns out to be the head of Hydra and the person Fury was stealing from in the first place. Going even further back, the only reason Hydra even lives is because the original founders of SHIELD thought they could trust Hydra scientist Arnim Zola to work with them after Hydra was destroyed, but Zola betrayed that trust by rebuilding Hydra within SHIELD. With SHIELD compromised, Steve, Nat, and Fury have nobody they can trust within SHIELD, which is why they recruit outsider Sam Wilson, who only agrees to help because he trusts that Captain America is fighting for a good cause and knows how to run a mission. And of course there’s Bucky, whom Cap tries to save from being the Winter Soldier in the final battle, and he succeeds enough that Bucky saves his life when the Helicarrier explodes.
