Bucky is the big wrinkle, because the film is pretty confident that SHIELD can’t be saved after it’s been compromised by Hydra, but it still believes that Bucky can be saved from being the Winter Soldier. However, it kinda works. SHIELD has to go because it can’t be trusted anymore as an organization, but the film demonstrates that not everyone in SHIELD is bad. Sure Hydra’s plan still works until Cap & Friends stop it, but there are several people in SHIELD who are loyal to that organization’s stated ideals and work to stop Hydra. They can be still be saved, as seen by Maria Hill joining Stark Industries, because they are just individuals caught up in the organization’s scheme. Similarly, Bucky is one man who has been literally mind controlled by Hydra, and as such, that man can be redeemed because he is just a man and not a massive organization with a focus on world security. Plus, even though we don’t see Bucky’s recovery, he goes to visit his museum exhibit, a strong indicator that he will recover from Hydra’s literal brainwashing.

The trust theme doesn’t have any solid conclusions, but between SHIELD and Bucky and Sam and Pierce, it really just comes down to saying that you can trust the little guy but not the people up top. Fury walks a tightrope on this because he does clearly withhold info from Cap, but he also works to earn Cap’s trust by revealing Project Insight and eventually agrees that SHIELD has to go. Him retiring adds to the film’s statement on this too, as it’s Fury realizing that he can’t be the man on top because the man on top is inherently untrustworthy. If that is the intended message, which I think it is, then it’s a lot more subtle than I’d like it to be.

Other miscellaneous things I liked: the fight scenes in this movie are all really really good with tight, frenetic choreography, especially the elevator fight and the aforementioned highway fight; the scene where Nat and Steve go undercover and Nat has to lead the operation because Steve just can’t do subtle is very fun; and Arnim Zola’s server room of a body is freaking awesome. Also, I think it’s really funny that Bucky visiting the Captain America exhibit still gets the evil Winter Soldier music even though this is Bucky trying to remember who he was before the brainwashing.

As part of the MCU, this is the Phase 2 film most directly connected to Avengers and the rest of the MCU. Black Widow and Fury play major roles, and the movie’s central twist only works as well as it does because we’ve spent so long getting to know SHIELD as a shady but generally well-intentioned organization. Since we’ve spent so long with this status quo, breaking it completely feels like we’re charting new territory without sacrificing our exploration of the present. Avengers is focused around SHIELD bringing together the Avengers, but since the Avengers aren’t part of SHIELD, their status quo hasn’t been changed. That said, it is funny that Nat never brings up Clint Barton at all, since he could in theory be a Hydra mole within SHIELD and that would mess her up. But it’s never mentioned because he’s out of scope of this movie, which is understandable.

It’s a very tight movie with almost no wasted parts. Every bit of dialogue and direction is purposeful, and the way that the characters untangle and reveal the conspiracy of Hydra is really cool. I like that we learn the big twist by the halfway point, so the rest of it is the characters trying to figure out how to stop Hydra. It’s primarily a spy-thriller movie, but Captain America is so superhuman that it still has that superhero flair. Despite being really competent, I don’t think the movie has that special je ne sais quoi to push it into being one of my favorites. The final fight is one of the weakest in my opinion, and I think the ending is understated, being more small character moments with a sequel hook instead of a solid conclusion. I do think that part of the reason it’s so popular is that it appeals to people who don’t like superhero movies, but that’s partly because it is a banger spy thriller film.

Avengers: Age of Ultron.title: Avengers: Age of Ultron
Avengers: Age of Ultron.blurb: A solid sequel to Avengers with a stronger focus on the Avengers as a team. It definitely isn’t as tight of a film as the first one, but it makes up for it with team dynamics and all the little conversations they have. The action scenes are also pretty good, which helps the film because it’s character arcs and plot are fairly weak.
Avengers: Age of Ultron.review:
A solid sequel to Avengers with a stronger focus on the Avengers as a team. It definitely isn’t as tight of a film as the first one, but it makes up for it with team dynamics and all the little conversations they have. Weirdly enough, aside from Thor, the character with the least focus is Captain America, with Tony Stark and Clint getting the most focus. The action scenes are also pretty good, which helps the film because it’s character arcs and plot are fairly weak. It is about the team in their status quo, even if it breaks that status quo at the end.

Starting with the characters, Captain America’s main job is to be the voice of reason who’s focusing on the mission, but the biggest thing he does is “recruit” Wanda and Pietro. Thor is the other least prominent member, but his job is to learn the plot and rally the others when Cap can’t. Specifically, I love that he ends the Tony/Steve argument about Vision by just activating Vision without debate because he’s the only one who knows what’s actually happening thanks to magic foreshadowing water. Natasha and Bruce have their weird little romance going on, which kinda works but never quite lands. I like that Nat likes Bruce because he’s always so reluctant to fight, in contrast to everyone else she knows, and yet she also talks to Hulk like a child. It makes the whole dynamic really weird. Bruce gets really nothing to do this movie aside from Hulk out and play second fiddle to Tony.

Speaking of Tony, he’s the most prominent Avenger, alongside Clint. Tony sets the whole film in motion by building Ultron, then devises the solution by building Vision, and is the one generally causing the most friction in the team by hiding his creations from them. He also should have the biggest arc, but more on that later. Clint is then the other focus as the grounding factor, being the one who brings the team to his house so they can recuperate and the one who motivates Wanda to become an Avenger even if he doesn’t initially trust her. Symbolically, his family are the normal people the Avengers are fighting for, and it’s his sense of normalcy along with Cap’s strength of heart that convinces Wanda and Pietro that the Avengers are heroes and not warmongers. This whole idea of the Avengers interacting with civilians is a recurring theme, first with the big Hulkbuster battle in Africa, then Clint’s family, and then Sokovia. It doesn’t really go anywhere in this movie, though, despite being an interesting throughline.

Wanda and Pietro have almost nothing going on, but I do like that they turn on Ultron as soon as they learn that he’s going to blow up the world. They're not genocidal, they just want revenge against Tony, and even that fades as they see him do everything he can to save people. Really, their lack of character is the most interesting part of the movie, and makes Quicksilver’s death way less impactful than it could be. The Avengers recruited these newbies and one of them immediately dies and it’s just, who cares. Vision is very fun, and I like that he’s the focused straight man. He is to the Avengers what Jarvis was to Tony, being the one who keeps them focused while supporting their mission. Him casually handing Mjolnir to Thor without realizing what it means is both really funny and really awesome. Fury and Maria Hill are pretty much just performing their supporting roles from Avengers just without SHIELD or character arcs, and Rhodey is somehow used better in this film than he is in Iron Man 3.

Ultron is a fun villain. I like that he’s frazzled initially, being naive and kinda funny since he’s based on Tony’s AIs, but becomes more and more serious over the course of the film. His goal evolving from killing the Avengers to killing humanity seems natural, since the Avengers are supposed to be the representation of the best humanity has to offer.

The action scenes are pretty good too. The Hulkbuster/Hulk fight is fun, and the Hulkbuster armor is cool. The Captain America/Ultron fight on the truck is also really good, keeping things on the move while letting Cap show off how persistent he is. I also like the finale, since even though the Avengers are fighting faceless robots, the focus is always on them working together to save civilians. My favorite fight though is the opening assault on the Hydra base. The no-cut scene focusing on each Avenger is an awesome showcase for all of their abilities. The fight has such a clear objective with enough variables to keep it interesting, and everyone gets to use their powers really well. Since we’re on Avengers 2 and MCU 10, we get to do cool shit with people’s powers like Thor making a shockwave off of Cap’s shield. It’s awesome, with a good twist climax by Wanda showing Tony the apocalypse.

Unfortunately, one of the film’s biggest problems is that it really has nothing else going on besides the awesome fights. The plot is incredibly simple, just tracking and fighting Ultron, and the character arcs are incredibly minimal. Almost everyone has an arc if you squint, but none of them get any real focus. Tony has a small one of finally leaving the Avengers behind, but his solution to stopping Ultron is Ultron But It Works This Time, so he doesn’t really learn anything. Cap finds a place to stay after Winter Soldier and has a team to protect the world with, but that’s an external arc instead of an internal one. Clint gets to retire to his home, but I literally didn’t know that was his endgame until the last scene, so is that really even an arc.

Bruce finally gives up and runs away again, which is fair, but it’s less impactful since we don’t see him between the two Avengers movies. It’s also definitely a negative arc, but it does contrast nicely to Nat who chooses to stay and fight despite also being a “monster”. I know people hate on this movie because Nat considers herself a monster because she can’t have kids, but it’s clear she thinks she’s a monster because she was raised to be a killer and doesn’t know anything else. It’s why she stays with Cap at the end, because she can’t just run away when she can turn those monstrous traits into something heroic. The movie never spells this out, but that’s the implication based on like three scenes.

The film’s other biggest problem is its connections to the wider MCU. While the first Avengers (not to be confused with The First Avenger) was a culmination of the preceding 5 films, Age of Ultron doesn’t connect as neatly. The movie doesn’t outright ignore the other films, providing references to threads from Dark World and Winter Soldier to show that they both still happened and affected the characters, (I like that the movie opens with finishing off Hydra from the end of Winter Soldier), but two of the characters feel like they immediately forget their arcs from their past movies.

The big inconsistent arc is Tony, partly because his arc in Iron Man 3 is a bit messy. I like that he’s still traumatized from the Chithauri Invasion, but his arc in Iron Man 3 is learning that he doesn’t need to rely on the Iron Man armor, which he demonstrates by blowing them all up. Here not only does he have a new suit, but he has a new legion of Iron Man drones that work like shitty versions of the suits from Iron Man 3, and then on top of that he wants to make Ultron as a totally autonomous Iron Man so he can stop being a hero. It’s completely counter to his arc from his last film, which is jarring. However, maybe that’s because Iron Man 3’s arc is messy. He did only survive that movie thanks to having an army of drone suits, so it seems natural that he would double down on building more and more autonomous suits so he and his friends don’t need to go into danger. Regardless of which arc the film wanted to go with, an explanation would have been nice.

The other character who forgot their lesson is Fury, this time from Winter Soldier. He agreed that SHIELD has to go because it was corrupted by Hydra, so here he learns nothing and instead makes SHIELD 2, complete with a second Helicarrier. We even see one of the SHIELD agents from Winter Soldier on the new Helicarrier, proving that this is just SHIELD 2. It is admittedly a very Fury thing to do, going behind Cap’s back and restarting SHIELD with his own hand-picked agents so there’s no corruption from Hydra, and I’m pretty sure he at least didn’t put instant death guns on the new Helicarrier so he kinda learned his lesson. However, Cap should have way more of a negative reaction to the reveal, but he doesn’t because it’s supposed to be a hype moment. Really the problem is that undoing Winter Soldier is supposed to be a hype moment. Granted it is very helpful in the particular scenario that we are trying to evacuate civilians from a flying city, but Fury really did just make SHIELD 2 after a whole film about the fact that government oversight organizations can’t be trusted.

Looking to the future, we get a completely new Avengers team since Tony, Thor, Bruce, and Clint quit. I like the lineup for the new team, although the film is so much about this team’s status quo that it feels weird to end it uncermoniously. It makes sense why each member quits individually, especially knowing that they have backup members, but still. We also get our second hints at the Infinity Stones, which is fun. Technically this film should come after Guardians of the Galaxy, but I’m not watching a whole movie just to explain 1 (one) magic rock. That movie will come later. Thor just pretty much says that the Stones are items of extreme power, which is enough because we see the familiar Tesseract and Aether. It’s also an expansion on the Collector’s line from the Dark World post-credits, so it’s more intrigue that provides just enough context for Vision and Ultron. Plus, Thor leaves to learn more about the Infinity Stones, so it’s a promise for a future film without taking away the conclusion to Ultron. Ultron is defeated, and Tony has seemingly maybe learned his lesson for real this time.

It’s still a good movie that utilizes almost all of its cast very well. The fight scenes are very fun, and the plot is a solid enough excuse to facilitate those fight scenes. The biggest downside versus the first Avengers is the lack of general character arcs. Age of Ultron is a big-screen experience with its plethora of great action scenes, but it definitely has elements of being an episode of an ongoing series versus a standalone film. Still worth a watch if you’re going through the MCU, even if it lacks the gravitas and big conclusion of its predecessor.

Peacemaker S1.title: Peacemaker S1
Peacemaker S1.blurb: An incredible show. Despite almost everyone being assholes, the show is all about dissecting why they’re assholes and what it’ll take to make them do better. This show is also about fighting alien butterflies who possess people in order to take over the world. It’s peak.
Peacemaker S1.review:
An incredible show. Despite almost everyone being assholes, the show is all about dissecting why they’re assholes and what it’ll take to make them do better. This comes partly in the form of Adebayo, the newbie and “nice one” who’s not used to how black ops works yet, and partly in the form of the characters learning how to be sincere about their feelings instead of treating everyone like a threat. This show is also about fighting alien butterflies who possess people in order to take over the world. It’s peak.

It helps that the show is hilarious. The characters are almost all super jaded, so they bounce off each other really well for the audience despite being grating to each other. It works because everyone uses humor as a coping mechanism, with Peacemaker especially using it to push people away and avoid being vulnerable, so none of the jokes feel forced. Peacemaker’s hurtful jokes clearly hurt the other characters, and their jokes hurt him in turn, so it feels real when the characters open up enough to talk about it. Harcourt and Economos use humor similarly, playing parallels to each other. They both learn to open up, but they’re closed off because Harcourt is arrogant and Economos is insecure. The big exception is Vigilante, who is just that stupid, which usually results in him hilariously misreading situations. Peacemaker also seems stupid, but he generally understands what’s going on around him and has depth while Vigilante just thinks that everything is literally one big joke. Adebayo also often cracks jokes, but they’re to try and break the ice and make friends since she’s the most openly friendly and trusting, even if she has secrets of her own. Pretty much the only one who doesn’t joke is Murn, which is because he is both level-headed enough to not need a coping mechanism and because he takes everything seriously.

Speaking of Murn, his reveal is pretty good. Everyone talks about how much of a bastard he is, but he seems like a pretty reasonable guy, so you’re just waiting for the shoe to drop. And then once we learn that Murn is a butterfly, it leaves you wondering what his deal is because there’s no reason for him to be a double agent since he’s the one who brought the butterfly job to Amanda Waller’s attention in the first place. It’s a great reveal, and the reveal that Murn is completely genuine still works because it blindsides the characters. Funnily enough, I don’t think Peacemaker ever learns Murn’s true identity.

The main character of our show is Peacemaker, the twist villain from The Suicide Squad, and he should be an absolutely insufferable protagonist. However, the show puts in the work to humanize him. It helps that we see him in private when he’s not putting on a face, and like Adebayo realizes, he’s completely miserable and alone. His best friend is a bird, and he only tolerates his self-proclaimed human best friend. But the big factor is that we learn where he comes from: his dad is a Nazi supervillain. The show not only makes it clear that he hates Peacemaker and is the one who gave Peacemaker his worst qualities, but also that Peacemaker recognizes his father’s faults and is clearly not a Nazi himself. Peacemaker may not be a good person, but he makes it clear from his second scene that he’s not trying to be racist or misogynist, he just doesn’t realize that he is. From there, Peacemaker confronting, rejecting, and finally killing his father is an externalization of him becoming a better person, providing a physical manifestation of his character arc for the audience to latch onto.

Adebayo is our other POV character, and I really like her. She’s kind while not incompetent, and quickly adjusts to being good at her job while not becoming an awful person. She genuinely feels bad about betraying her team to Waller, and makes it up to them by exposing Waller to the world. I don’t have much more to say about her, but I really like her relatively simple arc.

A character I think is interesting is Detective Song. She clearly hates Peacemaker’s dad, and yet is committed enough to the law that she lets him go when she realizes that he’s been framed by Peacemaker’s allies. Despite him being a Nazi, it’s her job to free him and bring Peacemaker to justice, and it’s this dedication to the legal system that ultimately gets her and her entire team killed by butterflies. It’s an extension of the themes from The Suicide Squad that doing what is right does not mean following the law or the government, but ensuring that those who are doing evil can’t do more evil. Adebayo exposing Waller is also a continuation of this theme, finally giving her the penance she deserves. Waller isn’t in the show much, but her shadow hangs over Peacemaker’s team, so her getting exposed as the bastard she is feels cathartic despite the show ostensibly being about the Butterflies.

The story of the show is also really good. Everything is interconnected, and actions taken in one episode affect the rest. Peacemaker’s dad only gets brought into the show because Economos frames him for Peacemaker’s murder of a Butterfly, and that whole arc spirals from there. Episodes feel episodic while still being part of a larger whole, giving the show great pacing where events play off each other while still getting periodically resolved. The plots tie into the characters’ arcs really well too, always taking the time to show how its characters react to their missions, which helps ground everything and keeps things feeling cohesive instead of rushed or disconnected.

The intro is also peak. There’s a full-ass dance number set to upbeat music where all the characters dance with emotionless expressions. It’s perfectly emblematic of the show’s simultaneous weirdness and sincerity, giving us insane events and characters while having the characters treat everything with the appropriate seriousness. Alien butterflies that possess people seem unhinged to us, but to the characters they’re a serious threat, so it makes sense that the characters treat them like one. The show balances these two aspects super well, blending them into the surprisingly lovable characters to make an excellent offbeat superhero series you won’t soon forget.

Fant4stic.title: Fant4stic
Fant4stic.blurb: Genuinely one of the worst movies I've ever watched. It's worse as a Fantastic Four adaptation than it is as a movie, but only barely. As an FF adaptation, it just completely flattens all of the characters into empty shells and misses the entire point of the team. As a movie, it has completely flat characters that barely change and a plot that skips over all the interesting bits.
Fant4stic.review:
Genuinely one of the worst movies I've ever watched. It's worse as a Fantastic Four adaptation than it is as a movie, but only barely. As an FF adaptation, it just completely flattens all of the characters into empty shells and misses the entire point of the team. As a movie, it has completely flat characters that barely change and a plot that skips over all the interesting bits in favor of establishing several status quos in a row before blowing them all up because the movie needed a supervillain fight scene.

At its core, the movie feels like a horror film. Everything is set up to emphasize the tragedy of a government experiment turning bright young scientists into body horror monsters. The government only recruits genius Reed instead of his best friend and helper Ben, so when Reed decides to go to the other dimension on his own instead of letting the government steal the glory, of course he invites Ben along. The only reason the head scientist’s son Johnny is there is because he has to pay off a debt for trashing his car, and the scientist’s daughter Sue that wants to be there is adopted. The only two who are “supposed” to be there are Reed and Victor, and Victor is an asshole who shouldn’t be there at all. So of course Victor is stranded in the other dimension and Reed escapes, leaving the three biggest casualties to be used by the government as weapons. The whole thing feels artificial and convoluted, which really rips away any tension and impact everyone getting powers should have.

Then of course the government decides to go back into the other dimension to create more superhumans, and this gets them all killed by Victor, who has become the embodiment of the other dimension. You’d think this would mean that Victor wins as the embodiment of humanity’s hubris is trying to control something they can’t and roping innocent people into it, but no the plucky young superhuman scientists beat them with the power of teamwork because this is supposed to be a superhero movie actually. It just doesn’t work. It's a classic tale of "just because they could, doesn't mean they should", except literally the only person who dies that we care about at all is the lead scientist, so it reads like a happy ending when the movie is not set up for it. Or maybe I just want everyone to die because I hate this movie.

Part of the problem is just how overpowered Victor is. He explodes people’s heads with a flick of his wrist, and yet never bothers to explode our protagonists’ heads because then they would lose and we can’t have that in our superhero movie. It’s not even like head exploding is an escalation of Victor’s powers: it’s literally the first thing he does after returning from the other dimension after not being mentioned for the entire middle hour of the film.

Honestly, our protagonists aren't much better. They barely feel like friends, and don't get a chance to interact after they get their powers because they're kept as government lab rats. The only one who really wants to be there is Johnny, but this literally goes nowhere because the finale is about Victor coming back to destroy the Earth. Ben is the one who wants to be there the least, but he and Johnny never interact for this to be a problem. Ben and Reed have like 1 fight about Reed kinda being responsible for turning Ben into The Thing, but then it also goes nowhere because the finale is about Victor coming back to destroy the Earth. Sue seems ambivalent about the whole thing to be honest. Reed is at least trying to cure everyone, but we literally don’t see any of his progress because it all happens during the 1-year time skip. Oh yeah, there’s a 1-year time skip after everyone gets their powers, so they’ve all adjusted to being superhuman government lab rats already. The time during that skip is potentially the most interesting part of the movie and the part with the most horror potential, but instead it’s glossed over entirely to show us the status quo and then advance to the next plot point, which in this case is Victor coming back to destroy the Earth.

FF as a horror movie is an interesting idea, but not as a big screen adaptation, and also not when it’s done really badly. The team's origin is stupid convoluted, making it so Sue doesn't even go on the mission and Ben just tags along because he's Reed's best friend as opposed to actually being part of the group. Victor von Doom is literally just some guy, and then he turns into the living embodiment of a hostile alien dimension. Everyone gets their powers because the elements just glomp onto them when they do the interdimensional travel, which is more complicated than it needs to be because it’s normally just random. Why does Ben become a rock man? Nobody cares except this movie, when they decide it’s because he gets covered in alien rocks while jumping between dimensions. Sue doesn’t even get her powers from the other dimension, she’s just hit with the teleportation energy. It's certainly not a film about superheroes, and it's barely a film about the characters. It's about a science experiment gone wrong that gets co-opted by the American government to use as weapons, which is not the Fantastic Four at all.

I will shout out the two things I like about this movie. There’s one scene where the team gets the interdimensional teleporter working, and Johnny tries to give Reed a fist bump, but Reed gives him a high five and it’s really awkward. It’s very funny. Also the reveal of Reed’s powers where his foot is stuck under some rubble and then he crawls towards Ben only to realize that his foot is still stuck and his legs are stretched is good. The special effects are also decent.

Everything feels hollow, like none of the movie's ideas are coalescing into anything greater, or really anything at all. There are vibes of a horror flick, but the movie never commits, especially in the ending. All of the acting, directing, and writing feel empty and unenthused, and none of the characters feel real. Also the movie spawned the "say that again" meme, which is a pretty good one. That scene really is the capstone to the whole movie, though: refusing to meaningfully engage with the source material while only gesturing at grounded character writing.

Ant-Man.title: Ant-Man
Ant-Man.blurb: Ant-Man is a simple yet delightful superhero comedy. It doesn't do anything particularly special in terms of characters or plots or themes, but it executes its simple ideas very well with some truly unique fight scenes that take full advantage of our hero’s powerset.
Ant-Man.review:
Ant-Man is a simple yet delightful superhero comedy. It doesn't do anything particularly special in terms of characters or plots or themes, but it executes its simple ideas very well with some truly unique fight scenes that take full advantage of our hero’s powerset. The film's main theme is redemption, with Scott trying to redeem himself in the eyes of his ex-wife after committing a crime, and Hank trying to redeem himself in the eyes of his daughter after pushing her away. In some strange way, Darren Cross is also trying to redeem himself in the eyes of Hank, but everything he's doing just makes Hank hate him more and he kinda knows it. It's not the most prevalent theme of all time, nor is it explored to its fullest, but it helps make everything feel cohesive.

Among other things, Ant-Man is a comedy, and like most Marvel movies, this primarily comes through in its character dialogue. Everyone is very funny, from Hank's sardonic wit to Scott's chill wisecracking to Cassie's overexcitedness to Luis' nigh-incoherent ramblings. Even Hope gets her moments, despite mostly being the straight man of the film. The only character who's really not funny is Darren, which makes sense for the villain. The movie sets the comedic tone in its second scene, when the prison fight Scott is in turns out to be a farewell ritual between a group of friends. It establishes that this is a lighthearted comedy where people are generally nicer than they seem on the surface, and this holds true for everyone except for Darren. Even Scott's ex-wife's new boyfriend cares deeply for Cassie and comes to respect Scott after realizing that Scott does too.

The characters are good as characters as well as comedians. Cassie is Scott's daughter and anchor and makes everything he does feel more heroic since he's doing it for her. Even if it's just so he can be with his daughter, it's very clear that Cassie loves Scott and that Scott cares about her deeply in a selfless way. Hank and Hope have a really interesting dynamic, with Hope resenting her father for pushing her away while Hank thinks he's doing everything he can to protect her. The reveal that Hank's wife died while being Ant-Man (or as she was called, Wasp) makes it abundantly clear why Hank refuses to let Hope in the suit. It's extremely selfish of him, to the point that he literally hires another man so he doesn't lose his daughter in case something goes wrong, but it's done from a place of love. Learning this makes Hope respect her father more, even if her negative feelings don't truly go away. Hank deciding to give Hope a new Wasp suit in the post-credits also shows that he's come to respect his daughter's autonomy more, treating her as a woman who can make her own choices instead of the little girl she was when her mom died. Even if she will get hurt, it's her choice, and it's worth the risk to break down the barriers so they can actually be family. This could maybe be connected to Scott doing everything he can to be with Cassie even if it hurts him, but the film never makes that connection so it's unclear if Scott actually impacted Hank’s development aside bringing his conflict with Hope to a fever pitch. Darren has the least going on, but he's just so punchably evil that you don't care that there's not much under the surface.

Maybe even more than the characters, Ant-Man's big selling point is its style. And I don't just mean that it's a heist movie instead of a normal action flick, but that it takes full advantage of its character being able to shrink and talk to ants. The ants are so fucking cool, which is a sentence I don't get to say about a lot of movies. It's really fun watching Scott learn to work with them after seeing how intimidating they can be up close, and when they're used as threats, it feels visceral because that's a lot of fucking ants. They’re also used so creatively, forming rafts through sewers and carrying EMPs to data centers. The other big thing is how well the film uses Scott's and Darren's small statures to craft unique fight scenes. Sure the choreography is mostly generic since the ants are only involved in the heists and not the big fights, but the setting is used to its fullest potential. There's a fight inside a half-full briefcase falling through the air, and a fight inside a little girl's bedroom where the characters throw Thomas the Tank Engine at each other and hide inside hairs on the rug. The first scene where Scott shrinks shows this so well, with him dodging under heels at a rave and then a vacuum cleaner as he falls through gaps in the floor of his apartment building. It gives the movie a vibe like no other, and really makes Ant-Man feel unique as both a film and a character.

The film is pretty separated from the rest of the MCU continuity-wise, aside from the cool Falcon fight. I like that the post-credits scene has Falcon suggest recruiting Ant-Man by saying that he "knows a guy", paralleling all of Luis' insane stories. SHIELD, Tony’s dad, Peggy Carter, and remnants of Hydra all get mentioned, but they don’t do anything aside from be recognizable faces that place this film in the world of the MCU. This is important because while the film isn’t connected continuity-wise, is takes excellent advantage of the established setting. We don't need to suspend our disbelief too hard for Ant-Man because this is already a world where Iron Man and Captain America exist. It makes Ant-Man fit right in, instead of being an anomaly in an otherwise normal world. It's also our first expansion into the smaller-scale MCU, with superheroes operating in mostly day-to-day life instead of being world-changers like Iron Man and Thor. It's very fun.

Overall, it's not the most complex movie, but it's an enjoyable one. The action setpieces are definitely my favorite part of the movie for how awesome and unique they are. The comedy is a standout, and both help elevate the simple plot and characters into a thoroughly enjoyable experience that stands out against the rest of the MCU's large-scale lineup.

Creature Commandos.title: Creature Commandos
Creature Commandos.blurb: Creature Commandos was a fun show with good characters and a strong personality. The whole main cast is solid, with special shoutouts to Phosphorus' and GI Robot's humor (intended or otherwise) and the Bride's simple but strong character arc.
Creature Commandos.review:
Creature Commandos was a fun show with good characters and a strong personality. The whole main cast is solid, with special shoutouts to Phosphorus' and GI Robot's humor (intended or otherwise) and the Bride's simple but strong character arc. The show's story is also generally good, but has a few too many twists for how little time the show spends on the main story.

Each episode aside from the first is split between the main narrative and flashbacks for each of the Commandos' backstories, which means the main narrative doesn't get a lot of focus. A lot still manages to happen each episode, but it doesn't feel as fleshed out as it could be. The last episode in particular feels like it doesn’t have enough time to tell the story it wants to tell because half of the episode is spent on Nina’s backstory. I wish the show was paced so the last episode is entirely the main plot, especially since it would give it more room to breathe. I do like that there is no big final battle and it’s just Bride killing the princess, but it does mean that a lot of the other characters don’t contribute much to the finale. Rick Flagg in particular does almost nothing despite being one of our main POV characters for the first half of the show.

The backstories themselves are great, and do a really good job of characterizing each Commando as a slightly different kind of fucked up outsider. However, they take up a lot of time that feels like it’s distracting from the main plot, especially since they run through the whole episode. What makes this worse is that some of them are only tangentially related to what’s happening in the main plot, namely Phosphorus' and Weasel’s. They’re still really good short films, they just don’t contribute much. Some of them are placed really well though, such as Bride’s, GI Robot’s, and Nina’s, even if I feel like Nina’s was placed where it was just to make her death hit harder. It does hit really hard, though, and nails home that society placed Nina with the likes of Phosphorus and Bride just because she looks like a fish person even though she’s actually a sweetheart.

Even with the pacing problems, the show is a fun start to the DCU proper, as opposed to being added retroactively like The Suicide Squad and Peacemaker. This show fits right in with the world that those two established, and is hopefully a sign of good things to come.

Captain America: Civil War.title: Captain America: Civil War
Captain America: Civil War.blurb: This movie beats the Avengers 2.5 allegations by being so squarely focused on Captain America and Bucky, but it’s also clearly the non-Avengers movie most connected to the rest of the MCU by far. It makes pretty good use of these connections, particularly to both provide the groundwork for the Sokovia Accords to make sense in-universe and to act as a strong moral framework.
Captain America: Civil War.review:
I don’t normally start with MCU connections, but I think it’s warranted here given how many MCU connections there are. I do think this movie beats the Avengers 2.5 allegations by being so squarely focused on Captain America and Bucky, but it’s also clearly the non-Avengers movie most connected to the rest of the MCU by far. In general it makes pretty good use of these connections, particularly to provide the groundwork for the Sokovia Accords to make sense in-universe. It also provides a strong moral framework for the film, as while Cap never says it out loud, the Sokovia Accords make the Avengers susceptible to be infiltrated by people like Hydra in the same way that SHIELD was.

However, many of the supporting Avengers characters feel underutilized. Wanda and Vision in particular aren’t explored as fully as they could be, and Clint almost doesn’t contribute to the film aside from freeing Wanda from Avengers Compound. I think my biggest complaint is that we just got a new Avengers team at the end of Age of Ultron, and we get to see them on one mission before the team is dismantled by the Sokovia Accords. I wish we got more of them, especially since they’re less powerful overall than the original team, outside of Vision and maybe Wanda. Black Widow also plays a major part of the film and then vanishes after helping Cap escape Tony, never to be seen again. It’s weird.

Thor and Hulk not being around fits Age of Ultron, but is also very convenient for the plot because there’s no way that either of them would agree with the Accords. Despite there being too many characters, there are also so many that leaving one out feels like a glaring omission: Nick Fury. I know the world thinks he’s dead, but you’d think either him or Maria Hill would have some kind of opinion about the Accords that they’d share with either Cap or Tony if not both. Fury being unmentioned is even weirder since Fury was a big part of Winter Soldier and this film is a direct sequel to that.

Outside of the prior connections, the movie also works to expand the world of the MCU, arguably even more than Age of Ultron, namely by introducing Black Panther and Spider-Man. I like Black Panther’s introduction, and he fits really well into this film’s themes and political plot. Spider-Man, on the other hand, is introduced so awkwardly. He’s just introduced in a 5-minute exposition dump so Tony can have him fight in the airport battle, and he doesn’t even really contribute much plotwise. It feels more like the higher-ups went “you gotta introduce Spider-Man”, and then the writers did it without changing their movie. If anything, it makes Iron Man look more like an asshole because he recruits outside help for what is basically an Avengers infighting conflict, but then Cap does the same thing with Ant-Man so whatever. It’s a net zero, like the rest of his appearance

As for the actual movie outside the MCU connections, it’s pretty good, if overly complex. There are a lot of moving parts, and they don’t all coalesce well. Like I said, most of the characters don’t contribute much outside of being necessary for the full force of the Accords to be felt, but the Accords themselves feel secondary to the Steve/Tony/Bucky conflict. The movie raises a lot of interesting questions about control and responsibility and government oversight, and while it doesn’t answer them concretely, it provides a pretty good idea of what it thinks the answers are. Cap is our protagonist, and while that doesn’t always mean he’s right, Winter Soldier pretty much answers that for us. Government needs less control because unlike people, it’s corruptible. There is the argument that the Avengers should be held responsible for the damages they cause, but the Avengers did not cause most of the problems that they are being held responsible for. Loki caused the Chithauri Invasion, Hydra was going to do a genocide when Cap dropped the Helicarriers in the lake, and while Tony did create Ultron, Ultron was also sentient and made the conscious choice to try and cause a mass extinction. If anything, the government’s emphasis is on the fact that they didn’t clean up after themselves, which means the logical thing to do is not control the Avengers, but ask them to help with the clean-up. So the government definitely just wants control of the Avengers, meaning the Accords are straight up a bad idea. Even Tony is only barely tolerating the Accords by the end.

Speaking of Tony, he’s kinda out of it in this movie, to the point of being almost out of character. I wish we got more of his spiral between Ultron and this film, because it’s clear he’s at a low point despite being at a high point at the end of Ultron. Instead he blames himself for Ultron and thinks he needs supervision, so he takes the first option available to him. I do get why he tries to kill Bucky at the end - he still blames himself for his past sins and so can’t forgive Bucky for his - but I wish we got more of that spiral.

The ending works thematically though because everything is about responsibility for past actions and revenge, from the Sokovia Accords being about prior incidents to Tony trying to atone for Ultron to Steve trying to save Bucky to T’Challa trying to avenge his father to Zemo trying to avenge his family. Through this theme, it’s fitting that Steve can look past Bucky’s time as the Winter Soldier while Tony can’t. Ironically, Tony the futurist is stuck in the past while the 80-year-old man out of time looks to the future. It’s an interesting intersection of their arcs, even if I don’t know if it works for Tony. He’s spent three movies fighting villains that are mirrors of his dark past, for him to be trapped in that past and not develop out of it feels wrong. T’Challa is the only one who really changes, letting go of revenge to help those in need because it’s what his father would have wanted. It’s thematically pretty cohesive once you ignore the fact that the government is involved, which is what makes the finale work emotionally even if Tony’s multi-film arc is slightly off.

The main villain is Zemo, and he’s so fucking petty that it’s enjoyable. He literally waterboards a man just so he could get a recording of Bucky killing Tony’s parents. And then mind controls Bucky for basically no reason except to make the Avengers suspicious of him so he could kill the other Winter Soldiers and then make Tony try to kill Steve and Bucky. His plan is so convoluted for no reason, it’s great. He also kinda wins because the Avengers break up, but Steve promises Tony that he can rely on him if he needs to, so Zemo still loses because Steve refuses to quit. It’s poetic, in a way. The film is about revenge and not letting go of the past, and Steve lets go of the past, causing Zemo to lose. T’Challa also lets go of the past and saves Zemo from killing himself, so Zemo double loses. The Accords still exist though, neutering the Avengers, so Zemo also kinda wins. The ending of this movie is very inconclusive aside from vaguely gesturing at “things will repair themselves eventually”.

The fight scenes are also pretty good. I was complaining that Spider-Man and Ant-Man don’t contribute anything, but they do contribute very well to the airport fight. It helps add moving pieces and makes the whole thing feel even more chaotic. Everyone gets to use their skills while still having small character moments, which makes it the standout fight. The final battle between Tony and Cap and Bucky is also really good. It feels appropriately weighty and dramatic, with two friends beating each other up over ideological and personal differences. Cap dropping the shield at the end shows that he will no longer be the symbol he used to be because the symbol has no meaning.

The movie’s biggest flaw and strength is just how many moving parts there are. The Sokovia Accords play a big role, but they’re really just a front for that personal battle between past and future that Tony and Steve represent. It generally works pretty well once everything coalesces, even if it feels like some characters and plot points aren’t used as well as they could be. The ending is also very up-in-the-air, even more so than Winter Soldier. While Winter Soldier makes you think about what the movie’s main message is, Civil War ends with a muddled victory that feels more inconclusive than anything. Steve and Tony have kinda repaired their relationship, but the evil Accords still exist and the Avengers are still broken. Of the five at the start of the film, only Vision remains. It’s a hollow ending that may be intentional, but feels even more like the ending to a TV arc than Age of Ultron did. That said, the film still mostly works as an exploration of revenge and past sins once you get past the plethora of moving parts.

Superman.title: Superman
Superman.blurb: A beautifully sincere film about overcoming corporate cynicism to do the right thing. Superman is packed to the brim with heart, which bursts through in its creative action sequences and seeps through the quiet character moments.
Superman.review:
A beautifully sincere film about overcoming corporate cynicism to do the right thing. Superman is packed to the brim with heart, which bursts through in its creative action sequences and seeps through the quiet character moments. The movie is very busy, both visually and plot-wise, yet manages to make everything feel connected and coherent by tying it all around its characters.

While the movie could feel crowded, I personally love that the world is unapologetically filled with superheroes and aliens and futuristic tech. The opening crawl immediately tells us that metahumans have been around for 300 years, cueing us in that this world is similar - but not quite the same - to our own. The opening crawl itself is kept interesting with the poetry of 300/30/3 timeskips, which helps keep the audience invested in the exposition. Once the crawl ends, we quickly understand that the characters understand that all the sci-fi stuff exists and that we should understand it too: an understanding that we know what a pocket universe is; what clones are; what nanotech is. There's a few throwaway lines about Guy Gardner being from space, and we’re expected to understand that this needs no further explanation. This unabashed sincerity and respect for the audience allows the movie to run free with its fantastical ideas that make the world feel alive.

Despite all the different sci-fi elements and plot threads, the story is surprisingly coherent. Every narrative thread centers around either Lex Luthor trying to take down Superman or Superman finding his place in the world in light of someone who opposes his ideals. Superman himself is bursting with idealism, believing he can save people instead of just beating villains, and follows through on those ideals when push comes to shove. My favorite example of this is the kaiju scene, where on top of trying to find a way to beat the monster without killing it, Superman is saving all the living beings in harm's way, including dogs and even squirrels. It’s an excellent showcase of who Superman is as a character, and is downright inspirational.

Opposite Superman is Lex Luthor, who is delightfully egotistical in this movie. He believes that humanity has to destroy what's better than them to prove themselves superior, which really means that he should get to engage in all of his worst impulses. He’s evil through and through, with no limits to what he'll do to kill Superman or stifle other human opponents. He traps ex-girlfriends and political opponents in an other-dimensional jail and enslaves monkeys to create anti-Superman bot accounts on social media. The end of the movie where Superman tells Lex that he could help humanity too, if he just put his mind to it, is so damn good for both their characters. Superman sees the best in people, and Lex is too blinded by his hate to actually prove to the world that humanity can compete with Superman. Lex getting mauled by Krypto is also really funny.

The rest of the supporting cast is really good too. Jimmy Olsen pulls through with the reporting, and his source sending him the photos that she's been taking all movie is such a good Chekhov's Gun. Lois Lane is on top of things, challenging Superman's ideals while never discouraging him or giving up on him. Mr Terrific is, well, terrific, doing the right thing despite what his team thinks and proving himself to be a badass while doing it. Guy Gardner is such an asshole, yet even he does the right thing when it comes down to it. Hawkgirl doesn't get enough to do, but Metamorpho shines in the few scenes he's in. His sun scene is one of my favorites in the film, being beautifully poignant in the way he literally creates light in the darkness, even if his light isn't perfect.

The fight scenes are also phenomenal. Engineer has a really interesting powerset that she puts to great effect, and it looks incredible visually. The Superman v Ultraman fight is also very good, showing how Superman’s creativity overcomes all of Lex’s meticulous planning because Lex lacks heart and allies. My favorite fight though is easily the Mr Terrific fight in the camp. The scene is shot beautifully, spinning around Lois in the bubble as Mr Terrific beats the crap out of Luthor’s grunts around her with his drones. One of my favorite fights in any James Gunn film.

Everything in this movie just comes together, despite its lightning-fast pace and lack of focus on Clark as a reporter. Superman is Clark, though, and that comes through in the quieter moments. An incredible superhero movie, an incredible Superman movie, and an incredible start to what will hopefully be an incredible DCU.

Spider-Man: Homecoming.title: Spider-Man: Homecoming
Spider-Man: Homecoming.blurb: Our second Spider-Man reboot in 5 years and our third series in 11 finally sticks the landing by making Peter Parker not an insufferable asshole. Instead, he comes across as an awkward nerd who genuinely means well but has too many of his own problems to really make friends. This charming version of Peter combines with a genuine sense of humor and great action sequences to make a focused, enjoyable action-comedy.
Spider-Man: Homecoming.review:
Our second Spider-Man reboot in 5 years and our third series in 11 finally sticks the landing by making Peter Parker not an insufferable asshole. Instead, he comes across as an awkward nerd who genuinely means well but has too many of his own problems to really make friends. This charming version of Peter combines with a genuine sense of humor and great action sequences to make a focused, enjoyable action-comedy.

The first half of the film teeters between being relatably funny and painfully relatable. Peter is too excellent of a teenager to the point where it makes me cringe to watch because he’s just too relatable in how little he thinks about the consequences of his actions. He already knows to be responsible, and his main arc is learning the limits of his abilities as a teenager instead of trying to be an adult like Iron Man. The humor is generally on point though, with it all feeling like very natural teenage humor. MJ in particular kills it with every line.

The first half is really all just buildup to the long finale, starting with us learning that ruthless supervillain Vulture is love interest Liz’s dad. That scene in the car as Peter has an internal panic attack while Vulture pieces together that Peter is Spider-Man is terrifying. Vulture plays it so well, protecting his daughter while threatening Peter with death. On top of that, Peter pretending to go along and then immediately apologizing to Liz that he has to leave is incredible. It’s such a small moment, but it’s the first time he really acts on the realization that being Spider-Man isn’t just being a famous hero, but has actual consequences on his life.

The ending is kinda weird though because Peter’s entire arc is internal and doesn’t affect the plot in any meaningful way. There’s the scene where he lifts the heavy thing and fully accepts that Spider-Man is him as opposed to him trying to be Spider-Man, which while a nice Iron Man 3 complement, is not the thing that beats Vulture because there’s a whole fight after that. He spends the whole movie sacrificing his school life to try and take down Vulture, and fails over and over. Then at the end, he sacrifices his school life to try and take down Vulture, and succeeds. You can argue that Peter stops trying to go it alone and accepts that he needs help, but Ned’s sole contribution is to help stop Shocker, and Peter calling Happy amounts to nothing because Happy doesn’t actually answer. Him turning down Tony’s offer to join the Avengers is probably because of his realization with Liz that he wants to have a personal life too, but again it feels like such a minor arc. My first draft of this paragraph was totally different because it took me like an hour to figure out what Peter’s actual arc was. There’s also a chance that he’s rejecting Stark to protect the little guy because Vulture and Liz were the little guys, and he’s supporting Vulture’s position that the government should let the little people take care of themselves. However, I’m not sure that Peter even knew what Vulture’s deal was so this would be entirely the writers’ position and not Peter’s.

While the plot and central character arc are fairly weak, the action scenes are awesome. Spider-Man is super kinetic and great at using the environments around him. The first two fights with Vulture are cut tragically short, but the final fight with him is really good. Having it take place on the outside of a plane is a really cool setpiece that the movie uses to full effect. The scene where Spider-Man tries to stitch the ferry back together is really tense, and the scene at the Washington Monument is really fun. There’s never a sense that anybody is in any danger, but it’s tense seeing how Spider-Man is going to figure out how to save everyone. And with the ferry scene, the twist is that he doesn’t, Iron Man does. It’s a good twist. Honestly, the movie almost feels like a plot strung together to hit these setpieces. Why is Vulture in DC? To have a Washington Monument setpiece. Why is he on a boat? To have a ferry setpiece. The fight scenes are good enough that the simple plot works for me though.

Like Ant-Man, this movie uses its MCU connections primarily in its setting. We’re reaching the point where the MCU is a setting and not just a plot, which I like, but Iron Man helps keep this film connected to the wider saga, which is probably a good thing for now. Stark plays a surprisingly minor role in the plot, serving primarily as the mentor figure for Peter: the one who can tell him that he’s trying too hard to prove himself and is working beyond his means. I do like that the final fight is done without Stark’s suit, and yet Stark approves of Peter enough to give him the suit back anyways. It’s a nice extension of him turning on the Sokovia Accords in Civil War. Also, Pepper is in this film but not Age of Ultron or Civil War, which is funny.

This film also naturally draws comparisons to the other Spider-Man first films, and I’m so glad this isn’t another Spider-Man origin story. We understand who Peter is, and we don’t need an explanation because the MCU is full of superheroes already. Plus, we don’t get another stupid, convoluted Uncle Ben death. Instead of Peter learning to be responsible, it’s about him learning how to deal with that responsibility. He can’t have a relationship, but he can trust his best friend to have his back. There’s less drama about Peter being Peter, and more about him trying to actually stop supervillains. Him being Spider-Man still affects his social life, but the film doesn’t really kick into high gear until Peter gets invested in the plot. The two colliding is still the most interesting part of the movie, but the plot feels actually relevant instead of tacked on like it does in most of the other Spider-Man films. I generally like this movie, even if the characters aren’t as good as I remember. Granted, I’m also not a teenager anymore, and this is the most teenage Spider-Man yet. It gives this film its own identity among both the other Spider-Man and MCU films, which helps it stand out despite its flaws.

Black Panther.title: Black Panther
Black Panther.blurb: A solid film with good characters, a well-structured plot, and awesome worldbuilding. Despite all the cool action sequences, this film is about the politics of how Wakanda should interact with the world. The first half of the film is a cautionary tale about what could happen if Wakanda exposes itself to the world and the second half is the reality of what happens when Wakanda sits back and does nothing.
Black Panther.review:
A solid film with good characters, a well-structured plot, and awesome worldbuilding. Despite all the cool action sequences, this film is about the politics of how Wakanda should interact with the world. The first half of the film is a cautionary tale about what could happen if Wakanda exposes itself to the world and the second half is the reality of what happens when Wakanda sits back and does nothing, with each anchored by their villains Klaue and Killmonger, respectively.

This transition is a little abrupt since Killmonger just kills Klaue, but it also feels inevitable. Killmonger could be an example of what Wakanda could do if it interacted with the rest of the world, but it’s important that he was created by Wakanda’s inaction instead of their action. He was left abandoned in the outside world and turned into a living weapon by the US government, growing to resent both being left behind and the world he was left behind in, because all he knows is war. To top it off, the only reason he’s able to amass so much power is because of Wakanda’s traditions of letting royalty and clan leaders engage the current king in ritual fights to the death. In order to prevent another Killmonger, Wakanda’s traditions need to change, and that means reaching out to the world to ensure that no black kids are left alone on the streets to be used and abused by the world’s governments. Killmonger is a force of nature, but he’s about as complex as a puddle of water, pretending to have deep philosophical motivations to mask the fact that he’s nothing more than a well of hate. He doesn’t care about Wakanda like he says, because if he did, he wouldn’t burn their heart-shaped herb. It’s not only one of their oldest traditions, but it’s one that represents unity; you can’t unite the world by destroying the herb that brought it together in the first place. Killmonger ultimately loses because he doesn’t understand Wakanda’s tech as well as the natives he’s trying to take it from. It’s beautiful that in Killmonger’s dying moments, T’Challa lets him see Wakanda for the beautiful place that it is as opposed to the instrument of war that he has always seen it as.

T’Challa himself is a good protagonist. He’s clearly conflicted about what the right thing is, whether that’s to keep Wakanda in the shadows or enter the rest of the world, especially since that world killed his dad. But he’s also in love with Nakia, the literal embodiment of “Wakanda should do more”. T’Challa and the movie are able to take Killmonger’s point that the outside world sucks and funnel it through Nakia’s altruistic worldview to create something that can actually help people instead of killing them all. She sees everyone as people, even outsiders like Ross, and it’s that love that makes her different from Killmonger. Nakia is the real hero of this movie, basically, even if T’Challa is king.

The plot is also really tight. Killmonger just killing Klaue and also his own girlfriend halfway into the movie is definitely the weakest part, but it’s also the moment when the film itself goes from good to great. Killmonger is straight up terrifying as he makes his way into Wakanda and uses Wakanda’s past mistakes coupled with his own strength of will to brute force his way onto the throne. I also love all the callbacks to earlier parts. T’Challa sees his dad, so Killmonger sees his dad, but the environment and conversations are different. M’Baku comes in clutch when he saves T’Challa and then the Dora Milaje, accepting T’Challa’s implicit offer that since Wakanda is going to de-isolate itself, M’Baku’s tribe can be a part of Wakanda if they wish to be. Killmonger gets the other version of T’Challa’s suit that Shuri made, and Ross gets to re-use the remote pilot car for a plane. Even the sonic train that the final fight takes place on was shown off earlier as part of the reveal to Ross that Wakanda is way more than he believed.

Also, of course the tribe that agrees with Killmonger is the border tribe, since they’re the ones who have to deal with the aggressions of the outside world all the time, meaning they’re the least insulated from the cruelty it has to offer. Them all standing down when they realize that they are destroying Wakanda from the inside instead of saving it is also such a good moment.

This film takes itself pretty seriously, although there are still moments of levity. Klaue in particular is delightfully insane, and Shuri’s enthusiasm is infectious. You know things are serious when even she gets scared. The action scenes are also really solid, if nothing special. The highlight is definitely the car chase in Busan, but I also like T’Challa defeating Killmonger by exploiting a weakness in the armor that Killmonger effectively stole. The worldbuilding is really good too, and makes Wakanda feel like a real place with a storied culture, even if we don’t see most of it.

As an MCU film, there isn’t much to say. This film incorporates the backstory from Civil War pretty well, showing us the flashback at an appropriate time early on. Aside from that, this film is pretty much standalone, with the only real reference to the rest of the MCU being Bucky showing up in the post-credit scene. It makes the film feel isolated in a good way, since it helps the movie feel complete. It also meta-narratively ties into the film’s story: Wakanda/Black Panther is isolated from the world/MCU, and then at the end, they join it. It’s a good movie, whether you like superheroes or not.

Peacemaker S2.title: Peacemaker S2
Peacemaker S2.blurb: An interesting season with some pretty good character work that is otherwise very messy in plot and pacing. The season also ends with a faceplant, but I think the rest of the season stands on its own without it, especially if you like the first season.
Peacemaker S2.review:
An interesting season with some pretty good character work that is otherwise very messy in plot and pacing. The season also ends with a faceplant, but I think the rest of the season stands on its own without it, especially if you like the first season.

I like that the first episode uses the Previously On segment to blatantly retcon Peacemaker into the new DCU, particularly replacing the Justice League with the Justice Gang. The Gang showing up in the first episode proper to interview Peacemaker really nails home that this is a DCU show now and you shouldn’t worry about it too much. I like it. Rick Flag Sr is a perfect addition from Creature Commandos as well, not because he’s tied to Argus, but because Peacemaker killed his son and this season is about Peacemaker facing his past even more directly than last season.

I like Peacemaker’s arc of admitting that he wants human connection and doing anything he needs to get it, even if it means abandoning all of his friends to go hang out in an alternate dimension where his father and brother are still alive and he’s dating the girl he likes. It’s not the best move, but you get where he’s coming from since he feels like he’d rather have his father and brother and the woman he loves, even if they aren’t really his father, brother, or girlfriend. The alternate world being a Nazi world only hammers home that Peacemaker can’t return to his past and needs to look for his future, which he gets when all his friends come to save him. This need for connection is also why he’s so insistent that he and Harcourt talk about what happened on the boat. It seems like he just wants more sex, but the reveal that they had a romantic kiss recontextualizes the whole thing into him wanting genuine human connection. I do think their romance arc takes up too much time this season, but I do like the way it climaxed with their big emotional talk in Nazi world mixed with the boat reveal.

I also really like how dedicated the characters are to each other season, after their ordeal against the Butterflies. Economos repeatedly puts his job on the line to protect Peacemaker, and Harcourt does the same once she has a job. Adebayo repeatedly speaks good of Peacemaker, and Vigilante is also here. He clearly wants to spend time with them all, even if they barely tolerate him at times. The characters getting fed up with his shit as the stakes get more dire is also a good indicator of their emotions, and Fleury indulging him at the end shows both that Fleury is new, but also that things are okay enough for them to put up with Vigilante’s tangents again. I love that the two Vigilantes are almost identical, down to killing people they think do wrong, and that they understand almost immediately that their universes’ Peacemakers are different people who shouldn’t be treated the same.

Harcourt has the strongest arc this season outside of Peacemaker himself, although the first half of the season is setting the stakes. She doesn’t think she’s good enough to be loved, which is why she keeps pushing Peacemaker away despite caring about him deeply. It’s a good parallel to Peacemaker’s arc, with Peacemaker doing anything to be loved and Harcourt doing everything to ensure that she isn’t. Economos and Adebayo don’t have strong arcs this season, but they still have strong presences, with Economos getting frequent opportunities to show his character growth from last season and Adebayo feeling like the heart of the team. Judomaster is also very fun this season, getting to interact with the main cast in a positive light and forming a tenuous friendship with them. Fleury I’m more mixed on, he’s so passive aggressive and his humor is hit or miss, but the hits are pretty good. I also like that he’s an asshole in such a different way from Economos and Harcourt last season, continuing the trend of Argus agents being obnoxious people.

The Nazi world also works pretty well for what the story is trying to do. You know something is up with the world because the civilians are way too celebratory of the Top Trio’s violence, regardless of if you notice the missing people of color or not. I’d have to go back and rewatch the crowd shots in the “real” world to see how many people of color are in them, but I wish we had more characters of color that are conspicuously absent in Nazi world. Fleury and Bordeaux aren’t in Argus, but we don’t meet their replacements to fully notice that they’re gone. That said, you know something is wrong due to the violence and Peacemaker’s dad being a hero, so the twist still works. I also like that Peacemaker’s dad isn’t really a Nazi, just someone who is trying to do what he can without rocking the boat. It’s a funny twist because Peacemaker’s real dad is a Nazi, so you don’t see it coming. Vigilante killing him also works very well, because despite not being a Nazi, he still works within that system and isn’t distinguishable from it to an outsider. I like that Peacemaker and Vigilante both turn on the world when they realize that Nazis are in charge. Despite loving it there, Peacemaker knows that it isn’t right, despite being raised by a Nazi. He also hated that Nazi by the end, but still, there’s no hesitation in leaving that world behind.

The Nazi World is also there to parallel the “real” world. The Nazi World put everybody who isn’t white and straight into labor camps, so the season ends with Flag Sr getting manipulated by Lex Luthor into building a prison to put all the metahumans, called Sanctuary. It’s a fairly on the nose parallel showing that the American government, even in our world, is corrupt, but because this happens in the last episode, nothing is done about it. Adebayo and the gang form their own spy agency, but they never actually do anything to counter or stop Flag Sr, which feels especially weird because Vigilante killed the Nazi World version of Peacemaker’s dad for trying to work within the system instead of fighting it outright. The parallels are there, but they make the finale even weaker than it already is.

The big problem is that Sanctuary kinda comes out of nowhere. Flag Sr going to Luthor for help finding the portal device is cool, but then Luthor seems to take over the plot from the shadows as he and his guys manipulate Flag Sr. Considering the whole last episode is dedicated to establishing Sanctuary, which does almost nothing in the show aside from parallel Nazi World. Flag Sr gets corrupted into completely ignoring his subordinates almost off-screen, and then that plot is never resolved, making the whole thing feel like DCU set-up.

Even worse is that, after Peacemaker’s big character arc and everyone forming their own spy agency to presumably stop Flag Sr, you still have a hopeful ending, except the show doesn’t end there. The very last scene is Peacemaker getting kidnapped and chucked in Salvation by Flag Sr. It’s a big sour note to end the season on, exacerbated by how poorly Salvation is integrated into the rest of the season. Sure if highlights how corrupt Argus, Flag Sr, and supermax prisons are, but it just feels like setup for future projects that may or may not come. The fact that season 1 ended so tightly and perfectly only makes this feeling worse.

Nearing the end of the review, I would be remiss not to mention the Eagly subplot. Eagly mauling the five Argus agents that break into his house is a great fight scene, and I like the subplot with the eagle hunter. It doesn’t really go anywhere, but it is really funny, especially the revelation that he was right about Eagly being the Prime Eagle. The various other fight scenes are also generally pretty good, especially the one where Peacemaker stops the Sons of Liberty from blowing up the DMV. The “fight” scene where the gang nearly kills Nazi Keith is also really good, despite it being less of a fight and more of a heartwrenching blowout. The show still has that trademark sense of humor from the first season, although it’s a lot more hit and miss this time around, which really goes for the whole season.

Ultimately, it's a season with a good amount of highs that just isn’t stitched together very well and fumbles really badly at the end. Ignoring that last scene though, it’s strong character arcs, humor, and setpieces make this season worth a watch if you like season 1.

Doctor Strange.title: Doctor Strange
Doctor Strange.blurb: A banger movie with a strong central character, beautifully trippy fight scenes, and one of the best final confrontations in a superhero film. Doctor Strange is a doctor, and by the end of the film, the Earth is his patient.
Doctor Strange.review:
A banger movie with a strong central character, beautifully trippy fight scenes, and one of the best final confrontations in a superhero film. Doctor Strange is a doctor, and by the end of the film, the Earth is his patient.

The most striking part of the film is its crazy fight scenes. The Mirror Dimension effects are excellent, and they make every fight they’re in a visual treat to watch as reality warps around itself. The time reverse effects in the final battle are also really good, and the characters play along with them so well. It’s probably just all CGI, but the effects are crazy enough that it doesn’t matter. I also like how creative the fight in the Sanctum is, forcing Dr Strange to use every available tool to his advantage, even if it makes the Sanctum’s guardian look like a chump.

That said, the best fight in this movie is easily the one that is no fight at all. Dr Strange killing himself over and over to trap Dormammu in a time loop is such an incredible scene. It’s not only a cool way to defeat an impossibly powerful adversary, but it’s such a good thematic ending as well. It’s an outside the box solution - something Strange has always excelled at - that requires him to think differently, losing over and over again when he refused to take risky patients earlier in the film. There’s a reason “Dormammu, I’ve come to bargain” became a meme, and it’s because this final confrontation is perfect.

Dr Strange himself is a really good protagonist, following the Tony Stark model of “insufferable genius who undergoes a great tragedy that changes their worldview and makes them become a better person”. Instead of realizing that he’s been hurting real people the whole time, Strange gets hurt himself. Once on the other end of the metaphorical (and in one instance, literal) operating table, he realizes that his patients are people too. So he is like Tony Stark in that regard, learning that the world doesn’t revolve around him, and like Tony Stark, he shifts his goals from just helping himself up to actually helping everyone he can. By the end of the film, he’s not just the Sorcerer Supreme, but the world’s surgeon. The biggest flaw with his arc is that most of his character development kinda happens off-screen, but it still happens gradually enough that you can see the steps he took even if you don’t see how he took those steps.

While Strange himself is really good, his supporting cast is kinda mid. Christine is your run-of-the-mill love interest, with the only real twist being that she’s an ex-girlfriend while still being a good person (which is okay because Strange is the asshole). She’s supportive and active when she needs to be, but doesn’t have much personality beyond that. Wong is in this movie way less than I remember, and Mordo doesn’t do much aside from mistrust Strange and become disillusioned with Kamar-Taj. He serves alright as Mentor #2, but he exists to set up that post-credits scene and eventual sequel (that is what the sequel’s gonna be about, right?).

The big secondary character is Mentor #1, the Ancient One. She’s the one who opens Dr Strange’s eyes to magic, and the one who guides him through what it means to be a Sorcerer. She’s a little soft on him, but she can literally see his future so it makes sense that she wants to train him well. Her death scene is also really good, showing that she wanted to protect the world so badly that she sacrificed her own morals to do it. Strange manages to break this “curse” without sacrificing his morals, because even if he does break the laws of reality, he doesn’t care about those. Maybe he should, but those are consequences for a future film (that is what the future film’s gonna be about, right?).

Dormammu and Kaecilius are both weak villains, but Kaecilius needs to be there to test Strange’s morals. Strange could “save” everyone via Dormammu, but he’s a doctor, so he knows that what Kaecilius wants isn’t living. Mordo manages to be a stronger villain in one 2-minute post-credits scene than they do the whole film. His desire to cull the unruly amount of Sorcerers is such a natural, yet surprising continuation of the film. Mordo was the mentor, but now he’s the villain, trying to tear down everything the Ancient One built up, presumably including Dr Strange.

As for worldbuilding, the magic system is pretty cool, if simple. It’s mostly magical constructs and the Mirror Dimension, along with a handful of magic artifacts. We don’t really see how those are created, but the library implies the existence of a magic system far more vast than we see. I like that the implications are there, and I like that this movie keeps it simple, because it doesn’t need to get more complex to tell its story.

As for MCU connections, there are basically none. The Avengers are mentioned once I think, and we see Stark Tower, firmly placing this film pre-Homecoming. I like it here though, because the big connection is that the Eye of Agamotto is an Infinity Stone. This is where things really turn cosmic, and the brand new magic system emphasizes that. Thor’s always been around, but the world of the MCU is far bigger than we thought we knew.

This film is one of my favorites for both its character arc, incredible action sequences, and awesome final battle. Plus, its unique premise helps it stand out amongst the rest of the superhero genre, making it a treat to revisit even outside the MCU.

Amazing Digital Circus.title: Amazing Digital Circus
Amazing Digital Circus.blurb: An animated psychological horror comedy about being trapped in a digital VR world with no known way to escape. The mystery of how the Digital Circus works and how to escape it drives the show, fuelled by excellently compelling characters and beautiful animation. The show starts off slow, but quickly gets better episode by episode, even if its finale falls a bit short of its potential.
Amazing Digital Circus.review:
An animated psychological horror comedy about being trapped in a digital VR world with no known way to escape. The mystery of how the Digital Circus works and how to escape it drives the show, fuelled by excellently compelling characters and beautiful animation. The show starts off slow, but quickly gets better episode by episode, even if its finale falls a bit short of its potential.

The animation is stunningly good, making great use of CGI models that always feel as fluid or solid as they need to be. The show mostly keeps things tame, but every character is incredibly expressive, even ones with minimal facial features like Zooble.
