There are also a few psychedelic sequences that stand out for their animation alone, such as Jax’s near-abstraction, Caine’s intermission, and Caine’s supervillain song.

Where the show really shines, though, is its characters. Despite seeming simple on the surface, every one of them is compellingly complex, with their own backstories and internal struggles that all complement one another. It’s delightful to learn about them all over time, especially since we learn about them naturally through dialogue, which makes it feel less like exposition and more like we’re learning about them alongside the other characters as they open up to each other to survive and get along in the Circus. The lightning round episode is particularly good at this, giving us glimpses into everyone’s backstories that are just deep enough to explain their characters without being so deep that they feel unnecessary. The show almost always feels like a proper ensemble, where even if some episodes highlight certain characters like Kinger or Gangle, everybody is always doing stuff that reveals things about their character, expands their character relationships, or progresses that episode’s plot. Even when the show starts more squarely focusing on Jax later on, the rest of the cast almost never loses their presence or relevance.

While I like all of the cast, my two favorites are easily Pomni and Kinger. Pomni is the glue that holds everyone together, connecting to the rest of the cast and gets them to open up to each other. She’s able to fit into the Circus knowing part of it is a game, but still treats the others like real people. In a sense, she’s the best of both Ragatha and Jax, and there’s a reason why she’s able to bring everyone together during the finale. Even though we don’t get much of her backstory, we learn a lot about her personality since she’s our POV character, and watching her develop from a scared, terrified girl into a natural leader is really cool. Her finally telling off Caine is incredibly cathartic, and her putting all her knowledge together to pull off insane feats like helping Kinger get control of the Circus and reaching through to Abstracted-Jax in the finale is awesome. It feels like we grow alongside Pomni from an outsider to a central core of the Cirus, and that’s part of what makes the show work so well.

If Pomni is the “hero”, then Kinger is the mentor. He’s delightfully funny when he’s insane, and heartwarmingly wise when he’s allowed to get his mind back. Learning about his past and how much he truly knows about the Circus is really cool, and aside from Pomni, he’s the best at comforting people. He’s the one who comforts Pomni, after all, and the first to start rebuilding the Circus after everything goes to shit. There’s a reason why Caine made Kinger insane, and it’s because Kinger would steal the show if he wasn’t. As is, he manages to steal the show anyways.

I really like most of the main cast though. Zooble is fun, and while Gangle is my least favorite, I do like that she grows to love herself, even through the depression. Ragatha’s uncompromising optimism contrasts well with Jax’s pessimism, and watching her and Jax fight over Pomni is fascinating. I wish she was more instrumental in the Jax conflict, because that dynamic feels ripe for strong character moments. I do like that she’s the first one to reconnect with Pomni during the finale, despite everything that’s happened.

Jax is one of the most interesting characters. I like how sadistically funny he is at the start, until that gets slowly pulled back to reveal that it’s a mask hiding his intense loneliness. Watching him spiral as he slowly re-associates with reality is fascinating, and I love that him pushing people away so he doesn’t have to be vulnerable makes him the most vulnerable one of all. He refuses to engage with the community positively, so without that community, he has nothing left. He becomes the central character alongside Pomni in the latter-third of the show, which makes sense since the whole show is about building community in a world where nothing matters. However, I do think the climax to his arc is handled pretty clumsily, with his backstory being shown via 10 minutes of exposition being told through Jax’s memories. It’s especially jarring compared to how natural and succinct everybody else’s backstories are, and it being the end of his arc means that there’s nothing to really do with this information. Jax can’t change anymore, so it’s just exposition for exposition’s sake. I like his backstory in a vacuum, and it compliments the show’s themes well, but the pacing makes it feel like a whimper instead of the bang it should have been.

Caine is a fun villain to watch develop. The cracks are there from the start, but learning just how far Caine will go to satisfy his ego as the cast stands up for themselves is both cool and terrifying. It’s awesome watching him go full supervillain by the end, even if he crosses the line earlier with the Fake Exit adventure. I do think his redemption is too quick, as he basically just realizes that he was wrong and moves on. Although he is an adaptive AI, so it makes sense that he can just change the dataset he’s pulling from to actually work with the humans instead of against them. I like where he ends up, even if I think getting there was rushed.

The driving force of the show, aside from the characters, is the underlying plot and mystery: how does the Circus work, and how does the cast leave it. It’s their goal from episode 1, even if they can’t always pursue it. The first episode also leaves us with several other unanswered questions, namely what abstraction is and what the Backrooms-type exit Pomni found is. The show is thematically about the characters finding meaning in a meaningless world, but too much focus is placed on the mystery elements for it to not be a major component of the story being told.

In general, watching the characters learn more about how the Circus works is really fun. We learn that the characters all came from different time periods, and that the Backrooms is something Caine had been making based on the real world. The plot really ramps up around the two-thirds point, with the Fake Exit adventure. It’s the first episode to really bring the escape plot back into focus, now that the characters have the chance to actually do something, and it ends with one of the greatest rugpulls in history when Caine reveals that the whole thing is fake. It’s an emotional gutpunch, and one that only matters if the plot - the mystery - is important. From there we learn about the creation of the Circus using brain scans, and how the cast can manipulate the Circus too, at least enough to stop Caine and gain control even if they can’t escape. We get a whole sequence dedicated to Caine’s creation, and the episode ends with his death and the near-destruction of the Circus. It’s an incredible buildup, escalating things quickly but with purpose, until things are on the brink of disaster.

From there, though, things kind of just lose their momentum. The characters just accept that they’re simply code without really saying it, even though it should raise several existential questions. Like, are they even people? As brain scans, their lives literally have no meaning, and their entire quest to escape is all for naught. It makes sense as a reveal - like how the fuck is Kinger’s body still alive otherwise - but it’s not particularly satisfying answer to the mystery.

Emotionally I really like it, as everyone breaks down and comes apart before Pomni, Kinger, and Ragatha slowly pull them back together. They have already accepted living forever in the Circus to some degree, but with them stuck there, they are able to find new meaning in each other. The scene of them slowly pulling back together as a team is one of my favorites in the show, and the scene where they learn about their real selves and Pomni’s little wave to the camera made me tear up.

As a climax to the mystery, though, it’s very unsatisfying, since the answer is that there is no answer. It’s all this buildup, and for nothing. I get that you have to choose your own meaning, but for me personally, it makes that whole half of the show fall short. It doesn’t help that we spend half the episode going through Jax’s memories and Caine’s overly-drawn-out-yet-also-rushed character arc, taking away time that I wish was spent on the rest of the cast adapting to their new, permanent reality. We also never learn what abstraction is, which is another big let down. I think it’s the code just getting corrupted, since Pomni can go into Abstracted-Jax’s memories, but that honestly just raises more questions. I think the finale’s emotional bits work really well, but the plot half of the finale is really weak compared to the rest of the show.

Really, this problem with the ending is so noticeable only because the rest of the show is able to perfectly balance the prevalence of the emotional and plot halves. I think prioritizing the emotional half over the plot half is the right choice, but I wish they had been able to nail them both.

Looking less at the individual details and more at the overall structure, I love that show’s transition from wacky comedy to psychological drama. It’s hilarious at the beginning, particularly Jax, Kinger, and Caine, but almost all of the humor is character focused, so as stakes get more dire, the humor goes away. I like that the humor is still mostly gone from the finale, as the people have control instead of Caine, but instead of being filled with despair, it’s filled with a quiet sense of normalcy and camaraderie. It’s a good emotional throughline, and the humor early on makes the dark moments hit even harder.

I highly recommend checking this one out. Gooseworx and GLITCH did an amazing job, even if the ending didn’t work as well for me as it did other people. It’s a banger show in a vacuum, but given the context of it being an indie webseries, I think this one is gonna go down in history as a major milestone and certified classic.

Guardians of the Galaxy.title: Guardians of the Galaxy
Guardians of the Galaxy.blurb: A fun film about a bunch of jackasses learning to work together to save the galaxy because they live in it too. The soundtrack is bopping but not super prevalent, the ragtag group of misfits come together too quickly, and the film is neither particularly funny nor particularly action-packed. There are still funny moments and the action is still decent, but nothing that compares to Gunn’s future films.
Guardians of the Galaxy.review:
A fun film about a bunch of jackasses learning to work together to save the galaxy because they live in it too. This film isn’t as good as I remember it being, but I think that’s because it inspired a whole bunch of films that do what it does better, including other films by James Gunn. The soundtrack is bopping but not super prevalent, the ragtag group of misfits come together too quickly, and the film is neither particularly funny nor particularly action-packed. There are still funny moments and the action is still decent, but nothing that compares to Gunn’s future films. This is the blueprint, and unfortunately that means that it’s been far-surpassed, even if it’s still good in its own right.

The plot is simple yet effective. It’s a MacGuffin chase, except our main characters have the MacGuffin the whole time and are just trying to figure out what the fuck to do with it. “Where do we safely put our pocket nuke” is a pretty good question, and it’s that immense sense of responsibility that is thrust upon our cast that drives their character arcs. The biggest downside to this plot is that neither the main antagonist nor the nominal “good guys” are particularly compelling. Ronan is an angry, intimidating zealot who has a motivation we never truly learn, and the Nova Corps are personality-less cops. We don’t even know anyone on Xandar to care about, even if the fact that we shouldn’t let a planet get blown up is obvious. The most interesting of our MacGuffin buyers is the Collector, and he’s only in one scene before the MacGuffin gets taken by Ronan.

This simple plot and lackluster supporting cast means that it falls to our main characters to carry the film. They’re decent, but unfortunately not great. Peter Quill is the obvious protagonist, and that’s because he’s the only one with any people skills. He’s a smug, charming rogue, and that works to bring people together, even if his initial goal is just to save his own ass. He’s pretty fun to watch, because even if his character arc is minimal, his job is to bring the best out of the rest of the cast. Despite how selfish he is, Quill does care about people, even if he couldn’t care less for the law, and that sense of responsibility and camaraderie is infectious to the others.

The rest of the cast is similarly fun, but underdeveloped. Everyone’s personalities are really strong, which makes it jarring that they get over their grudges and become friends so fast. I get that everyone except maybe Groot is lonely, but there are way too many lines about how these are the only friends they’ve ever had when they just tried to kill each other 5 minutes ago. It kinda works for Gamora and Drax because they were in states of trauma when the movie starts, but it still feels underdeveloped, especially for Rocket. Don’t get me wrong, everyone coming together to hold the Power Stone with Quill is awesome, but the road they take to get there happens way too quickly.

Part of the problem is that Gamora and Quill are already mid-character arc, having betrayed both Yondu and Thanos respectively by the start of the movie. Because of this, we never really see how they hit their breaking points, only that they’re already there. Then, only a few days have passed before deciding that they’re ride or die for their new friends. As much as I love the Power Stone scene, some of the emotional weight is taken away since the tight-knit friendship feels forced.

Yondu and Nebula also don’t feel as emotionally developed as they should be. They both have their moments, but they’re very small. Yondu shows up out of nowhere, and Nebula has one fight with almost no dialogue before leaving. Her and Gamora both clearly hate Thanos, and yet can’t work together because Nebula is filled with hate and Gamora is filled with… not hate. I don’t think it’s quite love yet, even if she clearly likes Quill. However, this conflict goes nowhere, and there’s only one small moment of Gamora trying to redeem Nebula before Nebula leaves the movie forever.

That said, there are still some things I really like about this movie. The opening is one of the MCU’s best, cutting from Quill watching his mom die of cancer to him being a rocking, kick-ass outlaw in space. It sets the tone of the movie as emotional yet irreverent, even if it doesn’t lean as heavily into that tone as it could. Quill’s dance-off moment is great, being so in-character and so egregious that it actually works. I love how protective Quill is of the music and headphones, it hammers in how much he misses home even if he seems perfectly content as a cosmic outlaw from the outside. I’ve already mentioned the Power Stone scene, and I like that Groot grows back in the credits. His death is really emotional, but he gets to live because this is a movie with a happy ending. I also like how much Yondu clearly cares for Quill by smiling stupidly whenever Quill outsmarts him. He has to put on a face for his crew, but he’s glad he doesn’t have to kill Quill for betraying him.

This is a fun addition to the MCU. It expands the world a whole bunch with beautiful and diverse alien worlds and species. We get to see the power of another Infinity Stone, this time with full knowledge that it is an Infinity Stone, and it’s terrifying. I love how destructive the Power Stone is. It sets up the Guardians as major players, even if they’re all in space. We also see Thanos in a non-post credits scene, even if its just so Ronan can tell him to go fuck himself. He is characterized pretty strongly here though, thanks to Gamora saying that he genocided her planet and that both Gamora and Nebula are so eager to betray him. It definitely sets him up as a menace. There is also plenty of foreshadowing for Guardians 2, mainly about Quill’s parentage.

Despite its flaws, I still like this movie. It's a fun romp that sets the stage for a whole bunch of future films that can take the zany vibes and classic rock music of this film to a whole nother level. I’m not super attached to any of the main characters yet, but it’s clear that the movie has plans for all of them down the line, and manages to make that exciting since the film itself still feels complete. Truthfully, this film’s biggest flaw is that it released in 2014, and since then, I’ve seen so many films that take what made this film stand out and do it so much better. Still, these idiots managed to save the universe with the power of classic rock, and that’s awesome.

Guardians of the Galaxy Vol 2.title: Guardians of the Galaxy Vol 2
Guardians of the Galaxy Vol 2.blurb: A fantastic action-comedy with a lot of heart and a love for classic rock. The soundtrack both tells the story of the film and injects every action scene with a heightened sense of adrenaline and awe. All of the characters feel more fleshed out with their own arcs, partly because we already have everyone’s characterizations from the first film.
Guardians of the Galaxy Vol 2.review:
A fantastic action-comedy with a lot of heart and a love for classic rock. The soundtrack both tells the story of the film and injects every action scene with a heightened sense of adrenaline and awe. All of the characters feel more fleshed out with their own arcs, partly because we already have everyone’s characterizations from the first film. Because the friend group is already established, we can trade generic prickliness for jabs that are a lot more personal. This makes them hit harder, but also makes them a lot funnier. These are people that know and like each other, even if they sometimes act like they want to kill each other.

The two main characters who hate each other the most are obviously Quill and Rocket. Both feel the need to prove themself as the best, especially Rocket, who is still really not used to working with a team. He’s an asshole through and through, and hasn’t quite learned how to show that he cares about his friends yet. It’s through Yondu that he learns that he’s not alone, and really gives him the determination to work together to ensure as many of his friends live as possible. Him giving Yondu the spacesuit and jetpack and then paralyzing Gamora to prevent her from going back for Quill because he can’t lose another friend is the capstone to his arc. It’s so good. Quill doesn’t have as much going on, but that’s because he’s still not used to relying on people either. He ignores them when they tell him that something is wrong with Ego because he wants to connect with the dad he never knew, but he regroups with his team a lot quicker than Rocket does. Once Rocket stops trying to prove himself, Quill is able to focus on leading the team instead of fighting with Rocket. I do love that what snaps Quill away from Ego’s influence is learning that Ego killed Quill’s mom. It’s all about family to him, and Ego isn’t part of that, but took it away.

Gamora and Nebula play out a miniature version of the Quill/Rocket arc, except they’re haunted by their pasts instead of trying to claim their place in the future. They both want family, which is why Nebula seeks out Gamora and why Gamora thinks Quill should go with Ego when they first meet up. Quill has helped her open up, and now she can better connect with Nebula. Even if Nebula leaves at the end to kill Thanos, she knows she has an ally in her sister. Drax and Mantis have the least going on, but I still like their dynamic. Drax also has to learn to show he cares about people, although in case it's about people who are very unlike him. Mantis is not his type of person at all, and it takes him a bit to adjust to how to treat her. Mantis doesn’t have a lot going on aside from betraying Ego, but she’s like character #8 so it's fine.

Yondu is also way more fleshed out this film. We knew he cared deeply about Quill from the last movie, but here we learn that he kept Quill around because he couldn’t stand to hand him off to Ego to die. He sees Quill as his son, even though he can’t show it due to being head of a Ravager squad. Also, because Quill actually would have let Ego complete his plan, Yondu’s sentimentality saved the whole universe. Quill’s sentimentality too, since he turns on Ego because Ego killed his mom.

Groot doesn’t have a lot going on because he’s a baby, but he ties into the whole theme of finding your family. Everyone openly cares about and protects him, even Drax and Gamora. The whole film is about finding your family and taking care of those around you, and the Guardians start the film off by taking care of Baby Groot. They are a family, and the rest of the film only enforces this. Rocket and Groot welcome Yondu onto the team, Yondu shows how much he cares for Quill, and Gamora is able to reconnect with Nebula. Ego, despite being Quill’s biological father, never truly cared about Quill and refused to let himself care about Quill’s mom, which is why he’s the villain. It’s the bonds that make family, not the blood.

Alongside the characters, the plot is also really tight. Even though Ego and the Sovereign have pretty much nothing to do with each other, it’s really Ego intruding on the Sovereign’s plot instead of them feeling like a tack-on to his. The Sovereign are only antagonists because of Rocket’s ego, and are not only how Ego gains the Guardians’ trust in the first place, but also the reason that the Ravagers get involved. Plus, they’re the focus of the post-credits scene. Ego intruding ends the Sovereign’s chance of being a real threat, playing into the bit that they’re way too self-important, but they never stop trying. Ego appearing works perfectly for his character too, since he’s someone who comes in and takes what he wants without caring about anybody else. It makes Ego feel like a big deal without making the Sovereign or the Ravagers feel like a B-plot, which helps the film feel cohesive.

Learning what Ego has been up to is really cool, and he lays out just enough pieces in the first half of the film to clue you in that something is wrong without letting you figure out exactly what. For example, Ego says he wants progeny, but only mentions falling in love with Quill’s mother, so you don’t realize that Ego has had thousands of children until Gamora and Nebula find the boneyard later in the movie. It’s a great set up, and even if the Ego plot is mostly the cast waiting around until they find out what’s happening, it's paired with the Rocket/Yondu plot where the characters can be active, meaning the movie never feels slow or stagnant.

On top of the writing, what makes this movie stand out is the music and action sequences. The film basically opens with an entire fight happening in the background while Groot dances to the credits sequence, and the movie only escalates from there. Rocket intentionally plays music while breaking out of the Ravager prison, partly because he seems to just like Quill’s music and partly to wake all the Ravagers up so he can Yondu can kill them all. Kraglin is listening to Wham Bam Shang-a-Lang when the Sovereign show up for the finale, and when they actually get to Ego’s core to fight the Guardians a few minutes later, the song kicks back in. It’s awesome.

The finale is an incredible capstone, as everybody tries to stall time to stop Ego and then escape. Baby Groot follows instructions for the first time to not immediately kill everybody (since he never really found Yondu’s fin on the Ravager ship), and Yondu gives Quill one last piece of fatherly advice to help him activate his power and fight Ego. Quill effectively sacrifices himself to save everyone before Yondu saves him, and Yondu gets the heroic send-off he deserves. It’s damn near perfect.

As an MCU film, this movie is pretty disconnected. After the first film has both Thanos and an Infinity Stone, this film has neither. Thanos influences Gamora’s and Nebula’s relationships and arcs, but his story doesn’t progress aside from Nebula ending the film by leaving to kill him. Ego also claims to be a Celestial, but we saw Celestials in the last movie and they don’t look like Ego, so either Celestials are weird or Ego is lying to inflate his own importance. I personally like the latter interpretation.

This film is a certified banger. It takes everything the first film is trying to do, and does it way better. It has the benefit of us already knowing these characters, but it takes all of their arcs further instead of taking them a step back. The first film is about these characters coming together, and this film is about what it means to be together. The action sequences and soundtrack are also just blended way better than the first film, which you can’t contribute to us already knowing the characters and world. If Guardians 1 is the blueprint, Guardians 2 is the finished product, and it’s freaking awesome.

Supergirl.title: Supergirl
Supergirl.blurb: A good action movie that doesn’t quite do anything more than that. The plot is incredibly simple and uninteresting, but there are enough character moments to keep you invested between the fast-paced but shaky fights.
Supergirl.review:
A good action movie that doesn’t quite do anything more than that. The plot is incredibly simple and uninteresting, but there are enough character moments to keep you invested between the fast-paced but shaky fights.

The best shot in the movie isn’t even an action shot, but instead the Supergirl space scream. She flies up there after a devastating loss and you expect to hear that gut-wrenching scream, it’s sound amplified because she’s Kryptonian, only for nothing to come out because, yeah, there’s no sound in space. But even without the sound, the anguish is clear on her face. It’s so damn good, and I think I’ll remember this scene if nothing else.

The other money-making shot is Supergirl smashing all the brigands around Ruthye while Jimmy Eat World's The Middle plays (today I learned that song is called The Middle). The focus isn’t on Supergirl, but instead on Ruthye realizing that Supergirl isn’t protecting her from the hollowness of revenge, but from the entire life of violence that it will bring. Kara has been broken to the point that she can’t save herself, but she can still save Ruthye, and she can save herself spiritually through her. Ruthye lost everything, but that doesn’t mean that she has to be alone, and this is the scene where both Kara and Ruthye realize that. The big flaw is that the lyrics are somehow too on the nose and yet not on the nose enough for how loud they are compared to the music, but it only takes away from the scene a little bit.

That last fight scene is also easily the best one in the movie. Most of the others feel too shaky or dark to really get invested in what’s going on. I really like the space fight, but it has the same problems. The last fight though is all in broad daylight, and every piece of choreography feels easy to follow and executed with intention. It’s a great cap to the film, even if the rest of the fights could be better. Also, the green sun making Kara lose her powers is hilarious. It makes no sense, but I’m down for it. I do like the implication that it’s not Kryptonite that kills Kryptonians, but whatever chemical makes them green that kills them, since that’s presumably what makes the sun green. Is it stupid? Yes. Is it funny? Also yes.

The heart of the film is Kara’s growing relationship with Ruthye, and honestly, it’s fine. They kinda go back and forth snipping at each other the whole movie, and while I do buy how close they get due to the life or death situations they're in (especially since Ruthye is not used to this), it just doesn’t really hit. Kara sees herself in Ruthye, as a young girl who lost everything, and Kara thinks she can save her from losing herself too. It’s a nice throughline, even if it’s really not fleshed out enough. I do like Supergirl’s take on why Ruthye shouldn’t kill though, not because it’s the right thing to do, but because it will make Ruthye worse, and her living is all the revenge she needs against the brigands. Kara kills them all too for good measure, since while the vengeance won’t heal Ruthye, it can’t make Kara any worse.

Most of Kara’s and Ruthye’s connection comes from the similarities between their backstories, and I do like Kara’s backstory. She’s born on a small pocket of Krypton her parents saved, and is sent to Earth because that too is fated to die. I do think it’s funny that Clark being sent to Earth before Krypton exploded made him better adjusted than Kara, who was born on “Krypton”. Trying to preserve what was just made things worse than fleeing before it went to shit. Granted, Kara was only born after Krypton exploded, so she wouldn’t exist if her parents hadn’t saved her city, but still, it's kinda funny. Her having a home to lose made her worse than losing it before she was born.

Lobo isn’t in the movie a lot, but it's clear that Jason Momoa is having the time of his life. Lobo’s gruff and brutal, but he isn’t dismissive. He respects that drive in other people, especially when they have a code of their own, and doesn’t go out of his way to kill people. He doesn’t care who gets caught in his collateral, but he doesn’t kill for no reason. He’s fun. The other aliens are really fun too. The designs all remind me of A New Hope in the best way possible. I think my favorite is the little Babu Frik bus driver with the really deep voice. He’s funny.

The weakest part of the movie is easily the plot. Despite it only being an hour-and-45-minutes, the plot still feels drawn out. I kept waiting for a new villain to pop up, but no it’s just the brigands from the beginning of the movie. They don’t feel like the threat they need to be for a Kryptonian, and Supergirl rightfully demolishes them once she actually gets a chance to fight them at full power. The plot is mostly just set dressing for the set pieces, with all the interesting connective tissue being handled by the characters. The villains being kidnapping rapists is surprisingly dark, and the movie never really tackles that. Maybe it doesn’t need to, because they’re just scum who exist to bring Kara and Ruthye together, but it makes them very boring.

The movie is a good time, and the action pieces mostly do their work. There are enough character moments that the film never feels empty, even if the plot is really weak. I’m excited to see this new Supergirl and Lobo in the future though, and I do hope Kara keeps some of her edge so she isn’t just Clark 2. It’s not the greatest film ever, but it’s a good enough expansion of the DCU if you’re looking for nothing more than a good time.

Thor: Ragnarok.title: Thor: Ragnarok
Thor: Ragnarok.blurb: A delightful action comedy with a lot of heart that is nothing like the previous two Thor movies. This movie is split between two plotlines, and when the two inevitably collide, the big Chekhov’s Gun comes from the prologue. It feels like the movie should be a mess, but those plotlines are secondary to the intense comedy and action that permeate the film.
Thor: Ragnarok.review:
A delightful action comedy with a lot of heart that is nothing like the previous two Thor movies. This movie is split between two plotlines, the one about Thor and Loki on Sakaar and the one about Hela taking over Asgard, and when the two inevitably collide, the big Chekhov’s Gun comes from the prologue about Thor fighting Surtr. It feels like the movie should be a mess, but since Thor spends his whole time there trying to gather allies to escape and fight Hela, it still feels cohesive. Really though, those plotlines are secondary to the intense comedy and action that permeates the film.

This movie is fucking hilarious. Not all of the jokes land, but a lot of them do, and the joke per minute ratio is so high that you hardly notice the flubs. Korg is delightfully deadpan, taking everything at face value and not understanding the gravity of what’s going on. Loki fully embodies his trickster persona, being funny without being malicious. He also gets to the butt of the joke a lot, like when Thor hits him in the head with a rock to see if he’s an illusion or when they do Get Help. It makes him appropriately pathetic while still letting him be cool and clever. Grandmaster is decent on his own, but his executioner Topaz being completely blunt while he tries to sugarcoat things is hilarious. Banner’s and Hulk’s humor somehow feels the most natural, keeping their goofy vibes from Avengers while having the seriousness of their arc played straight. The weakest part of the humor is definitely Thor. He gets to be very funny when he’s the one making the joke, but he’s also made the butt of a lot of jokes that rely on him being weaker or dumber than he should be. It’s those jokes that don’t really land for me, since they’re going against Thor’s character instead of supporting it.

The action is also phenomenal. The movie takes some cues from Guardians by using pop songs, but instead of littering the whole soundtrack with it, it just uses one. Immigration Song is played during Thor’s opening battle with Surtr, and is played once again when Thor powers up to battle Hela’s forces. It’s an awesome full circle moment that lets you know that this is the kick-ass climax. The fights aren’t super kinetic or deeply choreographed, but every hit feels weighty, especially in the Hulk/Thor fight. It feels like gods punching each other, and that carries into every fight in the film. Hela’s actions feel so fluid and calculated, while Hulk and Thor rely on brute strength and Valkyrie is winging it. Every character feels unique, which helps spice up the otherwise simple fights.

Outside of the action/comedy, Loki is the most interesting part of this film. He starts the film pretending to rule as Odin, but his rule seems pretty peaceful and not despotic at all. He takes steps to glorify himself, but everybody seems into it and there doesn’t seem to be any problems. Thor mentions that the other Realms are in chaos, but we never see any of that. Loki gets the rule he wants, and is chill to leave it that way. Even when he arrives on Sakaar, he rises in favor with the Grandmaster and just chills as one of his VIPs. He tries to betray Thor like once, but there is barely any malicious intent at all. He just wants to be adored, not rule with an iron fist, and once he gets that, he mellows out. If we had seen the other Realms in chaos, it would lend more credence to the idea that Loki did a bad job as ruler of Asgard, but we don’t, so he seems fine. Also, one of the ideas in the film is that Asgard got its power by intervening and taking over the other Realms, so Loki being isolationist might be a good thing, actually. Also also, despite this being the film where Loki completes his redemption arc to wind up back as Thor’s best friend from before Thor 1, this film also retcons in more malicious pranks that make him seem more evil, which is weirdly contradictory. His redemption arc here is still really well done, but it’s not handled as well as it could have been.

Thor goes through his arc from Dark World again, learning to trust his allies and draw out his own power, but this movie isn’t about his arc. He’s already the Hero of the Realms, and his job is to rally everyone else into fighting for their people again. The scene where he gets his new Thunder powers is awesome, but it’s really just the cherry on top to his more static arc. His subtle arc is about gathering allies to save his people, so it is fitting that he gets someone else (Surtr) to destroy Hela so he can save his people even if he destroys their homes.

Sakaar is a planet of lost things, which is why Valkyrie, Loki, and Hulk all have positions of power there. They’re all lost, running from their sorrows and failures, and Thor is able to pull them out to lead a revolution by giving them a goal to aspire to and people to protect. It’s why the two halves of the film feel like they fit, because everything is about protecting the people. Thor destroys Asgard to save the Asgardians, and Korg overthrows the Grandmaster to save the people of Sakaar. I like that Thor plans to take all his people to his second people, moving the Asgardians to Earth so they can have a new home with the rest of his allies. The film isn’t super deep, but it is narratively and thematically cohesive.

The movie’s biggest flaw is how loosely it plays with continuity. It is firmly an action-comedy versus the original two films being dramas, and it makes Thor in particular feel out of character. Loki is normal and Heimdall and Odin stay serious, but Thor feels like a different character in a way that can’t be explained by his character development in Dark World and Age of Ultron. Thor and Jane broke up off-screen again, Thor never found the Infinity Stones that he went looking for at the end of Age of Ultron, the Warriors Three die ignominious deaths that Thor never acknowledges, Sif is never acknowledged, and the entire “Loki is pretending to be Odin” plot gets resolved in the first 20 minutes. Despite being a banger film, it feels disrespectful of what came before, caring little for continuity in favor of telling its own story, which is something of a problem when you’re three films into a trilogy and ~18 films into a franchise.

This film is almost better standalone than as Thor 3, but it’s still a banger. The plot and characters are just good enough to let the thrilling popcorn setpieces and laugh-out-loud jokes take center stage without leaving you empty in the aftermath.

Avengers: Infinity War.title: Avengers: Infinity War
Avengers: Infinity War.blurb: The first half of the grand finale to the Infinity Saga can’t be viewed as anything but. As a standalone film, this movie is nigh-incomprehensible in a way that the first Avengers simply isn’t. As the finale in a series, though, it’s nearly perfect. By assuming you already know who everybody is, the film is able to hit the ground running and tell its sprawling story without ever feeling like there are pieces missing.
Avengers: Infinity War.review:
The first half of the grand finale to the Infinity Saga can’t be viewed as anything but. As a standalone film, this movie is nigh-incomprehensible in a way that the first Avengers simply isn’t. The movie expects you to know who everyone is and what their deal is when they appear, sparing no time for introductions. As the finale in a series, though, it’s nearly perfect. By assuming you already know who everybody is, the film is able to hit the ground running and tell its sprawling story without ever feeling like there are pieces missing. Every scene is important, and almost every line of dialogue pushes the plot forward or further characterizes the characters since we’ve last seen them. There are maybe a few too many jokes, but they always come from characters who aren’t taking things as seriously as they should be, and the jokes dwindle over the course of the film to let the serious scenes be serious.

The way the movie handles its sprawling cast is by splitting them into groups, each led by one or two focus characters that the supporting cast is there to support. By and large, this works, with everyone feeling as important as they should be. Falcon and Bucky for example don’t do much, but they’re there to support Captain America like they always have. Arguably, Captain America is there to support Wanda and Vision, since while he leads the new Avengers, he doesn’t have specific stakes in the battle against Thanos in the same way that Wanda and Vision do. We see them before we see Cap, and while Cap gets his moment holding off Thanos, the big emotional moment with this group is between Wanda and Vision when she breaks the Soul Stone out of his head.

It goes like this for the rest of the characters, too. Tony Stark gets a lot of focus because he’s the original hero of the MCU, but he doesn’t really do a lot except kill Ebony Maw. The star of his little group is instead Dr Strange, being the one who explains how all the Stones work and the one who comes up with the plan to stop Thanos by sacrificing the Time Stone to save Tony. Drax and Mantis don’t do a lot (Drax is maybe the one character who should do more), but the focus is placed on Quill and Gamora since Gamora has the most direct tie to Thanos, and they get some of the most emotional scenes in the movie. The scene where Quill tries to fulfill Gamora’s wish to kill her but is stopped when Thanos turns his gun into a bubble blower is heartbreaking. Gamora later trying to sacrifice herself again and Thanos doing the same thing is equally gut wrenching.

In my head, the star of the movie, aside from Thanos, is Thor. The movie starts Thanos slaughtering all the Asgardians that Thor spent Ragnarok saving, and then Loki sacrifices himself to save Thor. Heimdall sends Hulk to Earth, basically kicking off that whole half of the plot, even if Thanos would have shown up anyways. Thor is the most proactive throughout the movie, undertaking his own adventure to stop Thanos instead of reacting to what he’s doing like many of the others. The Guardians are also proactive, but only because Thor alerts them to what’s going on. Thor’s the one who turns the tide in the Battle of Wakanda, and the climax of the film is him coming within an inch of stopping Thanos by overpowering the Infinity Gauntlet. There’s a reason why “you should have gone for the head” became a meme, and it’s because it’s not the moment where Thanos wins, but the moment where Thor loses. He does the Goku arc of training off-world while everybody holds off the villain for as long as possible, and then fails to follow through by snatching defeat from the jaws of victory at the last moment. If Thor stops Thanos, this is his movie, his equivalent of flying the nuke into the portal above New York.

Thanos is arguably the main character of this film, but that’s really only because he wins at the end. As seemingly committed to his noble goals of universal balance as he is, the man is also a right bastard. He straight up tortures Nebula to get information out of her and Gamora, and is fully willing to sacrifice Gamora to get what he wants. He does seem to love her, but his love is so twisted in pragmatism that it doesn’t have any emotional weight and ruined both Gamora’s and Nebula’s lives. They don’t want to be heartless warriors, they just wanted to be with their families, and Thanos ruined that for them in pursuit of his own ideals. The most damning evidence that Thanos is pure evil is the fact that he kills every dwarf but 1 on Nidavellir, presumably because they have the power to stop him. It completely breaks his half rule, and proves that he’s willing to break his own rules to get what he wants, even if what he wants is seemingly noble. The movie also ends with the harrowing shot of him sitting in that field of flowers, showing him content with his victory just like he said he’d be. He achieved inner peace, regardless of how many lives he had to take to get there.

This movie isn’t really about character arcs, but about the distances people are willing to go to get what they want. People have argued that the reason the heroes lose is because they aren’t willing to make any sacrifices - or “trade lives” as Cap puts it - but that is just untrue. Both Wanda and Quill try to kill their partner, and Thanos stops them both times. You could argue that if they had just killed their partner sooner, then Thanos wouldn’t have been able to stop them, which is probably true, but the point stands that they were willing to make the sacrifice when they needed to. Even Gamora is willing to sacrifice herself to stop Thanos, but Thanos stops that too. Plus, with the context of Endgame, Strange sacrificing the Stone to save Tony is the only reason the heroes win at all.

The stronger argument is that the heroes lose because they are more emotional than Thanos, following their hearts instead of being purely pragmatic. Quill and Wanda really don’t want to kill their loved ones, not because they aren’t willing to make the sacrifice, but because it really hurts, and they believe there has to be another way. Gamora would rather sacrifice herself than Nebula, and Tony can’t make the call to Cap to warn him and Vision about Thanos’ Black Order. If he makes that call, then maybe Vision never destabilizes and they’re able to remove the Stone from his head before Thanos arrives. Hulk is also too scared to help after getting his ass kicked by Thanos in the opening scene, depriving the Avengers of one of their biggest guns.

The two biggest pieces of evidence for this theme, though, are Quill on Titan and Thor not going for the head. Thanos killed the love of Quill’s life, and Quill loses it, enabling Thanos to break free from Mantis’ control and win. Mantis also controls emotions, and Thanos is the only character able to resist her - he resists even better than Ego did - because he’s simply not in touch with his emotions at all. Thor then misses his opportunity to kill Thanos because he wants to make him suffer for killing Loki, which he swore to do at the start of the film. Thor’s path has been doomed from the start because he and Thanos are on opposite ends of the emotional/pragmatic spectrum and Thanos is the one who wins. The thing that will let the heroes eventually win - Strange saving Tony - isn’t done out of emotions, but because Strange knows that this is the practical play in the long term. This emotionality even runs down to their armies. The Wakandans have to hype themselves up with chants and rallying cries, while Thanos’ army is a mass of identical unthinking monsters willing to slaughter and die for their master. That’s why Thanos wins: because he’s an emotionless pragmatist, and he surrounds himself with people who feel the same.

The movie is basically a 150 minute long action scene, and the action almost always works. The characters feel like they’re fighting like themselves, using their own unique abilities to pull out everything they’ve got. Everything feels intense, yet you’re always able to understand what’s going on. The fights also almost never cut around, so even though events kinda happen at the same time, you’re almost never focused on more than one thing at once. Even when the two final fights happen at the same time, they’re always cut where it always feels like a natural break in the fight choreography. It makes things easy to understand and follow, which is good because of just how many moving parts there are.

There are a few things I don’t like. I do wish Hulk got to come back in this movie, even if that’s probably partly because I know they skip his arc between this movie and Endgame. Hawkeye feels like he should be here since he’s the only Avenger missing. Him being there would lend more to the idea that this is the last movie, but since we miss out on the Avengers reunion, there has to be more. I’m fine with Ant-Man being absent because, really, he wasn’t gonna do much, and Fury at least gets his post-credits to contribute.

The Infinity Stones also seem inconsistent. The Power Stone and Space Stone seem to have permanent effects, but the Reality Stone’s effects are undone as soon as Thanos leaves the area. You could argue he’s undoing them, but that doesn’t seem like something he would do, or you could argue that he has to keep the effects active, but that’s still inconsistent with the other Stones. I’m also literally not sure what the Soul Stone does, which is bizarre when a whole chunk of the movie is dedicated to Thanos killing Gamora to get it. It probably helps him delete half the universe, but that seems more like a Reality/Space/Power effect than Soul, especially since the bodies are disintegrated and not rendered lifeless. That said, they’re really minor complaints in the grand scheme of things. Of course the six Stones being together makes them powerful, and I understand why the characters are absent even if I wish they were there.

This movie is a certified banger in the context of what it is. This is what the whole MCU has been building towards, and it's a perfect juggling act of every single character to craft a tightly-knit yet sprawling story that is somehow easy to follow. Everyone gets their moment, and Thanos gets to be the threat that he was built up to be in the two Guardians films. The heroes lose, but it doesn’t feel unearned because you can see the path that they could have taken to win. The MCU is all about humans trying to be gods, and when a god-like threat shows up, even the real god acts all too human to truly stop him.

Ant-Man and the Wasp.title: Ant-Man and the Wasp
Ant-Man and the Wasp.blurb: A solid follow-up to the original Ant-Man that keeps its focus on the comedy, unique action, and family ties. It doesn’t do anything particularly unique, but it does everything it does extremely well. It takes the action in a unique direction while ramping up the comedy and embracing the inspirational heart of the first film.
Ant-Man and the Wasp.review:
A solid follow-up to the original Ant-Man that keeps its focus on the comedy, unique action, and family ties. It doesn’t do anything particularly unique, but it does everything it does extremely well. It takes the action in a unique direction while ramping up the comedy and embracing the inspirational heart of the first film by showing its heroes helping even their adversaries out of the rut that the law has stuck them all in.

I don't think the action is quite as good in this movie as the original, partly because it's mostly characters swapping sizes in normal spaces instead of fully utilizing the ant-sized world. The ants are also almost barely used, which is disappointing considering how cool they are. There are some banger action scenes, namely Wasp's first fight in the kitchen and Ant-Man growing to giant size over the boat, but generally the fights are a downgrade from the first movie.

The comedy, though, is on point. Everybody is hilarious in this movie, both in the dialogue and just the general scenarios they find themselves in. Like, Agent Woo trying to learn Scott's card tricks is funny enough, but his subordinate barging in on him doing them is hilarious. Sonny Burch is a wise-cracking asshole, Scott is just a generally chill and funny guy as demonstrated in the excellent opening where he and Cassie do a fake heist, Luis is as unhinged as ever, and even Hank Pym gets in some good one-liners. Hope and Ava are the most serious characters, which tracks for both of their circumstances. One of my favorite bits in the movie is Luis going on one of his signature tangents while on a drug the villains swear isn’t truth serum, and revealing a boatload of sensitive yet irrelevant information, and then Luis putting the villains on the truth serum later to make them incriminate themselves and finally admit that it is in fact truth serum. It's so damn funny. Wasp throws a giant Pez dispenser as a projectile weapon. A human-sized ant plays drums. What more do you want?

Oh, you want good characters? Okay, take your pick. Scott is trying to do right by everyone around him, even as his loyalties to Cassie and the Pyms tear him in two separate directions. Cassie is fucking adorable and not only proves that Scott is actually a good dad to her, but is able to inspire him in turn to save the Pyms after she covers for him in front of the FBI. She's like 10, for context, and she already understands how to be a hero. The scene of her mom and boyfriend being horrified to see Ant-Man breaking his house arrest on TV while Cassie just grins like an idiot is one of my favorites in the movie. Speaking of Cassie’s mom and boyfriend, I love that they continue to get along with Scott after repairing their relationship in the last movie. There's no conflict there at all; everybody knows exactly where they stand in the relationship and is perfectly happy with it. It’s such a good dynamic, even if it's a small part of the movie.

Hope and Pym are pissed at Scott for sending them on the run, but they can't truly hate him once they get back in touch with him. Even if it's just to save Hope’s mom at the start, they see Scott as family too, even if he messed up big time. Hell, part of Hope's problem is that he didn't invite her to do crime in Civil War, meaning they're basically perfect for each other. We get to explore Pym being kind of a bitch in his past while still leaving it ambiguous how much was actually his fault and how much was just three brilliant men disagreeing with each other. And in the present, Hank does his best to make it up to them, even if he's focused on saving his wife first. His reunion with Janet in the Quantum Realm is so good.

I love that this movie has no real supervillain. Agent Woo is trying to arrest Scott and the Pyms because they're wanted fugitives, but he seems like a generally chill guy, even if he's a bit too eager to score an arrest. He also winds up being the one who solves the Sonny Burch problem for good after Luis' guys tase him. Sonny Burch is the only real villain, being a capitalist interested in nothing but profit. He has no morals and no higher goals, leaving him as just an asshat with guns instead of a true supervillain with a plan like Aldrich Killian or even Baron Zemo. He’s a petty representation of the system of power, which is perfect for this movie.

Ava Starr aka Ghost is the main villain for most of the movie, but really she's just a parallel to Scott from the first movie if he was even worse off. The film never draws direct comparisons between her and Scott, but it can't be a coincidence that she's a down-on-her-luck criminal just trying to survive by stealing Hank Pym's tech. She even has a quantum scientist mentor in the form of Bill Foster. She’s even more down-on-her-luck since she’s about to die due to magic quantum bullshit, so it makes sense why her crimes are more heinous than Scott’s were. Still though, because the team knows what it’s like to be in Ava’s shoes, they never lose sympathy for her. Hank still wants to save his wife before he cures Ava, but it’s that very wife who saves Ava thanks to her magic quantum bullshit powers. Hank does help her, even if not the way he intended. She can live her life now, and now that she's not dying, she can be her own person instead of the desperate weapon that SHIELD made her. It's a perfect parallel, and a happy ending for everyone except the immoral businessman.

Even Agent Woo wins by arresting Burch, and making an arrest seems to be his main goal because he's a representation of the force of nature that is The System. He wants friends too, though, because as much power as he has, he doesn't have the friends that the normal people like Scott do. The little people help the little people, taking down corrupt businessmen and surviving within the unchangeable system. Hank Pym being like a genius and former CEO does play against that, but he’s also on the run from the cops in this movie, so it still mostly works. All he has is his wits, his tech, and his daughter to support him, and his daughter has the same.

As an MCU film, it’s an interesting fit. It has to go after Infinity War due to that devastating post-credits scene, but it could really go anywhere after Civil War aside from that. Like the first Ant-Man, this film uses the MCU as a setting, taking the idea of the Sokovia Accords and making Scott and Hope navigate them and their consequences. Heroes, powers, and weird tech exist, and we can just accept that because their ramifications are explored in other movies. It’s a perfect use of the expanded universe, and that post-credits proves that it is still part of that universe.

I love this movie, genuinely. It’s not the best movie ever, and maybe not even as good as the first Ant-Man, but it’s close. The Scott/Cassie relationship is so wholesome, and exemplifies why I love these movies. They’re about powerless people doing everything in their power to make the world better for those around them, and inspiring those who will take after them. They’re not the biggest films, or the most morally complex, but they’re freaking awesome and genuinely inspirational. I can’t be Tony Stark or Thor, but I could be Scott, because everyone has a Cassie.

Captain Marvel.title: Captain Marvel
Captain Marvel.blurb: A decent action movie with a decent plot twist, decent thematic twist, and really good looking shapeshifter visuals. Who do you trust when you’re fighting shapeshifters in an interplanetary war? The only people you can trust: yourself and your brand new allies that aren’t suspicious at all. It’s also the 21st movie in the Infinity Saga, and maybe the 19th best.
Captain Marvel.review:
A decent action movie with a decent plot twist, decent thematic twist, and really good looking shapeshifter visuals. Who do you trust when you’re fighting shapeshifters in an interplanetary war? The only people you can trust: yourself and your brand new allies that aren’t suspicious at all. It’s also the 21st movie in the Infinity Saga, and maybe the 19th best.

The movie seems to be about the idea that you’re allowed to show emotions, and that’s what makes you a good person instead of a good soldier. Lots of movies do the “lose your emotions to become the ultimate warrior” thing, and this movie looks like it’s going in that direction, with Yon-Rogg telling Carol that she has to control her emotions to control her powers. This seems poised to be her arc, but with the reveal that Yon-Rogg is evil, it naturally follows that her arc would be the reverse. She goes against her training to harness her emotions and the full range of her powers. However, her personality doesn’t change that much after learning that Yon-Rogg betrayed her, and she doesn’t show any new emotions aside from maybe rage. There’s an argument that she’s showing compassion, but that doesn’t seem to power her emotions at all. Plus, the finale is Yon-Rogg trying to bait her into him fighting hand-to-hand with no powers or weapons because he can’t win otherwise, and her solution is to not give into her anger or ego and just blast him. It’s the practical thing to do, not the emotional thing, which means that Carol’s arc is almost entirely switching sides. Arguably, the entire movie is instead about learning who the true enemies are, with the Kree actually being evil, the original bad guys being shapeshifters, said shapeshifters turning out to be good guys, and Fury being part of an international spy agency, but that theme doesn’t really change any of the characters at all.

None of the characters really gripped me in this movie. Carol’s snark is decently funny, and I like her arc of finding her true self, but it happens so casually, like these revelations barely leave any impact on her. She doesn’t have a breakdown about it, or really interrogate her sense of self, or really change at all. She just changes sides. Fury is also decently funny, feeling very much like a different character from his appearances in Iron Man 2 and Avengers. I think it works - it takes time for a man to get that jaded - but it is a bizarre choice. As much as Fury’s adventures with Carol shape his belief in heroes, they don’t turn him into the paranoid superspy he becomes later. That happens after this movie, with his personality also being barely different from the beginning of this film to the end. Yon-Rogg is really really boring. I like him trying to bait Carol into fighting without powers because he knows he’ll lose, but that’s it. Maria is also, unfortunately, kinda boring. She learns her dead best friend is alive and has like one scene of shock before she just rolls with it and goes to space.

The two best characters are Telos and Monica, and they don’t have arcs either. Rather, they’re just written very well. Telos is proven to be smart and crafty and even cruel when he still thinks Carol is a villain, but his general demeanor after the fact really sells that he’s the good guy. He’s so chill, readily admitting to making mistakes and speaking naturally instead of in a pre-planned, authoritative way like Yon-Rogg does. Despite being a shapeshifter, you believe that he’s telling the truth about his goals. Monica is just super fun, and I do like how quickly she takes to Carol being back. Unlike Maria, she’s still a kid, so of course she believes Carol survived, and is thrilled to have her back. She wants to be a hero, and encourages her mom to do the same. Between this and Ant-Man and the Wasp, we’re 2 for 2 on based 12-year-olds. Also, Goose is really funny. Him being revealed to be an actual alien by casually eating people is probably the best joke payoff in the movie.

The plot is also just decent. The big twist is that the Kree are evil and the Skrulls are good, which does work. I don’t think the characters really give it the weight it deserves, but to some degree I do like that Carol just flips on the Kree. Fury just learned that the Skrulls are evil (and exist) like 24 hours ago, so I’m down with him just believing that they’re the good guys based on more evidence. The double twist that Wendy Lawson was a Kree, but a Kree traitor, is also pretty good. There are pieces to put together all these twists pretty early on, but they still work. Nothing is phenomenal, but it works. The plot has to carry the characters because they barely change at all, but it’s engaging enough to do that, alongside the Fury/Carol banter. I could see this movie being eye-opening for a 12-year-old who hasn’t had exposure to the horrors of war. The “bad guys” aren’t always the bad guys, and I think this movie will make this message land if you haven’t already been exposed to it a hundred times.

As an MCU movie, I think this movie is worse than it is standalone. It’s cool seeing Fury’s backstory and where the idea for the Avengers comes from, but it still doesn’t really show us how he becomes the no-nonsense Fury we see as the head of SHIELD. Carol getting her powers from the Tesseract is a nice touch to explain how strong she is, but it does make the Tesseract’s history unnecessarily complicated. Fury’s and the Tesseract’s backstories are added to, but instead of being elegantly simple like they were before, they’re now more complex than they need to be. Also, we’ve only ever seen the Kree as bad guys in Guardians 1, which really lessens the impact of the twist. We know these guys as genocidal bastards, so of course they’re genocidal bastards. This film is also another origin story with snarky humor, laser beam fight scenes, and a message about becoming your best self to be a hero. We’ve seen this like 5 times already, and the plot twist that the good guys are actually the bad guys is literally just Winter Soldier but worse.

This movie really just exists to explain Carol’s presence in Endgame, and it does work in that regard. The post-credits scene of her showing up on Earth and demanding to know where Fury is really works. Carol’s pissed, but you know she’ll be able to help. It also elevates Fury’s non-existent presence in Infinity War to actually being relevant, since his job is to do what he’s always done: gather heroes to save the day. Also, I don’t think Carol is ever called Captain Marvel in the movie, and why would she be? It’s not even her name, but that of her mentor, which she didn’t know until 6 years after she died. Weird.

Captain Marvel is a decent movie. It’s not as bad as all the haters say, but it’s definitely a lower tier Infinity Saga film, made even worse by how late it comes in continuity. Everything it does is good enough to keep you entertained, and I do think the movie would be more impactful if you haven’t seen other movies that do the same thing but better, but this film doesn’t do enough to make it stand out amongst the others in its genre or even series.

Avengers: Endgame.title: Avengers: Endgame
Avengers: Endgame.blurb: The perfect ending to the Infinity Saga. This isn’t a movie that happens to be the last one, this is a movie that was written from the ground up to be the last one. This is celebrating the whole franchise, putting its characters in old situations to extract new meaning out of them. Its themes and character arcs aren’t particularly deep on their own, but they’re instead building on the themes and arcs from previous movies to make something cohesive in context.
Avengers: Endgame.review:
The perfect ending to the Infinity Saga. This isn’t a movie that happens to be the last one, this is a movie that was written from the ground up to be the last one. This is celebrating the whole franchise, putting its characters in old situations to extract new meaning out of them. Its themes and character arcs aren’t particularly deep on their own, but they’re instead building on the themes and arcs from previous movies to make something cohesive in context. It’s a celebration of the whole saga, even if it focuses on some characters more than others. Fortunately, the ones it focuses on are the ones who get focus in Infinity War, so the duology balances itself out. I don’t think all the characters are done excellently in this movie, mostly because we just see the ends of their journeys and not the path they took during the Snap, but we learn enough about the intervening years that it works for most of them.

The stars of the show this time are Captain America and Iron Man, followed secondarily by Thor, Nebula, and Ant-Man of all people. Thor is the only character who’s really focused on in both Infinity War and Endgame, so it makes sense that he’s the most depressed because he’s the one who personally lost. I love his talk with his mom about becoming who he is instead of who he’s meant to be, and he puts up quite a fight against Thanos in the finale. He’s the only one of the big three still left at the film’s close, and I like that even he leaves Earth to find himself among the stars with his new friends, the Guardians of the Galaxy. He’s always been Asgard’s protector, and then Earth’s even if the role was in some ways placed upon him. With everything he loved gone, it makes sense that he’d leave to find a new sense of purpose, yet becoming a Guardian of the Galaxy means his responsibilities are even bigger than they were on Earth. Even if he no longer has to bear these heroics alone, even if he still feels lost, Thor is still growing into the hero he’s always been.

Nebula gets a surprising amount to do in this movie given that she’s a side character from the Guardians films, but it makes perfect sense considering that Thanos is her adoptive dad. I love that the Avengers’ plan goes wrong because Nebula didn’t predict that she’d connect to her past self, and I love that she takes this opportunity to bond with past Gamora. Gamora is already in the middle of betraying Thanos, so it makes sense that she’d help future Nebula so willingly. She wants them to get along, after all, even if she kinda hates past Nebula. Past Nebula was also on the verge of betraying Thanos, but I buy that she would fully lock in once she has the chance to prove herself more useful than Gamora. Present Nebula killing her past self is also really good, symbolizing that she’s not the villain she once was. It really completes her redemption arc from the Guardians films, both physically and symbolically, despite her not even being an Avenger.

Ant-Man is a bit underutilized, but I do like how he’s the lynchpin. It’s so funny that the time travel solution comes from the Ant-Man movies of all places, and it really makes everything feel connected. Scott emerging from the quantum tunnel five years later and just being completely blindsided by what happened is a great set of emotional scenes. I like that he’s the one who really sets things in motion, because he literally didn’t experience the despair of losing Infinity War. He still has hope, and that’s what brings everyone together, even if he doesn’t do much after telling Cap and Nat how quantum mechanics work.

If Scott is the spark that gives the Avengers hope, then Captain America is the fire. He’s the one who gets Tony to execute Scott’s plan, because he’s Captain Goddamn America. He’s always held out hope that things can be fixed, because that’s what he does. He and Nat still have hope, and once Scott gives them a way to fulfill that hope, Cap is able to bring the team back together by being the natural leader that he is. Him wielding Mjolnir is the perfect capstone to his arc, showing that he’s finally worthy of walking amongst the gods by standing up to a god-killer after weathering despair for five long years. Cap never stopped fighting, and at the end, when the world is finally saved, he gets to take his hard-earned dance with Peggy. He always believed in saving the past, and when it’s all over, Steve finally gets to live the past he lost when he went in the ice all those years ago.

Tony, then, is the opposite. Like Thor, he gives into despair and hides away, but unlike Thor, he still has people. He seems to mostly give up his work and heroing, but puts all his effort into raising his daughter. The old world is dead, but he still has the new one. It’s why it takes Cap to pull him back in, because he needs someone else to give him hope that he can fix things. He makes one last stand to save the universe, and while he can’t fix what’s been done, he can stop the future from being destroyed. He is the futurist, and his daughter is that future, so he sacrifices himself to destroy Thanos and secure that future. He can’t bring people back because he doesn’t believe he can fix the past, which is why Hulk has to be the one to undo the Snap.

Banner and Hulk have integrated their two disparate halves together into one unified whole, so of course Banner is able to reunite the half of humanity that was Snapped away with the half that remained and moved on. It’s perfect poetry. I also like that even though Banner is in Hulk’s body, he never fights with it, only ever using Hulk’s strength to wield the Infinity Gauntlet and bring back half the universe. Hulk is no longer an agent of destruction, but a true heroic extension of Banner’s will.

I do think Banner is hurt pretty bad by not seeing the path he took to merging himself and Hulk. We get a line or two, but it doesn’t feel complete enough for such a radical change. The whole thing feels really goofy and kinda out of place, even if I do like the idea and what it means thematically..

The Avengers who are given the least attention, though, are definitely Black Widow and Hawkeye. Clint specifically wasn’t in Infinity War, and here he turns into a murderous, rage-filled vigilante during the time skip. This should be a huge deal, but nobody really talks about it, and there are no real repercussions for him going all Punisher on the mafias of the world. He’s in the movie, but aside from Nat sacrificing herself on Vormir, he doesn’t really change or contribute. Nat herself is basically just a second Cap, pouring everything she has into fixing the world because she not only believes that she can, but doesn’t know what she’ll do if she doesn’t. Her whole life since Clint saved her has been SHIELD and the Avengers, and without them, she’s lost. It’s the reason she dies on Vormir instead of Clint, even if I don’t really think it’s handled the most elegantly.

I do really like the Vormir fight - you don’t see a lot of fights where two people are fighting each other to sacrifice themself - but it relegates Nat to being not just a second Cap, but also a second Tony. The whole movie is the end of the original Avengers, and this is where Nat meets her end. Clint has a family to go back to, but Nat is an Avenger through and through, so she sacrifices herself so Clint and everyone else after her can go home. It’s a nice sentiment, but it means that Nat never gets her happy ending. Tony dies too, but he had his time during the Snap to live the future he ensured for his daughter. Nat spends her whole time fighting, but unlike Cap, she has to die for it. It also means that Clint saving Nat in Budapest ultimately saves himself, instead of Nat getting to live the life he wanted for her. Of course, Clint being the one to sacrifice himself would mean that he isn’t in Infinity War, then shows up in this movie just to die, so it’s kind of a no-win scenario from a writing perspective. Ultimately, I think if Clint had died instead, this paragraph would have been about how Nat should have died, so I think the only thing the writers could have done would be to have Nat’s death carry more weight in the aftermath. Really, she’s the first of the original Avengers to go, and the one who lets the others live out their futures, which is poetic in its own way. Clint saved one person, and that person saved the world.

Thanos is also in this movie. Unlike Infinity War where he’s almost the main character, his job here is just to be an asshole for a final boss fight. I like how he gets to the present time, and it lines up with his motivation, but he doesn’t really do much beyond that. It works here because this film isn’t about him, but I do think Endgame Thanos is the weakest of the four Avengers villains, writing-wise.

I actually think Thanos is too strong in-universe, like he should not be tanking Stormbreaker and Mjolnir with no Infinity Stones, but whatever. The final fight is still pretty good, with almost everyone having a chance to shine and break out their best abilities. Everyone also feels pretty appropriately powered and useful except for Thor, who is relegated to the same level as Iron Man and Captain Goddamn America when he was the tide-turner in Infinity War. Those five years really did a number on him.

I’ve mentioned before that Endgame is just the second half of Infinity War, and that’s partly because of how it interacts with the themes from that movie. I said in my Infinity War review that the heroes lose there because they’re too emotional while Thanos is logical, and that doesn’t really change in this movie. What does though, and what lines up with Infinity War, is that the heroes become unified. In Infinity War, the heroes are broken apart due to Civil War and also the Guardians are here, and it means that they can’t coordinate anything. Thanos and his army, meanwhile, operate like a well-oiled machine, getting every Stone in the exact order Thanos needs to get the next one. In Endgame, the heroes are working together, executing a perfect plan near-flawlessly and getting mass back-up from all of their allies while Thanos gets betrayed by one of his own (Gamora) and decides to bomb his own soldiers to kill the Avengers. He isn’t fighting as a team while the Avengers are, and that’s why he loses. Even in the finale, the Avengers doing a relay race with the Infinity Gauntlet is the perfect example of how they’re working together to overcome their own weaknesses.

Endgame is the perfect ending to the MCU. It feels like it knows the MCU intimately, to Hank Pym working with Howard Stark in the 70s to the Ancient One helping secretly assist against the Chithauri Invasion of New York to literally reusing the opening of Guardians 1 for Quill dancing on the Power Stone planet, and uses that to show how far our cast has come and progress them even further. Thor gets closure with his mother and Tony with his father, Cap gets to take advantage of his future knowledge to outsmart both himself and Hydra in the past, and Nebula gets to form a bond with Gamora before they try to kill each other.

Even the film’s final one-liner is a callback to the first film, and even that is done with intention. “I am Iron Man” works as the finale here not just because Thanos says “I am inevitable”, but because it shows the completion of Tony’s saga-long arc. Before, he was supporting his own ego because he couldn’t just not tell people that he was a superhero, but here he’s making a statement: he is a superhero, and that means the Earth is protected. Everyone gets their happy endings, as the heroic mantles are passed onto a new generation. Tony saves the future, Steve gets to regain his past, Thor breaks out of the cycle of despair to find new allies and become his own hero, and Spider-Man, Falcon, and Valkyrie will carry on their mantles of heroism.

Even Captain Marvel contributes to make this even more of a finale. Fury learned there were aliens in the 90s, and with the best hero he knows off in space, he crafted the ultimate team of heroes to fight the ultimate alien. Avengers is the test run for Infinity War, both in-universe and out, and the Avengers’ success in-universe proves that Fury’s idea works, proves that heroes are what’s needed to save the world from those who would destroy it. There are really only two unresolved threads, that being Loki escaping with the Tesseract and the whereabouts of past Gamora in the present, but everything else is resolved. The heroes won, fighting the battles nobody else ever could.

Endgame isn’t perfect. It’s thematically pretty shallow on its own, and it doesn’t have the chance to do many of its characters justice, even the one that kicks off the plot in the first place (Scott). What it does have is a clear love for everything that’s come before, and it’s channeling all that love to create the perfect ending for the main characters of the whole saga. It doesn’t need a deep plot or its own themes, because we have those from 21 previous movies. We know this world is about heroes, about overcoming corrupt institutions and genocidal dictators to use your powers for the greater good. Even if that means making sacrifices, one day those sacrifices will pay off, because you’ll have put everything you’ve got into making the world a better place for everyone in it. The only thing stronger than a mad god is a bunch of idiots standing in a circle with nothing but a reckless plan, a heart of gold, and enough hope to carry them through to the end. This is that end, and it’s a damn good one.

X-Men: Apocalypse.title: X-Men: Apocalypse
X-Men: Apocalypse.blurb: An action movie bordering on so-bad-its-good that’s kept out of that group by actually being good due to the banger special effects used for stupid-ass action sequences. This movie exists purely to aura farm, and it damn well succeeds.
X-Men: Apocalypse.review:
An action movie bordering on so-bad-its-good that’s kept out of that group by actually being good due to the banger special effects used for stupid-ass action sequences. This movie exists purely to aura farm, and it damn well succeeds. The plot is paper-thin and the characters are thinner, yet there’s just enough there to keep everything cohesive while pushing things forward.

The opening is this dramatic shot of a masked pharaoh being marched through the city while throes of people bow and chant, and then he starts doing some magic ritual deep in the heart of his pyramid. It’s all very dramatic and impressive, and then two guards smash pillars with hammers to make this pair of giant bricks slide down perfectly cut ramps into the underground part of the pyramid and start smashing through all of its foundations like a Rube Goldberg machine. It’s so unbelievably silly while being played so straight that it becomes cool again.
