You can’t help but laugh and be in awe at the same time, because the characters never pretend that this is anything but the most serious shit. The whole movie is like this, and just expects you to get onboard. You’re also expected to just understand the superpowers and superhumans are real, and the movie jumps right in with the stuff they can do. Some guy disintegrates some other guys by using a force push to smash them into a wall at the five minute mark, and the movie never even pauses to emphasize how fantastical and intense this is. This is the world the X-Men live in, and things only escalate from there..

Other highlights of generally awesome yet also really goofy shit include Apocalypse just decapitating three people with sand, Cyclops obliterating a tree and then Xavier remarking that that was his favorite tree, Magneto making giant rotating rock structures all over the world at once, Jean casually walking on air, Xavier going bald because Apocalypse tries to possess him, and the entire Quicksilver mansion scene. The Quicksilver scene in particular is exceptionally goofy. Havoc literally dies 2 seconds earlier, but Quicksilver doesn’t know that, so he saves everybody in perfectly-timed slow motion while still chugging energy drinks and setting up sheets on trees to throw people into to slow their fall. It’s not quite as good as the Days of Future Past scene, but this one is still both really cool and also really really silly.

There’s a whole scene dedicated to just murdering a whole bunch of military guys. The X-Men get kidnapped for like twenty minutes and I’m pretty sure the whole thing exists as an excuse to have Wolverine murder a whole bunch of people. The scene where Jean calms him down is pretty cool, legitimately, but everything else is an excuse.

The final battle is also legitimately good, even if it’s still very goofy at parts. The X-Men are getting defeated so Magneto betrays Apocalypse by throwing two giant girders between Apocalypse and the X-Men. Girders that land in the shape of an X. For X-Men. Angel dies in a plane crash, and Psylocke just walks away while nobody’s looking. Quicksilver almost solos Apocalypse before Apocalypse telepathically traps his foot in rock because Quicksilver is just that fast. Xavier and Apocalypse have a psychic duel that ends with Apocalypse getting really big and ragdolling Xavier, and somehow the effects for this look good. Jean does the aforementioned walking on air thing, and then emits this sick-ass fiery aura in the shape of a Phoenix while she uses her flaming telepathy to disintegrate Apocalypse one layer at a time. It’s actually sick as fuck, no comedy at all, and is the perfect cap to the movie.

The special effects in this movie in general are pretty good. There’s like 5 minutes that are just dedicated to Magneto ripping rocks out of the ground at various points in the movie, and it all looks fantastic. The makeup is also really good, except for Apocalypse. Nightcrawler, Psylocke, Mystique, Storm, and Angel look phenomenal, yet Apocalypse’s comic-accurate makeup looks really bad whenever we get a closeup of him talking. His obvious drawn-on lips just don’t match his real lips at all. It makes him hard to take seriously, which is fine considering the rest of the movie is so goofy.

Normally I talk about the plot and characters first and then the action, but there’s honestly not a lot going on in this movie. There’s like twenty characters and maybe three character arcs. Jean and Mystique learn to embrace their powers, and Magneto learns to not commit genocide (again). Cyclops and Nightcrawler get some friends, but like, this is never acknowledged as an arc for them, it just happens. Nightcrawler just gets enrolled into the X-Men on accident during his first day at the school because the plot just so happens to occur while he’s there. The fact that he probably really shouldn’t be there is never acknowledged. It’s just “Nightcrawler’s here, woo!”. Cyclops’ brother dies and he’s sad about it for two scenes and then doesn’t mention it again. Nobody else is that torn up, either, even the characters who’ve known Havoc for years. It probably should be dramatic, but then the X-Men get kidnapped by the government, so we have bigger fish to fry.

I’m pretty sure the sudden government subplot is just an excuse for Wolverine to show up, but it’s also a connection to Days of Future Past and the original trilogy. It shows that the timeline is following similar paths even though Magneto was stopped in Days of Future Past, which is legit cool. Some thought went into this plot, even if it’s not the movie’s focus. It’s also completely irrelevant to the Apocalypse storyline. The Apocalypse storyline is, by the way: Apocalypse gets some recruits, blows up the world’s nukes in 30 seconds, kidnaps Xavier in less, then does mild terraforming until the X-Men show up to fight him. It’s so unbelievably simple, I genuinely don’t know how this movie is 2.5 hours. It doesn’t feel that long, though, because things still somehow never stop moving.

I think a big part of the pacing never feeling off is that despite how goofy everything is, nothing comes out of nowhere. We’re introduced to Nightcrawler and Angel fighting in a cage match so Mystique can save them, and then Nightcrawler and Angel join the X-Men and Apocalypse, respectively. Magneto’s family gets a whole dedicated scene before we cut away to another scene, allowing their presence to breathe before we cut back to the scene where they die. Cyclops gets an appropriate amount of buildup, and Storm gets her own scene before running into Apocalypse. It allows everything to be introduced once before being forced into fight scenes, so nothing feels like it’s pulled out of the movie’s ass just to blow shit up. Nothing except the government, anyway, and even that’s tangentially connected to the X-Men’s whole thing of being hated and feared by the government.

I understand why people don’t like this film. Almost all the other X-Men films are serious superhero dramas about bigotry, heroism, and deep characters, and Apocalypse is a straight action film veering on action-comedy. As an action-comedy, though, it does a damn good job. The fights are good, and the large cast feels well-balanced. Nobody feels underutilized in the fights, and everyone’s powers are unique enough that every fight feels like it could only be fought by the characters in it. If First Class and Days of Future Past are full meals, then Apocalypse is a well-crafted dessert, and if you go into it with that mindset, you’re gonna have a good time.

X-Men: Dark Phoenix.title: X-Men: Dark Phoenix
X-Men: Dark Phoenix.blurb: This is not a good movie. It tries to be a serious drama about the fall of a hero and how overwhelming power and oversensitivity makes you a danger to those around you. What it feels like is the world and characters being mean to each other for no real reason.
X-Men: Dark Phoenix.review:
This is not a good movie. It tries to be a serious drama about the fall of a hero and how overwhelming power and oversensitivity makes you a danger to those around you. What it feels like is the world and characters being mean to each other for no real reason. The special effects are really good, but they aren’t utilized nearly enough to carry the film’s abysmal plot and unlikeable characters.

The core problem is that nobody is likeable. People are understandable, maybe, but nobody is likeable. Jean is one of the most sympathetic because none of this is really her fault, but she does not handle things well. She doesn’t communicate at all with her boyfriend, refuses to take responsibility for any of the problems she causes, even if she is under duress, and goes to Magneto to get advice after she just killed his best friend. Also, Jean is under duress! The only reason she’s dangerous is because she’s experiencing the trauma of killing her parents for the first time because Xavier blocked those emotions off, and almost all the bad things she does happen when she gets sensory overload. Like, her fighting the military guys and torturing Magneto and Xavier isn’t great, but they are kinda trying to kill her. She’s both evil and the victim, which is a weird-ass dichotomy that the film never reconciles. You’re supposed to feel bad for her, but also she clearly crosses the line at several points.

Then there’s Xavier. This movie goes the route of making him a jerk again, which is annoying. It mainly does this by having him block Jean’s trauma of her father abandoning her after she killed their mother, and this gives Jean sensory overload when it comes back all at once in the present. Everything is kinda his fault due to this, and it takes him way too long to admit it. It makes him unsympathetic when he’s supposed to be the hero. However, his big critic is Mystique, who also comes across as unsympathetic. She blames Xavier for putting the X-Men in danger just to save humanity, when the X-Men being heroes is the only thing keeping mutantkind in humanity’s good graces. As soon as one thing goes wrong, Xavier is excommunicated from the government after 10 years of heroism, which means that Xavier was right about putting the X-Men in danger. Jean is unsympathetic, Xavier is unsympathetic, and Mystique is unsympathetic, which means the most sympathetic one is Magneto. He’s chilling on his own mutant haven island, and only emerges to kill Jean after she killed Mystique. However, she killed Mystique by accident, so Magneto isn’t super sympathetic either. Who am I supposed to root for? Cyclops? He has no personality outside of being Jean’s boyfriend and Xavier’s lackey. Him, Storm, and Nightcrawler all just feel like Xavier’s henchmen in the same way that the two random mutants Magneto takes with him to fight Jean feel like henchmen. Nobody is likeable, so all the big moral dilemmas just fall flat on their face because I don’t care. I don’t want anybody to win, I just want these people to get over themselves and stop fighting.

To the film’s credit, the final battle is pretty good. Everybody gets their shit together to fight the aliens that want to use Jean to destroy the world (yes that’s the plot), and the action is very intense. Nightcrawler gets to kick ass, Storm gets to obliterate a bunch of people, and Magneto gets to crush a train car. Also, the scene prior to the finale of Jean making Xavier walk is appropriately horrifying. The actual ending to the battle is kinda lame because Jean just sacrifices herself to make the villain explode, but at least the big battle leading up to that is cool. The problem is that aside from the final battle, there’s basically no other action sequences. There’s the intro scene, the very brief scene where Jean mauls the X-Men and kills Mystique, and the two part final battle, the first of which is cool only because of how much the individual fights intersect. Xavier’s henchmen fight Magneto’s henchmen, and it actually feels like a proper 4v4 instead of 4 1v1s.

The lack of action sequences is even more disappointing because the special effects department goes all out for the powers. The Phoenix effects are awesome, and I love how Jean’s skin cracks and her hair flows with power when she loses control. Nightcrawler’s teleportation is awesome, as are the effects for Magneto. The makeup is also still on point, with both Beast and Nightcrawler looking really good. If the film made better use of these powers, it could at least have some merit as a spectacle film, but it doesn’t.

As an X-Men movie, this film is even worse than it is standalone. Mainly, it just does not treat the X-Men well. This is primarily because of the aforementioned asshole-ification of Xavier and Mystique, but Mystique’s death is also incredibly lame. She dies trying to talk Jean down, and only makes things worse. It’s cool that Mystique goes out trying to be a hero, but she accomplishes nothing, so it feels like a disappointing end for the tritagonist of this new set of movies. Oh and Quicksilver gets hospitalized in the same fight where Mystique dies, so we’re left with Cyclops, Storm, and Nightcrawler as our three X-Men, and none of them feel like people. They all have better characterization in Apocalypse somehow, and that movie gives no fucks.

The plot, too, hates the X-Men. They’ve been international heroes for 10 years after stopping Apocalypse, then the president rescinds their status after Jean goes rogue and attacks some cops. All that progress, gone for no reason, and this is never rectified. It’s barely even part of the story, except to have the X-Men get kidnapped (again) and to make Xavier look like more of a jerk. The movie ends with Xavier quitting and Beast taking over as the X-Men rebuild, but for what. This is the last X-Men movie, and it ends with the X-Men destroyed and mutantkind in a worse place than it was two movies ago. Like Last Stand, the franchise ends with mutants losing their battle for equality.

I do not like this movie. It tries to be the same type of character drama about bigotry and responsibility as the rest of the franchise, except it can’t write characters to save its life. It can only create drama by making everybody incapable of basic social problem solving. This movie could be solved in like 5 minutes if people just talked to each other. Mystique didn’t die because it was the perfect ending to her arc, she died because it would cause more drama and character conflict. I truly think this movie would be better if it wasn’t an X-Men film, because then at least it would be clear that everybody in this world just sucks instead of likeable characters becoming assholes because the writers need a conflict. Dark Phoenix makes the same mistakes Last Stand to end its series on a dud, with no third chance to rise from the ashes. Fortunately, as the audience, we have the power to watch things out of order and give the X-Men that chance. This franchise has spin-offs, after all, and ones that provide a better ending to the franchise than Dark Phoenix’s flickering ashes.

Deadpool.title: Deadpool
Deadpool.blurb: A raunchy, gory comedy with a decent plot and not much in the way of character development. The comedy mostly hits, despite the overreliance on sex jokes, but if the comedy doesn’t hit, there’s not much here for you.
Deadpool.review:
A raunchy, gory comedy with a decent plot and not much in the way of character development. The comedy mostly hits, despite the overreliance on sex jokes, but if the comedy doesn’t hit, there’s not much here for you. The action is pretty good, even if it’s not as zany or out-there as you might expect from a Deadpool movie. Still, there’s enough fast-paced action mixed with the frequent quips and infrequent moments of heart to smooth over the shallow plot and characters.

The comedy is mostly sex jokes and reference comedy, and they mostly work, even if you get a bit sick of them by the end. There are a few good jokes of other types though, such as Deadpool convincing Dopinder the Taxi Driver to kill his cousin to steal his wife, and Deadpool spelling the main villain’s name using the bodies of his dead soldiers. Deadpool living with Al the Old Blind Lady Who Does Coke is also hilarious. The comedy has a lot of momentum that makes each joke funnier than the last as you get swept up in it all, but the improvised quips in particular feel all over the place instead of feeling like a natural escalation of comedic intensity.

As for the action, it’s mostly standard if over-the-top gun and sword play without a lot of use of superpowers. The best use of Deadpool’s healing factor is probably when he cuts his hand off to escape Colossus, which is cool but not nearly the coolest thing they could have done. Negasonic Teenage Warhead gets one good use of her explosive energy powers to bomb the shipyard where the final battle takes place, but that’s about it. Aside from the lack of powers, the sword and gunplay are both very good. The fight where Deadpool is counting his bullets is hilarious.

The plot is very simple, being a simple love/revenge story with an element of tragedy. I actually like Deadpool’s backstory here, with him willing to try an experimental treatment to cure his cancer because he cares more about not dying than he does about living life to its fullest with his fiancee Vanessa. The treatment does make him immortal, but also makes him hideous, and he believes he can never face Vanessa again, so he goes on a revenge murder spree against Francis, the guy who transformed him. It’s a simple revenge plot, but Deadpool knowing that Vanessa is alive adds a cool layer of the story being as much about revenge as it is about Deadpool’s self-loathing. He refuses to see her because he thinks she won’t love him, so he goes and kills a whole bunch of people, when really he never needed to do that because she just wanted him. It’s a simple plot and nobody really changes that much, but it’s fine for the type of movie this is.

The movie does really make you hate Francis due to how much he tortures Deadpool and how much glee he takes in it, but there’s not much to him beyond that. Deadpool’s friends Al and Weasel are similarly one-note, although I do like how far Weasel goes to protect Deadpool’s identity.

Colossus and Negasonic Teenage Warhead also don’t have much going on, although Negasonic gets the teensy tiny character arc of deciding she kinda likes Deadpool’s vibe. The two are pretty funny, and try to add an element of whether Deadpool should choose revenge or be a hero and not murder everybody who wronged him. Of course, Deadpool gets to murder everybody and be a hero because the people he’s murdering are just that awful. Vanessa always knowing he was a hired assassin also helps, because she’s all he really wanted. So he gets his happy ending despite all the murder. He makes the choice to stay himself, and doesn’t change at all because he never needed to. So uh, I guess the experimental treatment did its job in curing Deadpool of cancer with no ill side effects.

The simple plot is mainly there to provide context for the comedy and action, and if it gets you invested in Deadpool’s romance/revenge story, all the better. It’s a violent, gory, raunchy comedy, and if that doesn’t do it for you, there isn’t much here. As one of those, though, it’s pretty unique for a superhero film, especially for when it released. You’ll probably know if this movie is for you based on the description alone, and that’s alright. Personally, I think it’s pretty good.

Deadpool 2.title: Deadpool 2
Deadpool 2.blurb: Deadpool 2 is pretty much the first one but better in every way. It’s way funnier, has better action sequences, more heart, and a stronger story. It’s still got the gory violence and sex jokes, but elevates it with an actually engaging story.
Deadpool 2.review:
Deadpool 2 is pretty much the first one but better in every way. It’s way funnier, has better action sequences, more heart, and a stronger story. It’s still got the gory violence and sex jokes, but elevates it with an actually engaging story.

The main draw of Deadpool is the humor, and this film knocks it out of the park. I was laughing out loud pretty frequently due to both the verbal and the visual comedy. My favorite general gag is how Domino uses her luck powers. Everytime she’s on screen something hilarious happens. Her fight in the orphanage and all the bad guys killing each other is great, but the highlight is her hijacking the train. It’s all the random things that cascade into being helpful, like her throwing a guy out the window to make the side mirror start spinning and then that temporarily blinds Cable and makes him miss. It’s an excellent showcase of luck powers, being both awesome and delightful to watch. I’m still mixed on the infamous X-Force genocide sequence, but the whole thing does make Domino’s bit way funnier. Her guessing the passcode at the end and it just being “7” is also a really good bit.

Some of the my other favorite jokes include everybody pointing guns at Cable and Blind Al not only reacting late but also pointing in the wrong direction, Deadpool bitches about there being no X-Men and then they shut themselves in a room to avoid him, and Yukio and Deadpool just cheerily greeting each other, and Deadpool ignoring the entire plot to ask Cable if dubstep is still a thing.

Not all of the humor lands, unfortunately. If the first film had an overreliance on sex jokes, this one was an overreliance on reference humor. I personally find many of the references funny, but the film does occasionally go too far and reference the same thing two or three times. Once you make the reference once, it stops being funny, because part of why it’s funny is that the reference is even being made in the first place.

The action is also on point in this movie. The fight scenes are very dynamic, and make far better use of Deadpool’s powers. Cable’s and Firefist’s abilities also make things more interesting than just guys with guns and swords, allowing things to feel far more intense. I don’t think any of the fight scenes top the bullet counting fight from the first movie, but they’re far better on average. The two Domino fights come close, especially the first one when you’re not quite expecting it yet. The weakest fight is probably the Colossus/Juggernaut fight because you can just feel that the characters aren’t real, but the ending to the fight being electrocuting Juggernaut in a pool is pretty funny.

The big thing that sets this movie apart from the first one is the characters and story. This film juggles a lot of characters and it leaves a handful of them underdeveloped, mostly the returning bit characters from Deadpool 1. Negasonic Teenage Warhead in particular adds almost nothing aside from a few good lines and the “Hi Yukio” bit. The rest of the cast also doesn’t have a lot going on, but they have just enough going on to do what they need to do, whether that’s add to the story like Cable and Russell, add to the fight scenes like Domino and Juggernaut, or just be really funny like Dopinder.

The film’s themes and central character conflict are a bit more complex than in the first movie, centering around Deadpool trying to find meaning now that Vanessa is gone and there’s nobody for him to get revenge on. Russell and Cable are in a similar place, with Cable trying to get vengeance for the torture he suffered, and Cable trying to get revenge for his own dead family. While Deadpool gets depressed, Russell becomes a violent terrorist, and Cable does everything he can to get his family back. The three fall down different paths, but end up at the same solution: you can’t get back what you lost, but you can still find meaning with the others who care about you. Of course, Deadpool does get Vanessa back, and Cable could have reunited with his family, but we don’t have time travel in real life, so eh.

The story still isn’t perfect. Killing Vanessa is certainly a decision, but Deadpool’s entire character is centered around her death so it doesn’t quite feel like fridging. Deadpool still tries to kill himself to the last, though, and only decides to keep living because Cable forces him too. He does find a reason to live, but he still immediately brings Vanessa back. I don’t blame him, but it does make it seem like Deadpool never really resolves his internal conflict. The first movie is similar, so this may just be a theme with this franchise.

Alongside Deadpool trying to kill himself, the film is all about what it means to do the right thing, and it never really answers that. Deadpool trying to kill Russell’s torturers in public is what leads to Russell becoming Firefist in the first place, and him killing all the criminals is what leads to Vanessa’s death. The movie also treats Cable trying to kill Russell as wrong, so the implication is that while bad guys need to be stopped, it’s better to talk them down than to just commit murder. That said, Dopinder still kills the guy who tortured Firefist and everybody’s chill with it, and the first movie is all about how it’s okay to kill people who deserve it. Deadpool isn’t supposed to be the best guy, but if he is a bad guy and murder is so wrong, then the X-Men are weirdly okay with it. That said, the other X-Men do shun Deadpool, so maybe Colossus and Negasonic Teenage Warhead are also towing the line of heroism.

I haven’t really talked about these movies as part of the X-Men franchise, and that’s because it doesn’t really matter. The X-Men are used as this idea of heroism that is more important to this movie than the first, but it doesn’t use any of the characters or plots from the main films. Instead, they use the franchise as a setting to have this heroic group and wacky mutant powers. This film makes better use of those powers than the first one, but I think both do benefit from assuming that audiences know and accept that superhumans live in this world.

Deadpool 2 isn’t perfect, but it’s still a damn good time. The comedy and action are excellent, and while the themes aren’t the strongest, the film’s heart is still in the right place.

New Mutants.title: New Mutants
New Mutants.blurb: The premise for this film is interesting, taking the horror aspects of mutants developing their powers for the first time and turning that into a full-blown superhero-horror film where the kids have to face the literal manifestation of the fears they developed when they used their powers for the first time. The problem is that the execution is kinda ass.
New Mutants.review:
The premise for this film is interesting, taking the horror aspects of mutants developing their powers for the first time and turning that into a full-blown superhero-horror film where the kids have to face the literal manifestation of the fears they developed when they used their powers for the first time. The problem is that the execution is kinda ass.

The whole setup of the film is that Dani is making everybody relive their worst nightmares through her powers, with everybody’s nightmare being hurting someone or being hurt because of their powers, and then everybody has to overcome their fears to embrace their powers and themselves. Except nobody really overcomes their fears except for Dani and Illyana, with everyone just making the conscious decision to use their powers to help their friends. The idea is there, but they never have to overcome the literal embodiment of their greatest fear, which is such a wasted opportunity. Instead, the apparitions serve to act as exposition and ramp up the tension with a bit of horror, with the only exceptions being Dani's and Illyana's. Illyana gets to actually activate her powers to beat the everliving shit out of her greatest fear, when only moments before she couldn't do anything but scream. It's an awesome moment that actually feels like it's delivering on the premise. The only other time this happens is the finale, where Dani faces her fears and commands the Demon Bear to stand down. It’s kinda disappointing, but I do like that because the Demon Bear is Dani’s fear, her facing her fear gives her control over her powers and the fears they manifest.

Part of the problem is just that the movie isn't scary. The Faceless Men are creepy and you do really feel like the kids have no chance of winning against their fears, especially the Demon Bear, but nothing is actually all that scary. There's some tension and it does peak, but like, I was never really scared watching this movie. I feel for the characters, but not for myself. Everything is just too telegraphed, too fast, and too one-and-done to actually have any impact. I do think this movie is better as a superhero-horror movie than a horror-superhero movie, which I do think helps it fit better into the X-Men franchise. It just really doesn't deliver on the horror aspect, which is disappointing since Dani’s power lends itself so well to it.

On the superhero aspect, the powers we see are pretty cool. Illyana's powers in particular are both gorgeous and thrilling to watch. She's so fast and so threatening that it's intense, and every one of her slices on the Demon Bear briefly opening a portal to Limbo is such a cool touch that they didn't need to add. Rahne doesn't do a lot in her wolf form, but her half-wolf form is really cool, both in how she uses it to track down Dani and in the visual effects. The Demon Bear itself looks incredible and is legitimately threatening, and the final fight is decent, especially for a movie of this caliber.

The other part where the movie is lacking is its characters. Sam and Roberto in particular get almost nothing to do aside from be the focus of first horror scenes we see, although I do like Sam snapping Illyana out of her panic response. Illyana is such a bitch early on, and there's no real point where she goes from being an asshole to being friends with everybody else. It's kinda when she realizes that Dr Reyes is planning to turn them all into weapons, but it feels like a flip switches instead of her actually becoming friends with them. I think the idea is that her bullying is a front to protect herself from getting close to others due to her trauma, but the movie doesn't really explore that, so the life-and-death friendship comes a bit too fast for me. It sucks the wind out of the hopeful ending when I don’t believe these characters actually like each other. The only really good relationship is that between Dani and Rahne, which is a good thing because it's the main relationship in the film. Even then, it's pretty much love at first sight and isn’t developed beyond that, but I do think Rahne sees herself in Dani when she reaches out. You do feel for the cast and they do kinda bond over the course of the film, but not enough for you to get fully invested in any of their relationships except for maybe Dani/Rahne. The actors are doing their best, it’s just not enough to save the writing. Dr Reyes is at least a decent villain due to the slow reveal of just how evil she is, and her death is good if a bit obvious.

This movie being an X-Men spin-off helps give it some weight, since you understand that superhumans exist and how they’re treated. Plus, the fact that Dr Reyes works for the same people who tortured Russell in Deadpool 2 and experimented on Wolverine in Apocalypse gives us more of a window into that universe. This film feels like the start of a series, and while I don't know if the sequels would necessarily have been better, I think the fact that we've spent this whole movie learning about these characters and watching them overcome their greatest fears would have helped. As it stands, this is the last X-Men movie ever made, although it's clearly not an ending point for the franchise.

I think if either the horror or the characters were good, this movie would be a lot better. Instead, it’s just a whole lot of nothing. All of the character arcs kinda work, and the horror kinda works, and the action mostly works, but almost none of it is interesting or engaging outside of the premise. As an X-Men movie, it’s an inoffensive addition, and as a standalone film, it's an experiment that simply didn’t pan out.

Logan.title: Logan
Logan.blurb: A very good end for Wolverine, showing a darker side of the X-Men universe while still leaving hope. The fight scenes are excellently bloody, and the character work is really well done, if a bit simpler than you might expect from a movie this dark.
Logan.review:
A very good end for Wolverine, showing a darker side of the X-Men universe while still leaving hope. The fight scenes are excellently bloody, and the character work is really well done, if a bit simpler than you might expect from a movie this dark.

Essentially, Logan has lost everything, and this movie is him learning to find hope and be a hero again. He’s accepted that he’s slowly dying and there’s no hope for himself or anyone around him, and yet he still can’t bring himself to put himself or the dementia-addled Xavier out of their misery. Instead, he reluctantly decides to be a hero again, bringing young Laura to North Dakota to save her from the evil military science people at Transigen. By the end of the film, he can’t stop himself from being a hero again, going after Laura when her friends are hunted by Transigen instead of abandoning her like he was going to when they attacked his house. He dies for this, but he dies satisfied, finally getting able to rest while feeling like he accomplished something for the first time in a long time. By having something new to fight for in the form of Laura, Logan is able to become the Wolverine again. As The Wolverine put it, he died holding his heart in his hand.

Laura is the tagalong for the first half of the movie, getting into more problems than she solves, and yet she exudes personality even before she reveals she can speak. She’s sassy in a way that only a self-interested child could be, which makes her a fun watch despite how objectively horrifying her circumstances are. She doesn’t know what love is and just wants to run away from the violence, yet switches to brutally efficient violence as her first resort. Even still, she clearly doesn’t like it, screaming the whole while. It’s cool watching her slowly warm up to Logan, even if she trusts him to some degree from the start thanks to talking to Xavier and reading the X-Men comics. Once she starts talking, she gets even better, as we get a better glimpse into her psyche. She just wants to run away with her friends and won’t take no for an answer, but she also clearly cares about Logan, making him rest when he’s too tired to drive. I like that her little eulogy to Wolverine is a quote from the one movie she’s watched, because it seemed profound and appropriate and she doesn’t know what else to say. Her turning the cross on Logan’s grave to an X devastates me, showing that she sees him not as the disgruntled old man he’s become, but as the X-Man he always was inside.

Xavier is also done pretty well. He’s clearly on edge and angry due to being locked away and drugged, but he still has that soft side to him, as seen with both Laura and the family they meet on the road. You feel bad for him because he’s only half there and has to constantly suppress his powers so he doesn’t kill everyone around him, but he still feels like Xavier when he’s able to do something other than be kept in confinement by Logan and Caliban.

The villains unfortunately kinda suck. They’re appropriately threatening, but they really don’t have a lot going on. They’re the embodiment of seeing mutants not as people but as weapons, willing to wipe them all out except for the ones that they grow in labs to be used as living weapons. They’re cruel and hateable, but there isn’t a lot going for them as characters, which is kinda disappointing. They’re just the villains, and even fellow clone X-24 remains loyal to his masters the whole time. X-24 being killed by the same adamantium bullet that gave Wolverine his amnesia initially is pretty cool, though, symbolically killing Logan twice at the same time. Of course, Laura lives, so the spirit of Wolverine the hero lives on.

The action is also phenomenal. It’s so bloody, and you can feel the pain in every slice and every gunshot. Logan is in pain the whole movie, yet he gets to finally cut loose in a way he never could in the X-Men films, amputating limbs and spraying blood at every opportunity. Laura herself is just as violent, and you really root for her to murder the shit out of her abusers even if a kid should never act like that. The villain being another counterpart to Wolverine flanked by guys with guns is kinda boring, but they’re perfect fodder for Logan and Laura to decimate. My favorite fight scene is probably the final one, when we get to watch all the kids use their powers while Wolverine tries not to die of exhaustion.

I also want to shout out the scene where Xavier has all the military guys paralyzed and Logan fights through the psychic strain to kill the guys and reach Xavier, which is just so cool to watch. I also love the scene where X-24 kills Xavier. It’s so tense, because you only barely realize something’s wrong before Xavier dies. The fact that it’s shot from Xavier’s perspective so you don’t fully realize that they’re not showing Logan only makes things more devastating.

Most of this film’s depth comes from it being an X-Men film, partly because this film was clearly made as the swan song for Wolverine, and partially Xavier and the X-Men. Wolverine’s arc across the X-Men films is great, going from being the new recruit in X-Men 1 to being the mentor and progenitor of the next generation here. Xavier fulfills a similar role, being the one to initially connect with Laura and lead Wolverine on the path to saving them. It’s why the villains in this film are tech villains and a clone of Wolverine, because it is his film and not an X-Men movie. Them making the future mutants is great too, because it means that through all the effort humanity went through to try and get rid of mutants, they wound up being the ones to ensure they survived. It’s delightfully ironic.

Despite being centered on Wolverine, this film still feels thematically tied to the rest of the X-Men franchise in a way that The Wolverine really doesn’t. Spiritually, this film feels like the counterpart to Days of Future Past, with Logan ending the timeline that that film created. Both are about dystopias where mutants no longer exist, but where Days of Future Past ends with a total reset, Logan ends with them being reborn through the same tech that killed them, making this far more hopeful. Assuming this takes place in the new timeline, though, it’s only a counterpart because it chooses to destroy the happy ending established at the end of Days of Future Past. However, that future can’t exist because Jean dies in Dark Phoenix, meaning this film and the Days of Future Past epilogue likely take place in their own timeline separate from the one seen in Apocalypse and Dark Phoenix. It’s unnecessarily complicated and muddies what this film actually means for the world as a whole. Still, though, I think it accomplishes what it’s trying to say very well, showing a world akin to Days of Future Past that nonetheless ends with hope because Wolverine is able to save his world instead of being forced to create another.

This movie is still a banger, despite how messy the X-Men timeline is. On rewatch, I’m not fully sure that it’s the perfect end to the X-Men franchise, but I think it still works as its own thing, as an end instead of the end. The cinematography is incredible, instilling in this whole film a vibe of dread, death, and destruction. The old is gone, the new is worse, and these kids are what will make the future whole again. The actors are all putting their best foot forward, even Dafne Keen as Laura, and the action is bloody incredible. It’s a damn good film, enhanced by being the last Wolverine movie if not the last X-Men movie.

One-Punch Man S1.title: One-Punch Man S1
One-Punch Man S1.blurb: A banger parody of the superhero genre that gets at the heart of what being a hero is despite having a guy who can one-shot everybody. The animation is also gorgeous, drawing out the best in every fight and making the world feel powerful and explosive.
One-Punch Man S1.review:
A banger parody of the superhero genre that gets at the heart of what being a hero is despite having a guy who can one-shot everybody. The animation is also gorgeous, drawing out the best in every fight and making the world feel powerful and explosive.

Almost every arc works out the same: some bad guys show up and gloat about how strong they are, then Saitama shows up and one-shots them. This works really well as a parody for the first few episodes since the way Saitama just casually upstages people is hilarious, and the supervillain types are really unique. Once the usual structure starts losing its luster, the show rightly pivots into more intense arcs, shining a spotlight on the world that Saitama disrupts just by existing.

Despite Saitama being the strongest guy in the world, the show is about him learning how to use that power. He’s comically destructive in the first few episodes, and doesn’t know what to do when he’s not fighting world-ending threats. The show is about him finding value in being a hero regardless, and learning that he can do more than just destroy people. The fact that Saitama got so strong from just training is a great addition to the bit, shaping his outlook that he should be able to do anything just by trying.

He passes this outlook to his new disciple, Genos, and Genos’ arrival is where the show really takes off. He forces Saitama to do something other than lounge around, both by making Saitama train him and by actually pushing for Saitama to be a hero. Genos is also incredibly strong, but never quite strong enough, so he wants to be stronger. He is also a cyborg, which means Saitama has no idea how to train this guy. Saitama is forced to spout generic, only barely useful advice, and Genos takes it as gospel. It’s really funny, and makes you feel for Genos as he tries and fails to live up to Saitama’s example. Genos losing nearly every fight he’s in makes me feel bad for the guy, because he is clearly powerful. You don’t get the impression that he’s powerful just because he’s flashy either; he blows up a mountain in one of his first appearances. He’s just never enough, but it is pretty funny that the visually stronger guy loses every fight while the boring guy wins every fight.

However, Genos losing is also the start of a larger trend: if you are a hero who isn’t Saitama, you will probably lose. Opening up the world from Saitama and Genos to the whole Hero Organization is a great idea, and I really like their concept and first few episodes. Joining their ranks gives Saitama something to do aside from fighting bad guys, and it's fun seeing other people adjust to Saitama’s power. While Saitama having to win nearly every fight could get boring and predictable, the show gives the heroes just enough to do that they feel like they’re pulling their own weight while Saitama handles the ridiculously overpowered bad guys that just happen to show up.

The last two arcs of the season are my favorite, showing just why the Heroes are heroes while still letting Saitama execute his one-punch strategy. The Sea King arc might be my favorite, and it’s all about how the heroes are utilized. We open with A-Class hero Stinger actually beating some guys, and then once the Sea King shows up, it’s all about weaker heroes holding him off to protect civilians until the stronger heroes arrive. Genos still has to lose, of course, but he’s the one who holds the line the longest, showing how far he’s come since he became Saitama’s disciple. The hero that finally arrives is Saitama, not one of the expected S-Class heroes, but it makes Saitama feel more heroic since he is the savior the other heroes and civilians have needed. The heroes buying time is epitomized by Mumen Rider’s “fight”, which is literally just him getting mauled until Saitama shows up, but it emphasizes what the heroes are doing and makes them feel worthwhile. Mumen Rider’s speech about never standing down and Saitama’s subsequent floor-wiping of the Sea King is probably my favorite moment in the show.

The finale is the Boros Arc, and it’s structured similarly to the Sea King Arc, except four S-Class heroes actually get a win against Boros’ right-hand while Saitama takes on Boros’s entire ship and Boros. The Saitama-Boros fight is great, as Boros is painted as such a parallel to Saitama in terms of personality and backstory that you almost think he’ll be a match for Saitama before Saitama gets serious and the viewer and Boros realize that the fight was over before it began. It’s a great finale to Season 1, and honestly not a bad end to the show as a whole, aside from the various dangling plothooks.

The side characters are also generally pretty good, with my favorites being Speed of Sound Sonic and Mumen Rider. I kinda want Sonic to catch up to Saitama, because he’s just motivated by spite and it’d be so fucking funny. Mumen Rider is also great, being the true embodiment of heroism as a guy with no powers. Although if normal humans like Saitama or even the Tanktop people can get strong just by training, it seems kinda silly that Mumen Rider is still normal. Maybe silly is the point, but it does make it seem like he’s slacking, especially given how much exercise he must get from riding everywhere on a bike. The S Rank heroes don’t get a lot to do and most of them just seem like strong guys, but they do their job of making the hero organization seem just the right blend of heroic and conceited.

This first season is a certified banger, and an absolute must-watch for any superhero fan. The parodic humor defines the show while still managing to deliver on good characters, great fight scenes, and absolutely beautiful animation. The later seasons may stumble, but the first season absolutely lives up to the hype.

Ghost in the Shell.title: Ghost in the Shell
Ghost in the Shell.blurb: This movie presents a fascinating sci-fi future with all these gorgeous visuals and flowing action, and uses that world to pointedly pose a bunch of interesting questions it doesn’t answer.
Ghost in the Shell.review:
This movie presents a fascinating sci-fi future with all these gorgeous visuals and flowing action, and uses that world to pointedly pose a bunch of interesting questions it doesn’t answer. The plot is good enough, but the movie fails to tie its ideas together in such a way that leaves you feeling like it’s fallen short of its potential.

The big idea for the first half of the movie is that memories are just things that can be changed and altered, and if you can rewrite a person’s memories like you can rewrite a file, then what even makes us human? The bad guy grunts have all been hacked and we get a full explanation of how this works, and the main character - Major Kusanagi - is a cyborg while her partner explicitly is not, and yet this idea gets basically dropped by the halfway mark aside from tying into the next idea. Said next idea is that if computers can functionally mimic humanity and humanity is basically a computer, then can an AI be human? The main antagonist is an AI called the Puppetmaster that wants to be truly alive, and to them that means reproducing and then dying, because that’s all that makes humanity special apparently. Kusanagi takes them into her mind so they share a body since Puppetmaster has none, and then the movie ends.

None of the questions about what it means to be human are answered at all, not even symbolically as far as I can tell. If there is some cool metaphorical explanation here, it’s too hidden for it to meaningfully tie the movie together. The idea may be that humanity really is no different from machines, but that concept still doesn’t feel fully explored by the time the credits roll. Frankly, I’d rather watch the movie about a cyborg with a sentient AI in their head anyway.

Themes and symbolism aside, the plot is decent. The mystery of who the Puppetmaster is is pretty good, and the movie throws a lot of red herrings at you while still making the reveal seem obvious in hindsight. The politicking between different government factions is pretty good too, and paints a frightful picture of what this tech-based future is like. I didn’t really connect to any of the characters, which is mostly because they just don’t get a lot of time to do stuff aside from philosophize and shoot people.

The movie is under an hour-and-a-half, and any time not spent on philosophy is spent on action scenes and panning shots. The action scenes and panning shots are really good, though. Everything is beautifully animated, even the horrifying stuff like Kusanagi getting her cyborg skin surgically replaced. The fight scenes are also excellent, being simple while still engaging, and make full use of the technology present in this future.

Ghost in the Shell feels more focused on presenting this world than it does about giving us engaging characters, a mind-blowing story, or even engaging with its own themes. The world itself is pretty cool, but worldbuilding does not a masterpiece make. I understand that this film is influential to cyberpunk as a genre, and the worldbuilding and animation should be praised, but it’s not doing enough special in the other departments to justify this film’s reputation to me. If you love cyberpunk, this is obviously worth a watch if you haven’t seen it already, but outside of its legacy, this film just isn’t drawing me in.

CITY The Animation.title: CITY The Animation
CITY The Animation.blurb: One of the most hilarious and heartfelt shows I’ve ever seen. A spiritual successor to Nichijou, CITY takes its formula of overexaggerating the emotions of mundane events for comedy and applies them to adult situations. The situations themselves are also absurd, amplifying the idea that how we feel about events is just as important as the events themselves.
CITY The Animation.review:
One of the most hilarious and heartfelt shows I’ve ever seen. A spiritual successor to Nichijou by the same writer and animation studio, CITY takes Nichijou’s formula of overexaggerating the emotions of mundane events for comedy and applies them to adult situations. Even the main pair of teenagers deal with more “adult” problems than those in Nichijou. The show also makes the situations themselves more absurd, amplifying the idea that how we feel about events is just as important as the events themselves. It’s cool seeing these more mature scenarios handled with the proper emotional weight while still being absolutely hilarious.

CITY is a masterclass at absurd comedy, with things taken to their logical emotional extremes. For example, a trio of business owners want a summer vacation like in their youth, so they literally brave a hurricane to get it. There’s the one girl who is so pretty that people like her effortlessly, so not only does she incapacitate people with a smile, but she herself is asleep all the time because she literally puts no effort into her appearance and presence. A woman wants to retrieve an important pendant that she lost, and she literally punches a strange, unyielding creature all day until she passes out before the creature yields and lets her have the pendant. The absurdism makes everything feel so powerful because it's focused on emotions and not the actual real events. The show is also aware that the events it's portraying on screen are absurd to the point of being hilarious, letting the absurdity heighten the comedy and the emotions at the same time. It’s an excellent formula that is only amplified by its well-rounded characters.

When I say that this show is a comedy series, I mean that very seriously. There is continuity and character arcs, but each episode is divided into several segments, each of which are centered around their own setup and punchline. Somehow, almost every segment hits, twisting the general formula in various ways on top of being really well written on their own. You’ll rarely get two sets of characters in back-to-back segments, so things never get stale. It does mean that “main” characters often won’t appear for almost a whole episode, but the rest of the cast feels fleshed out enough that you barely even notice.

Most of the characters are defined by their main bits, but they all have depth once you get to know them. Nagumo is greedy and will do anything for money, but she used to be super driven and just doesn’t see the point anymore. Matsuri and Ecchan seem like the perfect best friends, but they struggle to show real emotions towards each other aside from positivity, even when the situation calls for them to be sad. Wako just seems absurdly weird and overly happy, but she has a consistent soft spot for helping others in need. Even the rich blonde lady who masterfully manipulates whole events in the city to get what she wants completely collapses into a nonverbal idiot when she is shown any hint of affection. It makes all the characters more memorable as you learn more about their intricacies on top of their usual quirk. And of course those intricacies are just used for more bits.

CITY has four main characters, Nagumo, Niikura, and Ecchan and Matsuri, and I really like all of them. Nagumo is really funny even if she is a selfish asshole most of the time, and Niikura is so genuine that her crashouts are always completely understandable. The standouts, though, are Ecchan and Matsuri, who ironically are the main teenagers in the show and not the adults. That said, they’re just so unbelievably wholesome. They can’t quite read each others’ minds, but they’re always on the same wavelength, and they just bounce off each other so well that it’s so obvious that they’re having the time of their lives. They also have the most heartfelt story, though, as Ecchan has to move away at the end of summer and needs to figure out how to tell Matsuri. And she just can’t. She tries, and can only manage it through a convoluted version of one of their bits that ends with both of them in tears. And it's the only way she can say goodbye, because she can’t deal with the immense sadness of leaving Matsuri behind, while all Matsuri wants is a proper goodbye. They get a (relatively) happy ending, of course, and the way it’s all handled makes it my favorite story in the show by a longshot.

The show is called CITY for a reason, as it really does feel like you’re watching not just the story of Nagumo, Niikura, Ecchan, and Matsuri, but the whole City (yes, the city in CITY is called City). I really like this, because it makes the whole setting feel alive, and you get to see characters interact with those outside their usual clique. Like, we see Ecchan get haircuts from an old man who gives short cuts for free, and she treats him really well too. Everything feels connected, and it gives the sense that there is no “main” character, but this whole community of people that all have their own problems and heightened emotions that they have to deal with. Niikura is just as funny on her own as she is with Nagumo, and Nagumo plays just as well of Niikura as she does her boss, and her boss is funny with her in a different way than he is with his friends. It’s such a complex yet simple web that makes everything feel so whole. It also means we get some really unique bits, like two that are just honest-to-god actual Japanese rap/stageplay segments. Its peak.

There are a few episodes, though, where CITY breaks its segmented formula to give us episode-long skits, bringing in every character in the show for some absolutely fantastic experiences. These episodes having no segments makes perfect sense too: a skit is centered on a specific character, and every character is experiencing this. These skits include the city-wide race where everyone competes for the prize, and the music number in the finale, but nothing compares to episode 5. What starts off as a one-off adventure spirals out to feature several ongoing, intersecting storylines that all happen at the same time. Not just in in-universe time, but in real world time. The screen gets divided up into smaller screens that all have their own events playing out in real-time. Usually only one or two have something important happening so you’re never lost, but it's so cool. It feels like the whole city is on the move, and it pays off beautifully at the end when every screen converges for a Where’s Waldo-like mosaic of everyone in the show. It feels like a season finale, and it’s episode 5. If you only watch one episode of CITY, watch this one.

Speaking of finales, CITY’s sticks the landing. The first half is the goodbye between Ecchan and Matsuri that manages to be really heartwrenching while still keeping the comedy. It’s the perfect ending to their storyline, ending the series longest arc. The second half starts out as a small musical number that slowly introduces more and more characters as everybody comes together to eat food and celebrate with an elaborate song and choreographed dance. It’s filled with its own emotional ups and downs, but the story takes a backseat to the fucking musical dance number that serves as the cast wrap-up season finale. Ending, of course, with Nagumo getting too greedy and making things literally explode, sending everyone joyously high into the sky in celebration of what they have and what’s yet to come. Perfect show, no notes.

Tron.title: Tron
Tron.blurb: Possibly the most 80s sci-fi movie to ever 80s sci-fi. It's a fairly standard adventure plot about getting captured and then escaping through enemy territory to kill the evil king, but it’s made cool by its premise and aesthetics. Traveling into a computer world to fight an evil computer program with the help of security programs is a fun idea, and the film looks incredible even by today's standards.
Tron.review:
Possibly the most 80s sci-fi movie to ever 80s sci-fi. It's a fairly standard adventure plot about getting captured and then escaping through enemy territory to kill the evil king, but it’s made cool by its premise and aesthetics. Traveling into a computer world to fight an evil computer program with the help of security programs is a fun idea, and the film looks incredible even by today's standards. The neon costumes perfectly match the vibe of a classic computer, and the CG makes the world feel like the video games it's trying to emulate. As the movie with the first real CG, setting it inside a computer is a genius idea, as the polygonal graphics add to the world instead of taking away from it like they might in a fantasy movie.

The movie's plot and characters are just okay, though. I mentioned the plot earlier, and while it has some fun twists and turns, it is really simplistic. The first half-hour of the movie is just setting up the premise and the dynamic between Flynn, Alan, and Lora, only for Alan and Lora to disappear up until the film's last moments. Their personalities influence that of their programs, but the actual dynamic is gone. Flynn himself isn't very interesting either, and doesn't really go through much of an arc, ending as the same self-interested guy he was at the start. He even kisses Lora’s program even though Lora herself loves Alan, which is just weird because the Lora and Alan programs seem to like each other in the same way that the real Lora and Alan do. It feels like Flynn is convincing Lora to cheat on Alan in a roundabout way, which isn’t a great look for our hero.

The main characters never even learn the bad guy's motivation. They're breaking in to steal Flynn's work back, which is a strong enough motivation since he should be paid for his work despite him being kinda a prick, but they have no clue that the Master Control program has basically developed sentience and its own evil schemes. Specifically, the Master Control’s plan is to "hit the Pentagon" to steal its security data (they mean hit its data banks, but it’s hilarious that they could just say “hit the Pentagon” in 1982 and nobody would bat an eye). Plus, the Master Control's motivations never come up again, so it's super irrelevant outside some light theming.

The theming, while not super important, is pretty good. The film is very anti-corporate, with the bad guy being a CEO who stole Flynn’s work, depriving Flynn of all credit and compensation. His Master Control program steals and destroys other people’s work, and absorbs the CEO’s personality to the point where it wants to amass power of its own. The movie ends with Flynn getting his work back and exposing all the other stuff the CEO has done, because programmers and workers deserve to be recognized for their work and not just swept under the corporate carpet. It’s not super deep, but that anti-corporate idea permeates the whole film.

The main things Tron has going for it, though, are the worldbuilding and visuals. Portraying computer programs as actual people with personalities is a cool idea, and simulating a computer network as an actual city is really fun. Showing how the programs drink from electricity and use actual weapons for anti-virus software makes the world feel more real, and every aspect of the digital world enforces this. The film takes this abstract concept of a computer network and makes it feel like a real, lived-in place, making the premise more digestible for the average audience while still feeling cool to people who understand how computers work. The movie rides or dies on its premise and visuals, and the plot and world are just interesting enough for those visuals to ride.
